paragraphs.text: [Mitsubishi UFJ Financial] [8306 JP / MUFG US ] Research Note
[PASTE EXCEL OUTPUT]
RECOMMENDATION

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Japan's largest bank and one of the largest financial institutions in world. Holds ~8.4% of all domestic loans and 11.8% of deposits in Japan as of March 2025, making it the largest non-Chinese bank group globally, with a balance sheet slightly larger than those of JPM and HSBC. Headquartered in Tokyo and with over 360 years of history, MUFG has a global network with over 2,700 locations in more than 50 countries and over 180,000 employees. One-stop financial supermarket: if you're a Japanese salaryman opening a savings account, a mid-size Japanese company getting a business loan, a multinational corporation doing a billion-dollar bond issuance, or a pension fund looking for asset management, MUFG likely has a product for you.

7 segments: Digital Services, Retail & Commercial Banking, Japanese Corporate & Investment Banking, Global Commercial Banking, Asset Management & Investor Services, Global Corporate & Investment Banking, and Global Markets.
the Japanese bank with the largest exposure to overseas operations.
Japan accounts for ~50% of total profit. Banking in Thailand and Indonesia contributes ~15%, and equity-method earnings from Morgan Stanley make up most of the rest.

MUFG and Morgan Stanley announced a definitive agreement on September 29, 2008, under which MUFG would invest $9bn in equity in Morgan Stanley for a 21% interest on a fully diluted basis. The structure was: $3bn for 9.9% of common stock at $25.25 per share, and $6bn of perpetual non-cumulative convertible preferred stock with a 10% dividend and a conversion price of $31.25 per share.
~22% stake in Morgan Stanley has contributed 25%+ of earnings in each of the past five years
INVESTMENT THESIS:

Rate Normalization Tailwind: After decades of near-zero interest rates destroying Japanese bank profitability, the Bank of Japan has finally begun normalizing rates. Even modest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan dramatically expands MUFG's net interest income given its enormous deposit base and domestic loan books.

Massively Undervalued vs. Global Peers: MUFG's valuation remains subdued relative to the earnings power that higher ROE would imply, suggesting the market has not fully priced in the impact of rate normalization and digital efficiency gains.

Shareholder Returns Improving:  MUFG is returning excess aggressively, ¥500 bn share buyback in 2025 plus ¥74 per share in divs, a 40% payout ratio directly addressing the long-standing critique that Japanese banks retain too much equity.
Morgan Stanley Stake: ~20 stake provides earnings exposure to U.S. investment banking and wealth management — a high-quality, recurring earnings contributor.

Southeast Asia Growth Platform: MUFG has meaningful ownership in fast-growing emerging market banks in Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines.  Has retained large positions in Southeast Asian banks including a major stake in Bank of Danamon in Indonesia and Krungsri in Thailand
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:
BOJ Rate Policy Risk: If Japan's central bank slows or reverses rate hikes. MUFG's earnings are highly sensitive to the domestic rate environment.
Yen Currency Risk: Yen appreciation would compress overseas earnings when translated back into yen. Much of MUFG's overseas business is USD-denominated.

Tariff & Trade Policy Uncertainty: MUFG management noted it is closely monitoring the impact of U.S. trade policies on its financial performance Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, particularly on Japanese export-oriented clients.
Asia Slowdown: An economic slowdown in Southeast Asia would directly hit Global Commercial Banking profits including the Thailand and Indonesia subsidiaries.
Execution Risk on Digital Transformation: Modernizing a 180,000-person institution is complex and the returns on AI investment are not guaranteed.
JGB Portfolio Risk: As Japan's largest holder of Japanese Government Bonds, MUFG is exposed to rising JGB yields increasing mark-to-market losses on its bond portfolio.
Governance / Regulatory Risk: MUFG has in the past faced regulatory scrutiny in Japan and internationally, including a Tokyo Stock Exchange sanction in October 2024.

paragraphs.text: [Tokyo Marine ] [8766 JP / TKOMY US] Research Note
[PASTE EXCEL OUTPUT]
RECOMMENDATION

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Japan's first insurance company founded in 1879, providing marine insurance to support Japan's burgeoning international trade. Today, over 50,000 employees in more than 40 countries work toward the realization of its purpose. The company offers a wide range of insurance and related services including non-life insurance, life insurance, reinsurance, asset management, risk management, health and wellness services, and financial services, covering sectors such as agriculture, aviation, marine, energy, and life sciences. It also generates income from fee-based services (risk management consulting, asset management) through its Financial & General segment, but this is a smaller contributor.
Segments:
Domestic non-life (~45% of rev): auto, home, travel, and accident insurance in Japan.
Domestic Life (~7% of rev): whole life, cancer, medical, and annuity products.

International Insurance (~51% of rev): P&C and specialty insurance across 40+ countries, including major U.S. subsidiaries (Philadelphia Insurance, Tokio Marine HCC, PURE Group, Delphi Financial) and reinsurance. This is the growth engine of the company.
Financial & General: investment consulting, investment trust management, derivatives trading, real estate, and healthcare services.
INVESTMENT THESIS:
Consistent compounder: TM has delivered ~20% EPS CAGR over the past 5 years.
13+ consecutive years of dividend growth: DPS have increased every year since 2011, with a 50% payout ratio policy.
Disciplined underwriting: Combined ratios in North America have averaged 90-91%, the underwriting business generates profit before even counting investment income.

Capital release story: Japan's regulators and governance reforms are pushing companies to unwind "cross-shareholdings" (the old practice of Japanese companies owning each other's stock). Tokio Marine is sitting on ~¥2.5 trillion (~UDS $17bn) in these holdings, a massive, multi-year capital return/M&A war chest.
Berkshire Hathaway endorsement:On March 24, 2026, Berkshire's National Indemnity Company announced a $1.8 billion (¥287.4bn) strategic stake, with plans to collaborate on reinsurance and global M&A
Global diversification at a reasonable valuation: Despite its scale and quality, trades at a discount to Western insurance peers.
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:
Catastrophe exposure: A severe earthquake in Japan or a bad Atlantic hurricane season causes large claims payouts and hits earnings

FX risk: ~ half of profits come from outside Japan (primarily USD-denominated). A strengthening yen erodes overseas earnings in JPY, and vice versa. FX was a significant swing factor in both FY2023 and FY2024.

M&A execution risk: The company is signaling $10+ billion in future acquisitions. Large deals can destroy value if done at the wrong price or if integration fails. The North American prior-year loss reserve charge in FY2024 (~$265M pre-tax) was a reminder that legacy liabilities from acquired businesses can surface unexpectedly.
Japan domestic stagnation: The home market is mature, with an aging population and slow economic growth. Auto penetration is flat; competition is intense.
Capital deployment uncertainty: Risk it overpays on acquisitions or struggles to find deals at attractive valuations.

Regulatory / IFRS transition: Japan is adopting new economic value-based solvency rules (similar to Solvency II in Europe). The transition could require capital adjustments and introduces reporting complexity.
Cyclicality of insurance pricing: The current "hard market" with rising premiums will eventually soften. When insurance pricing cycles turn, underwriting margins compress.
Concentration in North America: ~80% of international profits come from North America, not as diversified as it may appear.
Management/Board

Masahiro Koike, 53, joined Tokio Marine in 1994 after graduating from university. Became CEO in 2025. His career includes a stint in New York, where he worked on the sale of the company's reinsurance business to RenaissanceRe Holdings in 2019. His professional background spans aerospace underwriting, ceded reinsurance management, and corporate strategy, with assignments in both Japan and the U.S. He is the most internationally focused CEO in the company's history — fitting, given his explicit goal of continued global M&A expansion.

Prior CEO was Satoru Komiya, and his departure was a routine, planned succession, not a firing or controversy. This was a textbook planned handoff at a Japanese company, with Komiya moving upstairs to Chairman (a very common pattern in Japanese corporate governance) rather than exiting entirely. Komiya was CEO for 6 years, from June 2019 until June 2025. He joined Tokio Marine in 1983 and held various roles including General Manager of Planning, Executive Officer, and Managing Executive Officer before rising to CEO. He holds an undergraduate degree in engineering from the University of Tokyo MarketScreener — an unusual background for an insurance CEO, but common in Japan where elite engineering graduates enter all industries.

Why he left: He didn't really "leave". It was a standard Japanese corporate succession. In June 2025, Komiya stepped down as Group CEO and assumed the position of Group Chairman. He continues to focus on developing future leaders and serves as Dean of the Tokio Marine Group Leadership Institute, which he founded in April 2023.

During his 6-year tenure, Tokio Marine grew from a predominantly Japan-focused insurer into a genuinely global operation, with international profits nearly doubling and the company hitting a ¥1 trillion profit milestone. He was also known for emphasizing corporate culture,

RECOMMENDATION: AstraZeneca is a world-class, large-cap, profitable business that is still in a high-growth phase, with a pipeline that provides visibility well into the 2030s. 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: One of the world's largest pharma companies, headquartered in Cambridge, UK focused on several major disease areas: cancer (oncology is the 
largest (~40% of rev), heart and kidney disease, respiratory conditions like asthma and COPD, and rare diseases. Key products: cancer drug Tagrisso ($7.3bn 2025 rev), 
cholesterol drug Farxiga ($8.4bn), COVID-19 vaccine developed with Oxford University. Stated goal to deliver $80bn in total rev by 2030 (vs $58.7bn in 2025) via growth in its 
existing oncology, biopharma, and rare disease portfolio, and by launching 20 new medicines.  
Oncology (~40% of rev): Largest, fastest-growing segment. Generated $24bn in 2025, +17% y-o-y. Key drugs include Tagrisso (lung cancer), Imfinzi (lung, liver, biliary cancers), 
Enhertu (HER2 cancers, ADC), Lynparza (ovarian, breast, prostate), and Calquence (blood cancers). 
Cardio, Renal & Metabolism (~22% of rev): Key drugs include Farxiga/Forxiga (heart failure, kidney disease, diabetes), Brilinta (heart attack prevention — now in decline due to 
generics), Lokelma (potassium management), and Roxadustat. 
Respiratory & Immunology (~15% of rev): Key drugs include Fasenra (severe asthma), Breztri (COPD), Saphnelo (lupus), and Airsupra (asthma rescue inhaler). Tozorakimab — 
currently in late-stage trials for COPD — is the major pipeline bet here. 
Rare Disease (~16% of rev): This segment was built through the $39 billion Alexion acq in 2021. Key drugs include Ultomiris and Soliris (complement inhibitors for rare blood and 
kidney disorders), Strensiq (bone disease), and Koselugo (neurofibromatosis).  
Vaccines & Immune Therapies: Primarily consists of legacy COVID-19 vaccine rev (now largely wound down) and Beyfortus (RSV prevention in infants), developed with Sanofi. 
Emerging Markets: EM outside China grew 22% in 2025, and geographic expansion — particularly in Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East — is a structural part of the growth 
story. Long-term themes include market expansion in emerging regions alongside transitions to advanced modalities like cell therapies and immune engagers.  
 
INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Size + Growth: ANZ is not just a dividend vehicle like many big pharmas. Rev grew 8% 
in FY2025, with core EPS up 11%.  
Execution record: CEO Pascal Soriot set a $45 billion rev target a decade ago and hit it. 
He then set the $80 bn target. The management team has delivered 16 positive Phase 
III readouts in the past year alone. Track records of pipeline execution are rare and 
worth paying for. The $80 bn by 2030 target assumes significant growth in the existing 
oncology, biopharmaceuticals, and rare disease portfolio, and by launching an 
expected 20 new medicines before the end of the decade.  
Strong pipeline: Broad portfolio of over 100 ongoing Phase III trials and over 20 late-
stage readouts slated for 2026. CEO called this an "unprecedented catalyst-rich 
period.” Mgmt has noted they've already achieved 10 of the 20 new medicines targeted 
as part of the 2030 roadmap. 
EM growth driver: EM ex-China grew 22% in 2025. As healthcare systems in Asia, 
Latin America, and the Middle East develop, AZN is well-positioned with an established 
commercial footprint in these regions. This could be a decades long tailwind 
Rare disease is high-margin: 2021 Alexion acq gave AZN a leading position in 
complement biology (treating ultra-rare diseases). These drugs face almost no generic 
competition, have high prices, & have loyal patient populations. Rare Disease grew 
15% in Q1 2026.  
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: 
Pipeline Failure: Phase III failures, particularly in high-profile programs would 
materially reset growth expectations.  
US Drug Pricing Risk: AZN has struck a Most Favored Nation pricing agreement with 
the US, with phased implementation starting through Medicaid. Political pressure on 
drug pricing in the US, AZN’s largest market at ~43% of rev, is an overhang.  
Tariffs: AZN manufactures in multiple countries and sells heavily into the US. Tariffs 
could compress margins or force expensive supply chain restructuring. Management 
has pledged $50 bn to continue to grow in the US, including the largest manufacturing 
investment in AZN's history set for Virginia, which partly mitigates this over time. 
China risk: ANZ’s China business has been under pressure from generic competition, 
mandatory price cuts, a gov anti-corruption crackdown that affected pharma sales 
practices, and broader US-China geopolitical tension.  
Patents: Growth from newer medicines has to more than offset the impact of patent 
expiries on mature brands including Brilinta, Pulmicort, and Soliris. Tagrisso, currently 
one of AstraZeneca's largest drugs, will eventually face patent expiry. The question is 
always whether the pipeline refills the bucket fast enough. 
F/X Risk: AZN reports in USD but generates rev across dozens of currencies — GBP, 
EUR, JPY, CNY, BRL and many more. F/X is a persistent drag in weak-dollar 
environments and can meaningfully distort reported results 
 
 
 
 
 
2026-03-09 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
 
OTHER POSITIVES: 
 
Leadership in Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs): ADCs are a new generation of cancer drugs that deliver chemotherapy precisely to tumor cells. 
AZN, through its partnership with Daiichi Sankyo, is a clear leader. Enhertu achieved sales growth of 34% on a constant exchange rate basis in Q1 
2026. The ADC platform has multiple drugs in development across different cancer types, giving it a multi-year runway.  
 
Oncology Dominance with Room to Expand: Oncology generates $25.6 bn, 44% of product revenue, growing at 17%.  
The key drugs — Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Enhertu, Calquence — are each expanding into new cancer types and earlier treatment lines, meaning the 
addressable market for drugs already approved keeps growing without needing new approvals.  
 
Operating Leverage: AZN is targeting mid-30s core operating margins, and Core EPS is consistently growing faster than rev.  
 
Progressive Dividend + Buyback Optionality: Modest yield (~2%), but the dividend has never been cut, and as the debt from the Alexion acq is paid 
down, there is increasing potential for capital returns to accelerate (divs or share repo) 
 
OTHER NEGATIVES: 
 
Debt Load from Alexion Acquisition: The $39 bn Alexion deal in 2021 left the balance sheet leveraged. While net debt has been declining, 
AstraZeneca still carries meaningful d+ebt, which constrains financial flexibility and leaves it more exposed to interest rate environments than a net-
cash pharma peer like Roche. 
 
ADC Platform Concentration: ADCs are a competitive space with Pfizer, Roche, and others investing heavily. If the platform disappoints, or a 
competitor leapfrogs AstraZeneca's technology, the growth premium embedded in the stock erodes quickly. 
 
MANAGEMENT: 
 
Sir Pascal Soriot CEO 
Sir Pascal Soriot is one of the most consequential pharmaceutical executives of his generation, a French-born Australian businessman who took over 
a British-Swedish pharma giant in crisis, rebuilt it into one of the world's most scientifically ambitious and commercially dynamic life sciences 
companies, and delivered one of the most remarkable corporate turnarounds of the twenty-first century. 
 
 
 
 
 
2026-03-09 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4 
 
 
Born on 23 May 1959 in France, Soriot studied veterinary medicine at the École nationale vétérinaire d'Alfort in Paris before obtaining an MBA from 
HEC Paris. The unconventional starting point, vet school before business school, is worth noting. It gives him genuine scientific fluency that many big 
pharma CEOs, who come purely from finance or sales, lack.  
 
He joined Roussel Uclaf as a salesman in Australia in 1986, became General Manager of Hoechst Marion Roussel in Australia in 1996, then moved to 
Tokyo in 1997.  
 
When the merger of Hoechst and Rhône-Poulenc created Aventis in 1999, Soriot joined the merged entity, serving as President and CEO of Aventis 
Asia Pacific and Japan — his first experience of full P&L accountability for a multinational pharmaceutical enterprise across the most commercially 
diverse and fastest-growing pharmaceutical markets in the world. 
 
He served as COO of Roche's pharmaceuticals division and, prior to that, as CEO of Genentech, where he was credited with leading the successful 
merger between the San Francisco-based biologics business and Roche. The Genentech role is particularly relevant — Genentech was the gold 
standard of oncology drug development, and running it gave Soriot a deep understanding of the science and commercial dynamics of cancer 
medicines that he brought directly to AstraZeneca.  
In August 2012 he was named the new CEO of AstraZeneca, taking up the post on 1 October 2012.  
 
When Soriot took over, AstraZeneca was in poor health. Profits had fallen 31% between the second and third quarters of 2012 as major product 
patents had expired (including Crestor and Nexium) with no new products to replace them. In short, AstraZeneca had for a number of years failed to 
invest in R&D.  
 
His turnaround strategy had three pillars: refocus R&D on oncology, biopharmaceuticals, and rare disease; relocate the company's headquarters to the 
Cambridge science hub; and push hard into emerging markets. One early example of his scientific instincts: he elected to revive the development of 
the ovarian cancer drug olaparib (Lynparza), which had been shelved after failing a Phase II trial, saying "it was a clear reflection of good science and 
poor management." Lynparza went on to become a major commercial success 
 
Under his leadership, AstraZeneca has grown from revenues of approximately $27 bn in his first year to more than $45 bn in 2024, with a market 
capitalization that has grown more than tenfold. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2026-03-09 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5 
 
In 2022, Pascal received a knighthood for services to life sciences and leadership in the global response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Oxford-
AstraZeneca COVID vaccine — developed and distributed at cost globally — was a significant part of that recognition.  
 
Soriot is one of the most important reasons to have confidence in AstraZeneca's $80 billion 2030 target. He has set ambitious long-range targets 
before and delivered. He has genuine scientific credibility (unusual for a big pharma CEO), deep experience across every major geography, and a track 
record of making bold calls — on olaparib, on the Alexion acquisition, on the ADC partnership with Daiichi Sankyo — that have compounded into a 
coherent and highly valuable portfolio. At 66, succession planning is a question worth monitoring, but for now the investment case and the CEO are 
closely intertwined.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN 1.75% POSITION IN IDVZ 
 
AstraZeneca remains a world-class, large-cap, profitable business that is still in a high-growth phase, with a pipeline that provides 
visibility well into the 2030s. The $80 bn in rev by 2030 remains intact. The pipeline, despite a setback this quarter, remains best in 
class. If anything, it is a candidate to add to. The stock was hit this quarter when a rumor came out they had talks to acquire Roche, 
which didn’t make any sense of the market or to me. Nothing has been substantiated.  
 
Q2 2026 Summary 
 
AstraZeneca's Q2 2026 performance met consensus expectations on the top line, while bottom-line results were bolstered by non-
operating factors. Revenue of $15.4 bn, representing 6% year-over-year growth (5% at constant exchange rates CER). 
Core EPS of $2.63, a 6% beat against consensus estimates. Earnings beat was largely driven by a much lower tax rate resulting from 
adjustments to deferred tax assets and internal legal entity changes. 
 
Core Operating Profit of $5,158 mm, in line with consensus. 
 
Core operating profit margin stood at 33.5%, while the gross margin of 83.6% was slightly ahead of expectations. 
 
Dividend: Increased its interim dividend by 3 cents to $1.06 per share. 
 
Business Segment and Product Performance 
Growth was led by the Oncology and Rare Disease units, which helped offset the sharp decline in Farxiga sales following its U.S. 
patent expiration. 
 
Oncology 
• 
Sales rose 13% (CER) to $6.71 bn 
o 
Imfinzi: Grew 27% (CER), benefiting from strong uptake in gastrointestinal and genitourinary cancers. 
o 
Calquence: Surpassed $1 bn in quarterly revenue for the first time, beating expectations by 4%. 
o 
Enhertu: Alliance revenue saw a 2% beat, driven by sustained demand for the therapy in HER2-positive and HER2-
low breast cancer. 
o 
Tagrisso and Lynparza: Both drugs experienced slight misses (~ 2%) relative to consensus forecasts. 
 
Cardiovascular, Renal, and Metabolism (CVRM) 
• 
The CVRM segment contracted significantly by 18% (CER) to $2.77 bn 
• 
This was primarily due to Farxiga, which saw a 19% (CER) decline as it faced its first quarter of generic competition in the 
U.S. starting in April 2026.  
• 
Analysts estimate that Farxiga's erosion will represent at least a 3% headwind to total revenue for the full year 2026. 
 
Rare Disease 
• 
Sales beat estimates by 3%, totaling $4.9 bn.

Strensiq was a standout performer, beating expectations by 13%, while Soliris missed and Ultomiris performed in line with 
projections. 
 
2026 Guidance and 2030 Ambition 
• 
AstraZeneca reiterated its FY2026 guidance, expecting total revenue growth in the mid-to-high single-digit percentage range 
and core EPS growth in the low double-digit percentage range (at CER). 
• 
Management also reaffirmed its target of $80 bn in total revenue by 2030. 
• 
This reaffirmation came despite the recent Phase III failure of Wainua (eplontersen) in the CARDIO-TTRansform trial for 
ATTR-CM, which management characterized as an anticipated risk in a broadly diversified portfolio. 
 
Broker Research and Analyst Commentary 
Sell-side reactions were generally neutral to positive, focusing on the company's ability to maintain growth through patent cliffs and 
its upcoming pipeline catalysts. 
 
• 
JPMorgan maintained an Overweight rating, noting that the Q2 results underpin their confidence in the 2030 revenue target. 
They highlighted that the 2026 pipeline readouts, including SERENA-4 and AVANZAR, offer further upside potential. 
• 
UBS reiterated a Buy rating, viewing AstraZeneca as a core portfolio holding for mid-term growth. However, they cut their 
mid-term EPS forecasts by an average of 4% to reflect the removal of Wainua in ATTR-CM from their model, partially offset 
by increased peak sales expectations for tozorakimab (now >$5 billion). 
• 
Bernstein raised its price target to £202 from £185, citing peer group multiple expansion and a leading R&D engine. Despite 
trimming 2026–2033 adjusted EPS by 1–4% due to lower expected income from Enhertu, they forecast a core EPS CAGR of 
10.70% through 2031, which is significantly ahead of European peers. 
• 
Deutsche Bank maintained a Sell rating, describing the revenue print as "mixed" and noting that while cash flow was decent, 
core operating expenses missed consensus. They viewed recent R&D newsflow, including the Wainua setback and the 
Ultomiris failure in HSCT-TMA, as net neutral to negative. 
• 
Shore Capital retained a Hold rating and lowered its price target to 13,000p from 15,000p. The broker noted that market 
speculation regarding a potential mega-merger with Bristol-Myers Squibb—rumored to be valued at over $400 billion—has 
recently weighed on AstraZeneca's market value by approximately $24 billion (-9%). 
• 
CFRA Research maintained a Strong Buy rating, citing the company's pipeline depth and projected 11.54% EPS growth for 
2027. They believe the stock justifies a premium valuation due to its post-2030 growth story involving ADCs and cell 
therapies. 
• 
ABG Sundal Collier maintained a Buy recommendation, observing that AstraZeneca successfully "weathered the Farxiga 
patent hit" and managed to expand gross margins by 100 basis points despite pricing headwinds. 
• 
Leerink Partners updated its price target to $215 from $214 and increased the probability of success for the internal ADC 
sone-ve to 80% following positive Phase III results in gastric cancer.

paragraphs.text: ALIBABA [BABA] Research Note

RECOMMENDATION:  SELL - with slowing sales and margin pressure as A.I./cloud spend ramps, BABA faces the same challenges faced by the U.S. cloud hyper scalers. Add in China risk and chip procurement risk, and despite a reasonable valuation, the risk/reward on BABA is not favorable. The ROI on cloud investment is uncertain and the momentum behind A.I. model releases and hype has faded.

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Alibaba is China's version of Amazon, Google Cloud, PayPal, and eBay all rolled into one. It is the biggest e-commerce company in the world by gross merchandise volume (GMV) and operates online shopping platforms including Tmall, Taobao, Alibaba.com, AliExpress, and Lazada. Beyond shopping, it runs a cloud computing business, a logistics network, digital media, and is pushing into A.I. Headquartered in Hangzhou, China. Founded in 1999 by Jack Ma. Alibaba doesn’t make things, it runs platforms that connect buyers and sellers and takes fees, ads, and services revenue.
Four Segments:

1. China E-commerce (~52% of rev): The heart of the company. Includes Taobao, Tmall, the B2B platform 1688, and food delivery service Ele.me. Forecast to generate around CN¥565 billion in 2026. Taobao is like a giant online flea market where anyone can sell. Tmall is like a premium digital mall for established brands. Makes money through seller advertising, transaction fees, merchant services

2. International Digital Commerce (~13 of rev): Replicating the China marketplace globally. Includes AliExpress and Lazada (Southeast Asia), Trendyol (Turkey), Daraz (South Asia), with a strategic focus on key regions including select European markets and the Gulf Region. Growing fast but still small.

3. Cloud Intelligence (~12% of rev): BABA’s version of AWS, cloud computing and AI services for businesses. Provides computing, data storage, AI services, enterprise software. Rev grew 26% y-o-y, driven by public cloud rev growth and the increasing adoption of AI-related products. Cloud and AI are among Alibaba’s fastest-growing areas.

4. All Others: Freshippo supermarkets, Cainiao (logistics network that coordinates warehouses, delivery partners, cross-border shipping helping merchants deliver goods faster), Alibaba Health, mapping app Amap, and digital media assets. Most of these businesses are still losing money but improving.
INVESTMENT THESIS:

AI and Cloud accelerating: Alibaba Cloud achieved double-digit rev growth in FY 2025, with AI-related product rev growing more than 100% for seven consecutive quarters positioning BABA as China's answer to AWS or Azure. Largest cloud provider in China.
Massive AI investment signals long-term ambition:
Plans to invest more than $50bn into AI infra over the next three years.

Beijing has shifted from foe to ally: Gov has signaled renewed support for its domestic tech champions via regulatory softening and public encouragement of private sector innovation, a big shift from the crackdown era.
Shareholder returns: Share repo authorization of $19.1bn as of Sep 30, 2025

Core e-commerce has stabilized: Showed clear signs of stabilization in 2025, with e-commerce customer management rev returning to 10% growth after years of concern that Taobao and Tmall were in structural decline.
Exposure to China Consumer: China has ~1.4 bn people, a huge middle class and a massive e-commerce market historically dominated by Alibaba.
Massive E-commerce Ecosystem: Alibaba’s platforms connect:
hundreds of millions of consumers with millions of merchants
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:
Significant investment required: Margins compressing and cap ex increasing to fund A.I. and cloud business.
Chinese regulatory risk: Faces significant risks from China's unpredictable regulatory environment, which can change its business operations overnight.
The government previously hit the company with a record $2.8bn antitrust fine and has the power to reshape or restrict the business at any time.
Domestic competition: Intense competition PDD Holdings (Pinduoduo) and Douyin (TikTok's competitor), JD.com, Pinduoduo (PDD), Meituan, Tencent, ByteDance
Geopolitical tensions: Risk of trade sanctions from the US & restrictions on Chinese companies' access to Western markets. Delisting concerns. Chip export restrictions.
Heavy investment hurts profits: FCF has turned negative amid investments in cloud and quick commerce
Dependence on China's economy: Majority of rev from China
US chip export restrictions: Access to advanced AI chips important to Alibaba's cloud and AI ambitions, trade policy around US chip exports is hard to predict.
VIE Structure: Foreign investors don’t actually own Alibaba’s Chinese operating company. They own a Variable Interest Entity (VIE) in the Cayman Islands. This structure carries legal uncertainty.
Management/Board 80

Eddie Wu (Wu Yongming) long-time insider and co-founder CEO since Sep 2023. One of Alibaba’s original 19 co-founders. First programmer at the company in 1999. Former CTO roles across several Alibaba businesses. Led Taobao and Tmall platforms. Founded a venture capital firm called Vision Plus Capital. Education: Zhejiang University of Technology (engineering). Strategic focus as CEO: heavy push into AI and cloud computing centralizing Alibaba’s strategy around AI infrastructure and models.

BB Seguridade Participações SA reported Q2 2026 earnings results were in-line. The company achieved a modest bottom-line beat 
compared to consensus, the stock price reacted negatively, dropping significantly in the days following the announcement due to 
concerns over weak premium growth and a challenging outlook for the rural and pension segments. However, it has since rebounded 
to close to pre-earnings levels. BB Seg underperformed significantly in 2025 and recently started making up the gap. 
 
Q2 2026 Earnings Summary 
Recurring net managerial income of R$2.15 bn for Q2 2026, a decline of 3.9% year-over-year and 3.1% quarter-over-quarter. Despite 
the year-over-year decline, the result was ~1% to 2% above consensus estimates. 
 
Key Segment Performance 
Brasilseg (Insurance):  
• 
Net income reached R$1.23 bn, up 10.8% from Q1 2026 but down 2.1% year-over-year. 
• 
Written premiums were weak, down 4.9% year-over-year to R$3.55 bn, primarily driven by a 11% drop in rural premiums. 
 
Brasilprev (Pension):  
• 
Net income fell sharply to R$337 mm, down 18.8% year-over-year and 37.3% sequentially. 
• 
This miss was attributed to a negative investment result of R$49 mm, impacted by the IGPM inflation index and negative 
mark-to-market adjustments. 
 
BB Corretora (Brokerage):  
• 
Net income was R$858 mm, down 3% year-over-year, as a 35% decline in premium bond revenues offset resilience in 
pension and insurance commissions. 
 
Brasilcap (Premium Bonds):  
• 
Net income was R$74.7 mm, slightly beating year-over-year figures by 1.4% but missing analyst estimates by roughly 7%. 
 
Dividends and Guidance 
• 
The company approved an interim dividend of R$3.85 bn (~ R$1.98 per share), representing an 88% payout ratio and a 4.8% 
dividend yield for the half-year. 
• 
Management reiterated its 2026 guidance, though it noted that premium growth is currently tracking at the bottom of the 
expected range. 
 
Broker Comments and Analysis 
UBS Research maintained a Neutral rating, noting that while the results were a "small beat" driven by financial results, the 2H26 
outlook for the rural sector remains uncertain and premiums are tracking below the lower range of guidance.

INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Strong moat: Exclusive distribution through Banco do Brasil's ~4,000 branches under an agreement running to 2033 
Capital-light: brokerage arm converts that access into commission income with minimal capital and ROEs in the stratosphere. 
Cash return: ~90-96% payout ratio, policy of returning a high share of profits.  
Dominant, defensible market positions: Dominant share in Brazilian insurance, especially rural, with wide moats and highly 
profitable, capital-light operations via its unique JV structure and exclusive distribution.  
Underpenetrated market: Brazilian insurance premiums are ~4% of GDP versus ~8-11% in developed markets; private pensions are 
structurally growing as Brazil's public pension is reformed and constrained.

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: BP is one of the world’s largest oil and gas companies, founded in 1908 as the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. BP finds oil and gas, extracts it, ships it 
around the world, refines it into fuel, and sells it to consumers and businesses. BP has operations in 61 countries, produced ~2.4 mm barrels per day of oil equivalent, and had 
total proven reserves of over 6bn barrels. BP also runs around 21,200 service stations worldwide under the BP, Amoco (US), and Aral (Germany) brands. 2025 replacement ratio 
increased to 90% from 50%. BP earns through three interlocking mechanisms. 1) sells crude oil and nat gas at market prices (highly sensitive to the Brent crude oil price and 
European/US natural gas benchmarks). 2) earns a refining margin — the spread between what it pays for crude and what it receives for refined products like petrol, diesel, and jet 
fuel. 3) earns retail and services income from Castrol lubricants, aviation fueling, and convenience stores.  
Geographical breakdown: BP's upstream production is split roughly 40% US, 25% Middle East, 15% North Sea (UK/Europe), and 20% Asia-Pacific. The US is the single largest 
geography through BPX Energy (shale) and Gulf of America operations. BP has committed to growing US production to approximately 1mm boe/d by decade's end. 
Dividend: Div cut 50% in 2020 during COVID, a significant trust-breaking event for income investors. The dividend has been rebuilt since but has not returned to pre-2020 levels.  
Buyback: BP suspended buybacks in 2025 to focus on debt reduction. It will resume once net debt hits the $14–18 bn target range 
3 segments:  
Oil Production & Operations (~60% of 2025 EBIT): Crude oil exploration and production, including BPX Energy (its US shale business), operations in the Gulf of America, the 
UAE, and the North Sea. Upstream remains dominant at ~70% of FCF generation 
Gas & Low Carbon Energy (~9.5% of 2025 EBIT): Natural gas production, LNG trading, offshore and onshore wind, solar, hydrogen, and carbon capture.  
Customers & Products (~29% of 2025 EBIT): the downstream business — the 21,200 petrol forecourts, Castrol lubricants, refining operations, oil trading, EV charging, and 
aviation fueling.  
 
INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Turnaround story: Growing upstream oil and gas production; focusing the downstream 
business by reshaping the portfolio around advantaged integrated positions; and 
disciplined, capital-light investment in biogas, biofuels, and EV charging. sec Cost 
reduction is also a major lever — BP has achieved $1.7bn in structural cost reductions, 
on track to meet or exceed its goal of $4–5bn by end-2027. 
$20 billion asset sale program: Divestments will generate cash that can be used to 
cut debt, fund buybacks, and grow the dividend. 
Commodity leverage: BP offers leveraged exposure to oil and gas prices.  
New CEO optionality: O'Neill has a track record of bold, value-creating restructuring at 
Woodside. If she can apply the same formula to BP, the upside could be significant. 
Depressed valuation: BP trades at a meaningful discount to Shell, ExxonMobil, and 
Chevron on most metrics. Significant re-rating potential. 
High dividend: ~5.5% yield is attractive particularly with a stated commitment to grow 
the dividend 4%+ annually. 
Elliott's presence: Having one of the world's most sophisticated activist investors as 
the 2nd-largest shareholder looking for value creation is a meaningful catalyst.  
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: 
CEO instability: 4 CEOs in 6 yrs signals strategic problems and board dysfunction.  
Debt level: Net debt of $22bn limits flexibility and is a problem if oil prices fall. 
Commodity price risk: Earnings are sensitive to oil prices. A sustained decline in Brent 
crude pricing would materially hurt earnings and threaten the dividend. 
Legacy liabilities: BP remains the most indebted of the major oil companies, partially 
because of the Deepwater Horizon disaster. That 2010 spill cost BP tens of billions in 
fines, settlements, and cleanup — and the financial hangover has never fully cleared. 
Operational risk: BP has a history of refinery incidents, which periodically hurt 
quarterly results. 
Energy transition uncertainty: BP's pivot back to fossil fuels creates long-term 
stranded asset risk if the energy transition accelerates faster than expected. 
Underperformance vs. peers: BP has been a very poor performer for a long time 
versus Shell, ExxonMobil, and Chevron. Can they close this gap? 
Reserves depletion: BP's reserves replacement ratio has at times remained below 
100%, leaving BP with less than seven years of proved reserves and mounting 
decommissioning liabilities

Management/Board 
The company just went through its fourth CEO change in six years. BP's board appointed Meg O'Neill as CEO, effective April 1, 2026. Murray 
Auchincloss stepped down in December 2025. O'Neill is BP's fourth CEO since 2020 and its first external hire for the role in more than a century. She 
is the first woman to lead a top-five oil major.  The 55-year-old executive transitions from Australia's Woodside Energy, where she held the CEO 
position starting in 2021. Her career includes a 23-year tenure at Exxon Mobil prior to joining Woodside. During her tenure at Woodside, she 
orchestrated a merger with BHP's petroleum division, creating a top-10 independent global oil and gas producer with a $40bn valuation, and 
successfully doubled Woodside's production capacity. She is known for financial discipline, LNG conviction, and bold strategic moves. As O'Neill 
takes over, she benefits from a war-driven surge in prices — but inherits what observers describe as the industry's toughest cleanup job, including a 
mountain of debt, an organizational structure many believe is too sprawling, and a portfolio cluttered with low-return units. Her predecessor Murray 
Auchincloss was a 30-year BP insider who had served as CFO before becoming CEO. He reversed BP's disastrous overreach into renewables under 
Bernard Looney but was ultimately replaced before finishing that turnaround.

orchestrated a merger with BHP's petroleum division, creating a top-10 independent global oil and gas producer with a $40bn valuation, and
successfully doubled Woodside's production capacity. She is known for financial discipline, LNG conviction, and bold strategic moves. As O'Neill
takes over, she benefits from a war-driven surge in prices — but inherits what observers describe as the industry's toughest cleanup job, including a
mountain of debt, an organizational structure many believe is too sprawling, and a portfolio cluttered with low-return units. Her predecessor Murray
Auchincloss was a 30-year BP insider who had served as CFO before becoming CEO. He reversed BP's disastrous overreach into renewables under
Bernard Looney but was ultimately replaced before finishing that turnaround.

paragraphs.text: RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN 2.25% POSITION IN IDVZ

BP remains a core IDVZ energy holding along with Total Energies and Petrobras (combined 8.75% position, for context EAFE has 3.75% in energy and M1WDUDY has 12.65%). BP while often rumored to be a takeover target, is undergoing a turnaround under the new CEO with a focus on streamlining the business and deleveraging. They have been unwinding the green energy initiatives undertaken by prior management and and returning their strategic focus to oil and gas production. Ideally this leads to multiple expansion to be in line with other oil and gas majors and there’s always a chance someone buys them.

BP delivered a strong financial performance in Q2 2026, with earnings of $0.369 beating consensus of $0.327 by12.9%. BP benefited from the increase in oil prices due to the war in Iran. They also increased the dividend by 4%.
The stock declined on the announcement (~ -4%), driven by operational reliability issues, production headwinds, and a lack of firm updates regarding the long-term financial framework.
Reasons for Stock Price Reaction:

Operational Reliability Concerns: The market was discouraged by the dip in upstream facility availability to 92.4% and refining utilization to 94.7%, suggesting internal execution remains a challenge.
Lack of Financial Guidance: Investors were disappointed by the absence of firm updates regarding a return to share buybacks, which remain suspended in favor of further debt reduction.
Production and Capex Outlook: BP raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance by $0.5 bn to $13.5-$14 bn while simultaneously lowering its upstream production guidance for the full year.
Lower Implied Future Cash Flow: Analysts noted that the inferred free cash flow for H2 2026 was ~$2 bn below previous forecasts, tempering enthusiasm for the Q2 beat.
Q2 2026 Earnings Summary
Q2 2026 results were characterized by robust cash generation and accelerated deleveraging, supported by favorable market conditions.
Underlying RC profit reached $5.73 bn, a 79.2% sequential increase from Q1 2026, driven by Middle East supply disruptions and elevated refining margins.
Adjusted earnings per ADS of $2.22 beat consensus estimates by 13.8%.
Operating cash flow reached $10.9 bn, facilitating a $3.1 billion reduction in net debt to $22.3 bn.
Total financial obligations (including hybrids and leases) fell by $6.9 bn to $53.6 bn.
The company increased its quarterly dividend by 4% to 8.66 cents per ordinary share ($0.52 per ADR).However, share buybacks remained suspended as management prioritized balance sheet strengthening.
Operational Headwinds:
Total upstream production fell 4% year-over-year to 2.20 Mboe/d, impacted by maintenance and Middle East tensions.
Upstream plant reliability dipped to 92.4% from 95.7% in the previous quarter.
Strategic Priorities:

New CEO Meg O'Neill introduced five priorities under the "get fit to grow" initiative: balance sheet strength, portfolio simplification, investment discipline, operational excellence, and accountability.
Broker Commentary and Ratings

HSBC (Hold, TP 570p): Analysts noted that while results were strong, operational performance "fell short" of expectations due to plant reliability issues. They highlighted that asset disposals are doing the "heavy lifting" for deleveraging and pushed their expectation for share buyback resumption to 2028.

UBS (Buy, TP 675p): UBS maintained a positive outlook, citing attractive "self-help" potential from cost savings and deleveraging. They argued that BP's shares remain inexpensive, trading at a 13% discount to peers on free cash flow yield.

TD Cowen (Hold, TP $41/504p): The firm characterized the update as "neutral," noting that while earnings beat expectations, the lack of firm updates on the financial framework and weaker-than-expected implied cash generation for the second half of 2026 weighed on the stock.

CFRA Research (Sell, TP 460p): CFRA maintained a Sell rating, citing concerns over a potential oil price downcycle in 2027 and BP's high (80%) correlation to Brent prices. They expressed sustainability concerns regarding the "windfall" performance driven by temporary market disruptions.

Wolfe Research (Outperform, TP $64): Wolfe viewed BP as a "deep value play," praising the new CEO's "candid, unemotional assessment" of the business and the company's ability to accelerate debt reduction.
Piper Sandler (Neutral, TP $43): Analysts noted that although the accelerated deleveraging is impressive, BP still has "more work to do" to bring its capital structure in line with European peers.

paragraphs.text: IMPERIAL BRANDS [IMB LN] Research Note
RECOMMENDATION: Potential ADD in IDVZ (currently ~2.5%)
Owned since inception in Dec 2024

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: 4th largest international tobacco company, located in Bristol, UK. It makes and sells cigarettes including Davidoff, Gauloises, JPS, West globally; Winston, Kool, Maverick & backwoods cigars in the US via its ITG Brands subsidiary), rolling tobacco and papers (Rizla), and a growing "next generation products" (NGP) portfolio: blu vapes, Zone nicotine pouches, and Pulze heated tobacco. Also owns 50.2% of Logista, a separately listed Spanish logistics company that distributes tobacco and convenience products to retailers across Southern Europe. Classic tobacco equation: volumes decline slowly, prices rise faster, margins expand, and nearly all of the resulting cash goes back to shareholders. In FY25, tobacco volumes fell 1.7% but price/mix added 5.4%, and the company generated £2.75bn of FCF vs a ~£21bn market cap.
Geography: Europe (~42% of rev), U.S. (~35% of rev), Africa/Asia/Australasia/C&E Europe (~23% of rev)
INVESTMENT THESIS:
Cash-return machine: ~6% div yield plus a large buyback (£1.25bn completed in FY25) & £1.45bn launched for FY26). FY21–FY25 £10bn returned to shareholders

Buyback compounding on a shrinking share count: Adjusted EPS grew 9.1% in FY25 on only ~4–5% operating profit growth; the share count reduction does heavy lifting and works better the cheaper the stock stays

Pricing power reliably outruns volume decline: +5.4% price/mix vs. -1.7% volumes is the durable pattern; market share is up 48bps across its five priority markets since FY20 (US, UK, Germany, Spain, Australia). Mgmt assumes volumes of roughly -3% to -5% a year offset by +5–7% price/mix through 2030.

Deliberately capital-light "fast follower" NGP (next gen products) strategy: Unlike PMI/BAT, Imperial didn’t try to lead the smoke-free transition. It has entered proven categories late and cheap. Zone pouches reached ~2.8% US share and ~100,000 stores with Americas NGP revenue up 69.8%, while NGP losses narrowed to £76m

Clean balance sheet for a Tobacco company: Net debt/EBITDA at 2.0x. By consolidating Logistica, IMT gets to borrow the Spanish, French and Italian governments' tobacco tax receipts for a few weeks on permanent rotation, at a floating rate below its bond curve equal to ~£2bn of quiet balance-sheet support
Litigation overhang resolved: Decade-long Florida MSA dispute with Reynolds settled in January 2026
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:
Structural volume decline: the core product's user base shrinks ~2–5% a year in developed markets; the model only works while pricing elasticity holds.

NGP losses and credibility: the April 2026 trading update warning that NGP adjusted operating losses would be "moderately higher" knocked the shares 7% in a day; investors are running out of patience on NGP profitability.

US competitive intensity: UBS downgraded the stock citing heightened competition, specifically Altria's price investments in the US; the US is ~35% of net revenue and skews to discount brands most exposed to down-trading wars.
Regulation: a future US menthol ban would hit Kool; UK/EU generational sales bans and disposable-vape restrictions; flavor bans for pouches.
ESG exclusion: tobacco is uninvestable for many mandates, capping the multiple
Leadership churn: new CEO (Oct 2025), new CFO, and a new chairman (John Rishton) effective Dec 1, 2026, the entire c-suite turned over in 14 months.
F/X : sterling reporting with large USD earnings
Litigation tail: Florida is settled, but tobacco litigation never fully ends.
NPG (as of year-end Sep 2025)
NGP net revenue was £368m, up 13.7% at constant currency (14.9% reported) accounting for 4.4% of group net revenue.

The five-year scorecard: NGP net rev growth of 83%, with adjusted operating losses reduced by 76% to £76m in FY25 as gross margin improvement was offset by investment behind the Zone rollout in the US.
Modern oral (Zone):

the one that matters most. Launched in the US in Febr 2024, now in ~100K stores with 2.8% of the modern oral category, and Americas NGP revenue accelerated into the second half (ZYN still owns roughly 2/3rds of the category, Imperial is going for the growth of the category, not challenging its leader).
Management called US modern oral one of its biggest opportunities.
Launched Zone in the UK in Nov 2025 and bought the 2ONE pouch brand for £40m in Mar 2025.
Vapour (blu):
quietly strong in Europe.

Pivot from disposables to pod-based kits after the UK/France bans worked: "In the last 12 months we've more than doubled our market share in the vaping segment," and UK vapour share crossed 10% for the first time.
blu holds double-digit share in the UK, Spain and France.
In the US, Imperial has deprioritized blu given weak enforcement against illicit vapes
Heated tobacco (Pulze):
smallest, most defensive.
Pulze 3.0 launched into Italy and Greece with iD tobacco and iSenzia non-tobacco sticks, gaining share in Southern/Eastern Europe, but is a distant follower vs IQOS.

The AAACE decline is strategy, not failure: they withdrew blu from the Czech Republic and exited vape in Poland after device taxes shrank the market, and expect NGP revenue to grow again once those withdrawals annualize. That's the "deliberate choices" framework applied honestly.
One structural proof point worth noting: in 8 European markets, NGP now accounts for more than 20% of Imperial's tobacco & NGP net revenue. Where the model works, it genuinely scales.
March 2025 Capital Markets Day set the 2030 frame:
Double-digit CAGR for NGP net revenue growth through 2030, alongside low-single-digit tobacco net revenue growth, within group guidance of 3–5% operating profit growth and £2.2–3bn annual FCF.
The underlying market view: NGP penetration across Imperial's footprint rises from ~19% in 2025 to ~25% in 2030, with all three categories contributing
Combustibles will still represent around 75% of total industry net revenue in 2030.
Imperial is explicitly betting the transition is slower than PMI's rhetoric implies, so a fast-follower loses little by waiting.

The market entry framework is unchanged, only markets where the category is established and where Imperial has a strong route to market supplemented by small bolt-on acquisitions focused on enhancing NGP capabilities.
NGP Profitability:

April trading update flagged NGP losses running moderately higher this year on R&D, marketing and distribution build-out (the proximate cause of the 7% share price drop), but recent management commentary points to NGP breakeven targeted by ~FY27 with growth expected to accelerate in the second half of FY26.
The Reality:
Building scale" has no hard number attached to it, which makes accountability soft.
The arithmetic of "double-digit growth from £368m": even 15% compounded to 2030 gets you to roughly £750m–800m, still under 10% of net revenue.
NGP will not change what Imperial is within this strategy period
It's an option and a narrative support for the multiple, not a second engine.
The value discount doesn't close on NGP alone.
ITG/Reynolds Florida MSA dispute (2015–2026)
When ITG bought Winston, Kool, Salem and Maverick from Reynolds in 2015, it never joined Florida's tobacco settlement, and Reynolds kept getting billed.
In March 2025 the Delaware Chancery Court ordered ITG to pay Reynolds $251.5mm, and in January 2026 the parties settled
ITG paid a $200mm lump sum on Jan 30, 2026, and will pay ~$234mm of contingent payments from Oct 2026–2028 and will reimburse Reynolds for future Florida payments on the acquired brands.
This is why H1 FY26 reported profit collapsed while adjusted profit grew.
DIVIDEND HISTORY (Cut/Re-based) in 2020
From 2009 through 2019, Imperial ran a mechanical "dividend +10% per annum" policy regardless of what earnings and cash flow were doing.
That was the company's whole equity story, and it's precisely what broke.
Cut in May 2020
The proximate announcement came with the H1 2020 results, but COVID was the occasion, not the cause.
The payout had outrun the business.

Ten years of formulaic 10% hikes against flat-to-declining underlying earnings pushed the payout ratio into the 90%+ range on earnings and left almost no free cash flow after the dividend. The policy was arithmetic, not economics.
Leverage was too high. Net debt sat around £14bn (~3x EBITDA), a legacy of the $7.1bn US brand acquisition from Reynolds/Lorillard in 2015 and heavy spending on blu.

The planned fix was a £2bn asset disposal program, anchored by the sale of the premium cigar business, which stalled and ultimately fetched less than hoped, closing off the non-dividend deleveraging route.
NGP investment was disappointing.
2019 brought a profit warning driven by the collapse of the US vaping market (the EVALI scare and flavor restrictions) just as Imperial had ramped blu investment.
The board, then between CEOs, after Alison Cooper's departure and before Bomhard's arrival in July 2020, needed to fund NGP and fix the balance sheet simultaneously.
The one-third cut freed up roughly £600mm a year, which went to debt paydown.
Notably, the board explicitly framed it as a rebasing to a sustainable level with a progressive policy thereafter andthat's exactly what has happened
the trajectory since is token growth (2021–22) while deleveraging, then a step-up to ~4.5% growth once net debt/EBITDA reached 2.0x, with buybacks layered on top from FY22 onward
MOATS/BARRIERS TO ENTRY
Paradoxically strong.
Advertising bans and plain packaging freeze existing brand equity in place
Excise structures favor incumbents with pricing power
In the US, FDA premarket authorization (PMTA) requirements make legal entry into vapes/pouches enormously expensive.
The oligopoly (PMI, BAT, JTI, Imperial) faces essentially no new legal combustible entrants.
The caveats: Imperial is the smallest of the four
is subscale in NGP (no answer to IQOS in heated tobacco at scale)
and the moat does not protect against the illicit vape market, which bypasses regulation entirely, or against deep-discount brands in the US.
MANAGEMENT
Lukas Paravicini, CEO since 1 October 2025, having been CFO since May 2021.
Career consumer-goods finance executive
~2 decades at Nestlé, then Fonterra, and joined Imperial from ED&F Man Holdings, where he was CFO.
As CFO he was credited with driving the consistent growth of the past four years and led the company's tech and data transformation program.
Continuity appointment
He co-authored the 2030 strategy he's now executing
the market initially reacted badly to Bomhard's departure announcement (shares fell 7.5% that day in May 2025) given Bomhard's strong five-year turnaround record.
LOGISTICA (50% owned by Imperial)
Logista Integral, S.A. trades on the Madrid Stock Exchange under ticker LOG
Distributes tobacco, convenience, and pharmaceutical products across Spain, France, Italy, Portugal and Poland.
The free float is essentially the ~50% Imperial doesn't own
Key current stats: ~€4.6bn market cap, ~15–16x P/E, dividend yield of ~6% at a 99% payout ratio, beta of ~0.4.
Accounting is misleading

Economics to IMT are modest. Imperial owns just 50.01% but fully consolidates Logista, control rests on 5 of 12 board seats and a Relationship Framework Agreement, and the FY25 accounts flag this as a key judgment.
£11.4bn of pass-through revenue inflates Imperial's top line while Distribution contributes only ~£323m of adjusted operating profit (~8% of group), half of which economically belongs to minorities.
The clean way to model it: strip Distribution out entirely and add back (a) Imperial's ~€105–110m share of Logista's dividend and (b) the stake's market value.
The hidden treasury function
arguably the real reason it's kept.

Logista collects excise duty from retailers before remitting it to governments, generating a large structural cash float, and per the FY25 accounts it lends this to Imperial through cash pooling: a daily average balance of ~£1.7bn, ranging from ~£0.5bn to ~£2.6bn with excise timing, standing at ~£2.2bn at year-end.
That's roughly a quarter of Imperial's adjusted net debt funded by its own subsidiary's working capital float.
Deconsolidation would surrender this, plus Logista's EBITDA from the leverage calculation, reported net debt/EBITDA would look worse overnight even with sale proceeds.
The SOTP tension.
Logista trades at roughly double Imperial's multiple (~15x vs ~7.5–8x)

Mechanically, the market pays €2.2bn for cash flows inside Logista that it implicitly values far lower inside Imperial meaning Imperial's core tobacco business trades at an even deeper discount than the headline multiple suggests, perhaps ~7x.
The activist case writes itself: sell or spin the stake, redeploy £1.9bn into the buyback at 7.5x.
The counter-case: the cash pool, control of its own route-to-market in Spain/France/Italy (Logista is effectively the distribution monopoly in France and dominant in Spain)
The dividend income, and a taxable gain on exit.
Management has zero appetite to monetize, it didn’t happen during the 2020 deleveraging crunch, which tells you how they weight the funding and strategic benefits.

Owning Imperial gives you a ~9% embedded Logista position with a look-through to Southern European convenience/pharma distribution. It's a modest diversifier and a quiet credit support, not a value driver unless capital allocation changes
LOGISTA
An income asset ~50 owned by Imperial Tobacco

Dominant, quasi-monopoly distribution infrastructure with negative working capital, a ~6% yield with a decade of stable-to-growing payments, beta of ~0.5, and a real diversification story with non-tobacco now over 50% of gross profit, pharma economic sales grew 10%, and FY26 guidance is mid-single-digit adjusted EBIT growth.
It screens like a toll road on Southern-Europe retail.
FY25 net profit fell 9% on restructuring and financial items
99% payout ratio leaves nearly nothing for reinvestment or deleveraging
dividend is the entire return, with little compounding behind it.
Earnings carry an underappreciated interest-rate sensitivity
cash-pool loan to Imperial earns interest income that fattened profits during the ECB hiking cycle and now works in reverse as rates fall
French tobacco volumes are declining sharply
Governance is constrained
Imperial's 50.01% means minorities never get a takeover premium and strategy serves the parent's interests first
Logista's float funds Imperial's balance sheet
Liquidity is thin (~€6–8m/day traded)
No US ADR and Spanish dividends carry 19% withholding (versus zero on Imperial's UK dividends)
HISTORICAL VALUATION
COMMON STOCK COMPARISON
WHY DOES IMPERIAL TRADE AT A DISCOUNT?
Smallest player, weakest hand in the endgame.
The market prices tobacco companies increasingly on the credibility of their post-cigarette future.
PMI has IQOS and ZYN, category leadership and a smoke-free business approaching half of revenue.
BAT has Vuse and Velo at scale.
Imperial has ~4.5% of net revenue from NGP and is a deliberate fast-follower with no proprietary category-winner.
Imperial's balance sheet is now stronger than BAT's (~2.0x net debt/EBITDA vs ~3.1x), but that doesn't override weaker competitive positioning
Risk for Imperial is being left behind as a sub-scale player in the future of nicotine.
Portfolio quality and mix

Imperial skews toward declining, high-excise, regulation-heavy markets (UK, Australia, Germany) and, in the US, toward the discount end of the price ladder, the segment most exposed to down-trading wars and with the least brand-equity protection.
PMI's Marlboro-ex-US and EM exposure is structurally better; even Altria owns the premium US franchise.
Second-tier brands in first-world declining markets earn a second-tier multiple.
Legacy issues
The 2019 profit warning, the ousted CEO, and the 2020 dividend cut permanently re-rated the equity.
A company that cut its dividend once is priced with the assumption it could again
A decade of value-destructive strategy (the blu overspend, the failed disposal program) taught investors to discount management promises.
Mechanical/flow factors
UK-listed, too small for some global staples mandates, and no US primary listing — the ADR trades OTC, thinning the natural US buyer base.
Fresh uncertainty premium
The complete leadership turnover (CEO, CFO, Chair within 14 months)

the April warning on NGP losses, and H1 FY26 share declines in four of five priority markets — US -20bps, Australia -55bps, UK -55bps, Spain -20bps — gave the market a reason in 2026 to reapply the skepticism that Bomhard had spent five years dispelling.
What management is doing about it
Bomhard's 2021–25 strategy was a credibility-rebuilding exercise, and the stock more than tripled on a total-return basis over five years
The Paravicini playbook continues it with four levers:

Shrinking the equity faster than anyone else. This is the core "answer" to the discount: rather than argue with the multiple, exploit it. The FY26 buyback of £1.45bn retires ~5.7% of shares annually, on top of a 6% yield and at 7.5x earnings, every repurchased share is enormously accretive. Management has committed to an "evergreen" buyback to 2030. The logic is self-reinforcing: the cheaper the stock stays, the faster EPS compounds, delivering the guided high-single-digit EPS growth from a ~1% organic top line.

Consistency as strategy. The 2030 plan (March 2025 CMD) deliberately promises modest, hittable numbers, low-single-digit tobacco revenue, 3–5% operating profit growth, £2.2bn+ FCF. The investment case rests on delivering them quarter after quarter until the market extends the duration it's willing to pay for. Five consecutive years of met guidance is what took the stock from 5x to 9x; the pitch is that another five does the rest.

Capital-light NGP credibility, not NGP leadership. Imperial isn't trying to out-IQOS PMI. The play is targeted positions where it has a right to win like Zone pouches in the US (the one genuinely fast-growing, high-margin category where it's gaining share from a standing start), blu pods in Western Europe, Pulze in Southern/Eastern Europe with losses capped (~£76m and guided to breakeven around the end of the decade). Narrowing the discount here means proving NGP is a manageable option, not a money pit.

Simplification and self-help. The 2030 transformation program (~£740m cost, ERP consolidation, factory footprint cuts like Langenhagen and Taiwan) targets efficiency-driven margin support, and the balance sheet is held at the low end of the 2.0–2.5x range specifically so no one can rerun the 2019 playbook against them.
What they're notably not doing
no Logista spin-off or monetization (the 50.01% stake is worth roughly €3.5bn+ at market and arguably gets zero credit inside the group)
no US listing migration
no transformative NGP M&A.

The bear case says the discount is therefore rational and permanent and Imperial is a melting asset harvesting itself. The bull case says you're being paid ~11–12% a year in cash returns to wait, and any re-rating from 7.5x toward even BAT's 9–10x is uncompensated upside on top.

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: 4th largest international tobacco company, located in Bristol, UK. It makes and sells cigarettes including Davidoff, Gauloises, JPS, West globally; Winston, Kool, Maverick & backwoods cigars in the US via its ITG Brands subsidiary), rolling tobacco and papers (Rizla), and a growing "next generation products" (NGP) portfolio: blu vapes, Zone nicotine pouches, and Pulze heated tobacco. Also owns 50.2% of Logista, a separately listed Spanish logistics company that distributes tobacco and convenience products to retailers across Southern Europe. Classic tobacco equation: volumes decline slowly, prices rise faster, margins expand, and nearly all of the resulting cash goes back to shareholders. In FY25, tobacco volumes fell 1.7% but price/mix added 5.4%, and the company generated £2.75bn of FCF vs a ~£21bn market cap. Geography: Europe (~42% of rev), U.S. (~35% of rev), Africa/Asia/Australasia/C&E Europe (~23% of rev)

INVESTMENT THESIS:  Cash-return machine: ~6% div yield plus a large buyback (£1.25bn completed in FY25) & £1.45bn launched for FY26). FY21–FY25 £10bn returned to shareholders  Buyback compounding on a shrinking share count: Adjusted EPS grew 9.1% in FY25 on only ~4–5% operating profit growth; the share count reduction does heavy lifting and works better the cheaper the stock stays Pricing power reliably outruns volume decline: +5.4% price/mix vs. -1.7% volumes is the durable pattern; market share is up 48bps across its five priority markets since FY20 (US, UK, Germany, Spain, Australia). Mgmt assumes volumes of roughly -3% to -5% a year offset by +5–7% price/mix through 2030. Deliberately capital-light "fast follower" NGP (next gen products) strategy: Unlike PMI/BAT, Imperial didn’t try to lead the smoke-free transition. It has entered proven categories late and cheap. Zone pouches reached ~2.8% US share and ~100,000 stores with Americas NGP revenue up 69.8%, while NGP losses narrowed to £76m Clean balance sheet for a Tobacco company: Net debt/EBITDA at 2.0x. By consolidating Logistica, IMT gets to borrow the Spanish, French and Italian governments' tobacco tax receipts for a few weeks on permanent rotation, at a floating rate below its bond curve equal to ~£2bn of quiet balance-sheet support Litigation overhang resolved: Decade-long Florida MSA dispute with Reynolds settled in January 2026

RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:  Structural volume decline: the core product's user base shrinks ~2–5% a year in developed markets; the model only works while pricing elasticity holds. NGP losses and credibility: the April 2026 trading update warning that NGP adjusted operating losses would be "moderately higher" knocked the shares 7% in a day; investors are running out of patience on NGP profitability. US competitive intensity: UBS downgraded the stock citing heightened competition, specifically Altria's price investments in the US; the US is ~35% of net revenue and skews to discount brands most exposed to down-trading wars. Regulation: a future US menthol ban would hit Kool; UK/EU generational sales bans and disposable-vape restrictions; flavor bans for pouches. ESG exclusion: tobacco is uninvestable for many mandates, capping the multiple  Leadership churn: new CEO (Oct 2025), new CFO, and a new chairman (John Rishton) effective Dec 1, 2026, the entire c-suite turned over in 14 months.  F/X : sterling reporting with large USD earnings Litigation tail: Florida is settled, but tobacco litigation never fully ends.

RECOMMENDATION

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Think of JD.com as Amazon meets BestBuy meets Uber Eats in China's, except JD owns and operates almost everything itself. It doesn't just run a marketplace where other sellers handle shipping; it has built its own nationwide fulfillment infrastructure and last-mile delivery network, staffed by its own employees, which supports both its online direct sales, marketplace, and omnichannel businesses. It sells electronics, appliances, groceries, fashion, health products, and more directly to consumers, and with same-day or next-day delivery across most of China. JD describes itself as a "leading supply chain-based technology and service provider," and has opened its logistics and technology infrastructure to outside partners, brands, and sectors under what it calls a "Retail as a Service" offering.

Generates rev in 2 ways. 1) Direct product sales, buys goods wholesale and resells them. 2) Service revenues, marketplace commissions from third-party sellers, logistics fees from external businesses using JD's fulfillment network, marketing/advertising, and financial services. Service revenue is faster-growing and higher-margin.
3 segments:
JD Retail (includes JD Health and JD Industrials, and mainly covers online retail, marketplace, and marketing services)
JD Logistics (both internal and external logistics businesses)
New Businesses (includes Dada on-demand retail, JD Property, Jingxi social commerce, and overseas businesses).
INVESTMENT THESIS:

Supply chain moat: JD's owned logistics network is hard to replicate. JD.com has been recognized in the Gartner Supply Chain Top 25 for 2025 for the 2nd consecutive year, ranking 22nd and being the only Chinese retailer on the list.
Expanding profitability: JD Retail's gross margin has risen for 13 consecutive quarters through Q2 2025, while operating margin has maintained a steady upward trajectory.
Accelerating user growth” Annual active customers exceeded 700mm in Oct 2025, and quarterly active customers increased by over 40% y-o-y in Q3 2025.
Shareholder returns: JD repurchased ~80.7mm Class A ordinary shares for ~$1.5bn in H1 2025 alone under a $5bn buyback program running through Aug 2027.
New revenue streams: Food delivery, international expansion (including the Ceconomy/MediaMarkt acquisition), and AI-powered logistics services
Valuation: Chinese tech stocks trade at significant discounts to US equivalents due to geopolitical risk
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:

VIE structure: Over the past 8 years, steps taken by the Chinese gov have had the effect of formalizing, if not legitimizing, the use of VIE structures for companies listing overseas. But legally, foreign investors hold shares in an offshore Cayman Islands entity with contractual claims on China operations, not actual equity in the underlying business. If China ever decided to invalidate VIE arrangements, shareholders would have limited legal recourse.

Regulatory crackdowns: Crackdowns from Chinese regulators need to be considered. In the past, the Chinese government has implemented sudden, severe regulatory crackdowns on certain companies. JD has been treated more favorably than some peers (it's a logistics and product company, not primarily a financial services or social media platform), but no Chinese tech company is immune.

PCAOB/delisting risk: US regulators gained full access to the audits of Chinese companies for the first time in 2022, reducing the threat of delisting for firms like Alibaba and JD.com. CNN That agreement holds for now, but it's subject to the broader US-China relationship: Competitive intensity. JD is third in Chinese e-commerce by GMV, behind Alibaba and Pinduoduo. The food delivery push puts it directly against Meituan — a formidable, entrenched incumbent.

Weighted voting: Shareholders and prospective investors should be aware of the potential risks of investing in a company with a weighted voting rights structure. Founder Richard Liu retains outsized control.
Management/Board

Sandy Ran Xu made history in May 2023 as she became the first woman to serve as CEO of JD.com. She served as the company's CFO from June 2020. Before joining JD.com in 2018, she spent nearly 20 years with PricewaterhouseCoopers in both Beijing and San Jose, as an audit partner. She holds a dual degree in information science and economics from Peking University and is a CPA in both China and the United States. She also serves as an independent director at Baidu. JD.com Her background is financial and operational.

JD.com's Q2 2026 was mixed. A decline in revenue paired with record-high profitability. Management highlighted an inflection point 
in margins, but the market focused on the revenue decline. It was the first revenue decline in company history, which may explain the 
outsized share price reaction. Top-line performance suffered from a high comparison base in electronics and home appliances, but the 
revenue decline was the story. Management expects revenue to return to growth in Q3.  
 
Company Description: 
JD.com ("Jingdong") is China's second-largest e-commerce company by revenue and, critically, it's built differently from Alibaba or 
Pinduoduo. Whereas those are asset-light marketplaces connecting buyers and sellers, JD is closer to an Amazon-style first-party 
retailer: it buys inventory (electronics, appliances, groceries, general merchandise), warehouses it, and delivers it over its own 
nationwide logistics network. The company describes itself as a supply chain-based technology and service provider operating in 
China and Europe. Its reputation in China rests on product authenticity (no counterfeits) and very fast delivery, often same-day or 
next-day. 80–85% of revenue is product sales (retail: JD buys goods and resells them, low-margin, high-volume), with the balance 
from services (marketplace commissions and advertising from third-party merchants, plus logistics services sold to external 
customers). In Q2 2026, net product revenues fell 5.4% while net service revenues grew 6.8%. The higher-margin service mix shift is 
a key part of the margin story

JD Retail maintained its momentum by achieving its 17th consecutive quarter of year-on-year gross margin expansion, reaching 
18.5%. The segment's operating margin rose by 7 basis points to 4.6% during a peak promotional season. Within product categories, 
General Merchandise grew 5.6% to RMB 79.4 bn, led by near double-digit growth in JD Supermarket, while Electronics and Home 
Appliances fell 11.8% to RMB 187.7 bn. 
 
JD Logistics reported a 24.3% revenue increase to RMB 68.1 bn, driven by strong demand for on-demand delivery services. The 
segment achieved a non-GAAP operating income of RMB 2.3 bn, representing a 3.5% margin. 
 
Management Commentary 
CEO Sandy Xu noted that the company is successfully transitioning from rapid user acquisition toward enhancing user quality and 
lifetime value. JD.com continues to see double-digit growth in Monthly Active Users (MAU) and Plus members while improving 
overall marketing efficiency. 
 
Strategic operational updates included: 
 
AI Integration 
• 
The company has deeply integrated AI into search recommendations and customer service, including the deployment of 24/7 
autonomous delivery routes in Shenzhen. 
New Businesses 
• 
Losses in JD Food Delivery narrowed by over 50% year-on-year, and the European Joybuy business doubled its revenue 
within two quarters. 
Shareholder Returns 
• 
CFO Ian Su Shan highlighted that the company repurchased approximately 69.9 million Class A ordinary shares for $1 bn 
during the first half of 2026. 
 
Broker Reactions and Analyst Perspectives 
Broker sentiment following the results was generally "better-than-feared," with many analysts praising the company's ability to drive 
efficiency despite macro headwinds, though some noted that a major valuation re-rating might be delayed until top-line growth 
recovers. 
 
• 
Jefferies: Analysts adjusted the price target for JD.com (9618.HK) to HK$194 from HK$190 while maintaining a Buy rating, 
citing solid execution and an expectation that non-GAAP earnings are back on a year-over-year growth trajectory. 
 
• 
CMB International: The broker maintained a Buy rating and raised its target price to US$48.30 from US$47.50, noting that 
JD Retail's operating profit and the narrowing of new business losses both exceeded their forecasts. 
 
• 
JPMorgan: While confirming that earnings are recovering, JPMorgan analysts noted that the timing for a stock re-rating has 
yet to arrive, as much of the profit improvement was driven by marketing expense cuts rather than fundamental top-line 
expansion; they maintained an Overweight rating with an H-share target of HK$148. 
 
• 
CLSA: Analysts suggested that "the worst is over" for JD.com and maintained an Outperform rating, although they 
previously lowered the target price to US$38.50 from US$41 due to weak overall consumption sentiment in China. 
 
• 
CFRA Research: Maintaining a Buy rating (4-Stars), CFRA highlighted the support provided by JD's $5 billion share 
buyback program and projected significant earnings growth for the 2027 fiscal year.

lines.text: JD.com's Q2 2026 was mixed. A decline in revenue paired with record-high profitability. Management highlighted an inflection point
in margins, but the market focused on the revenue decline. It was the first revenue decline in company history, which may explain the
outsized share price reaction. Top-line performance suffered from a high comparison base in electronics and home appliances, but the
revenue decline was the story. Management expects revenue to return to growth in Q3.
JD.com ("Jingdong") is China's second-largest e-commerce company by revenue and, critically, it's built differently from Alibaba or
Pinduoduo. Whereas those are asset-light marketplaces connecting buyers and sellers, JD is closer to an Amazon-style first-party
retailer: it buys inventory (electronics, appliances, groceries, general merchandise), warehouses it, and delivers it over its own
nationwide logistics network. The company describes itself as a supply chain-based technology and service provider operating in
China and Europe. Its reputation in China rests on product authenticity (no counterfeits) and very fast delivery, often same-day or
next-day. 80–85% of revenue is product sales (retail: JD buys goods and resells them, low-margin, high-volume), with the balance
from services (marketplace commissions and advertising from third-party merchants, plus logistics services sold to external
customers). In Q2 2026, net product revenues fell 5.4% while net service revenues grew 6.8%. The higher-margin service mix shift is
a key part of the margin story
Non-GAAP diluted net income per ADS was RMB 6.29 vs consensus of 5.61 and RMB 4.97 for Q2 2025.
Revenue decreased to RMB 346.4 bn down 2.95 from Q2 2025 but still topped consensus of RMB 342.33 bn.
