RMB 13.5 bn (US$2.0 bn) vs RMB 13.9 bn for Q2 2025.
JD Retail maintained its momentum by achieving its 17th consecutive quarter of year-on-year gross margin expansion, reaching
18.5%. The segment's operating margin rose by 7 basis points to 4.6% during a peak promotional season. Within product categories,
General Merchandise grew 5.6% to RMB 79.4 bn, led by near double-digit growth in JD Supermarket, while Electronics and Home
JD Logistics reported a 24.3% revenue increase to RMB 68.1 bn, driven by strong demand for on-demand delivery services. The
segment achieved a non-GAAP operating income of RMB 2.3 bn, representing a 3.5% margin.
CEO Sandy Xu noted that the company is successfully transitioning from rapid user acquisition toward enhancing user quality and
lifetime value. JD.com continues to see double-digit growth in Monthly Active Users (MAU) and Plus members while improving
The company has deeply integrated AI into search recommendations and customer service, including the deployment of 24/7
Losses in JD Food Delivery narrowed by over 50% year-on-year, and the European Joybuy business doubled its revenue
CFO Ian Su Shan highlighted that the company repurchased approximately 69.9 million Class A ordinary shares for $1 bn
Broker sentiment following the results was generally "better-than-feared," with many analysts praising the company's ability to drive
efficiency despite macro headwinds, though some noted that a major valuation re-rating might be delayed until top-line growth
Jefferies: Analysts adjusted the price target for JD.com (9618.HK) to HK$194 from HK$190 while maintaining a Buy rating,
citing solid execution and an expectation that non-GAAP earnings are back on a year-over-year growth trajectory.
CMB International: The broker maintained a Buy rating and raised its target price to US$48.30 from US$47.50, noting that
JD Retail's operating profit and the narrowing of new business losses both exceeded their forecasts.
JPMorgan: While confirming that earnings are recovering, JPMorgan analysts noted that the timing for a stock re-rating has
yet to arrive, as much of the profit improvement was driven by marketing expense cuts rather than fundamental top-line
expansion; they maintained an Overweight rating with an H-share target of HK$148.
CLSA: Analysts suggested that "the worst is over" for JD.com and maintained an Outperform rating, although they
previously lowered the target price to US$38.50 from US$41 due to weak overall consumption sentiment in China.
CFRA Research: Maintaining a Buy rating (4-Stars), CFRA highlighted the support provided by JD's $5 billion share
buyback program and projected significant earnings growth for the 2027 fiscal year.

Eli Lilly and Company (LLY-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
  
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE  
Eli Lilly delivered a substantial "beat-and-raise" performance in its Q2 2026 earnings, reporting 48% revenue growth driven by 
unprecedented demand for its incretin portfolio. Total revenue of $22.97bn exceeded consensus expectations by 11%, with 
outperformance primarily fueled by the cardiometabolic health segment, which reached $18.35bn in revenue for the quarter. 
Mounjaro and Zepbound grew 91% and 46% year-over-year, respectively, beating consensus by 11% and 6%. While the company 
significantly raised its full-year revenue and performance margin guidance, a large acquired IPR&D charge resulted in a slight 
reduction to the reported EPS midpoint, which analysts largely viewed as a non-recurring accounting event that does not detract 
from robust underlying fundamentals. The investment community has responded with aggressive upward revisions to long-term 
forecasts, with some analysts now seeing $50 in EPS as achievable by 2027.  
 
Headline results 
Positives 
- 
Broad-based revenue beat, with sales of $23.0bn growing 48% year-over-year, beating consensus and continuing the beat-and-
raise pattern of the prior several quarters. H1 2026 revenue reached $42.8 billion, up 51%. Incretin franchise momentum 
continued as combined Mounjaro and Zepbound sales hit $14.9bn in the quarter (Mounjaro $9.9B, +91%, Zepbound $4.9B, 
+46%), underscoring the incretin franchise's continued scale-up. Margins expanded with non-GAAP gross margin expanding to 
86.3% (+130 bps y/y) on better production costs and favorable mix, partly offsetting price declines. Guidance was raised again, 
with full-year revenue guidance raised to $85-87bn from $82-85bn previously, the second consecutive quarterly raise this year 
(following the Q1 2026 raise). Pipeline products are scaling meaningfully, with newer launches including Ebglyss (+131% to 
$201M), Kisunla (from $49M to $167M) and Jaypirca (+56% to $192M), diversifying growth beyond the incretins. 
Negatives 
- 
EPS was diluted by deal charges. GAAP EPS growth (+26%) lagged revenue growth (+48%) and non-GAAP EPS growth (+33%), 
reflecting $3.03/share of acquired IPR&D charges tied to the Orna, Ajax, Centessa and Kelonia deals plus a $703M asset-
impairment/restructuring charge. Tax rate stepped up, as the reported effective tax rate rose to 23.3% from 16.5% a year ago 
(non-GAAP rate to 22.2% from 16.5%), largely because IPR&D charges are mostly non-deductible, a drag that recurs with each 
bolt-on acquisition. Pricing declined across both regions, and growth was “entirely from volume,” per the release. US net pricing 
fell roughly 3% (about 9% excluding one-time rebate adjustments) and international pricing fell approximately 36%, mainly from 
Mounjaro's addition to China's National Reimbursement Drug List (NRDL). Non-GAAP EPS guidance ceiling was actually lowered

to $35.50-36.50 from $35.50-37.00 even as revenue guidance rose, because the $2.78/share of operational upside was more 
than offset by the $3.03/share of new IPR&D charges. While the operational trend is favorable, further bolt-on M&A could 
repeat this pattern in future quarters. Oral GLP-1 launch is off to a slow start. Foundayo (oral orforglipron) launch in the US was 
described by management as slower than anticipated despite heavy promotional spend, though new-patient share had recently 
“inflected.” 
 
Geographic highlights 
- 
Rest of world had most impact with 136% constant currency growth, followed by China at 93%. Europe grew 55%, US 33%, and 
Japan 30%. International incretin market expanded 74% YoY with Lilly maintaining 55% global market share leadership. The US 
remains the larger profit pool (37% volume growth at a much smaller price decline), while ex-US growth is increasingly a volume 
story funded by steep price concessions, most visibly in China, where NRDL inclusion traded price for a much larger addressable 
population.  
 
Segment highlights 
- 
Within Mounjaro, US revenue was $4.8B (+45%) and international revenue $5.2B (+172%). International now contributes more 
than half of Mounjaro sales, a mix shift toward the lower-price, higher-volume international book. Zepbound remains US-only at 
this stage ($4.9B, +44% domestically), so its growth is a purer read on US obesity-market share versus compounded/generic 
competition and payer access. On the oral GLP-1 franchise, Foundayo (oral orforglipron) was submitted to the FDA for type 2 
diabetes during the quarter and generated its first meaningful revenue post-launch, though management flagged a slower-than-
expected US ramp. Oncology, Immunology, and Neuroscience collectively grew 121% YoY. Legacy products (Trulicity, Verzenio, 
Jardiance, Taltz, Humalog/Humulin, Cyramza, Alimta, Olumiant, Emgality, Cymbalta) were not broken out individually in the 
release as growth continues to be dominated by the incretin and newer-launch portfolio. 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Pricing/rebate pressure and growth impact – Realized price is falling across both US and international books (down 9% and 36%, 
respectively, on the metrics disclosed). The release and call both frame current growth as “entirely from volume.” As it relates to 
formulary/channel mix, the Zepbound “medical exception” channel is expected to shrink as CVS Caremark returns the product to 
standard formulary status, which should pressure realized price per prescription even as volumes hold up. Continued 
acceleration of price erosion is flagged by outside analysts as the most likely mechanism to break the bull thesis. Management 
guided to slower H2 2026 growth on tougher comparisons, one-time rebate adjustments unwinding, and seasonal effects 
(European summer vacation impact on Q3 volumes, diabetes seasonality in Q4).  
- 
Emerging generic competition – Generic/compounded semaglutide competition is emerging in markets such as India and Brazil. 
While Mounjaro is still growing in those markets, it is a reminder that incretin pricing power is not uniform globally. 
- 
Oral GLP-1 launch execution and retatrutide regulatory timeline – Foundayo's US launch trajectory has been slower than the 
company initially anticipated, an early signal worth monitoring given how central the oral GLP-1 opportunity is to the long-term 
thesis. Retatrutide's regulatory pathway is the subject of active discussion with the FDA. Management now expects a BLA 
submission in Q1 2027 rather than sooner, pushing out a key pipeline catalyst. 
- 
M&A/IPR&D charges – The company disclosed $2.8B of acquired IPR&D charges in the quarter (Orna, Ajax, Centessa, Kelonia) 
plus $703M of asset impairment/restructuring, versus a combined $154M a year ago, a direct drag on GAAP and non-GAAP EPS 
and, via non-deductibility, on the effective tax rate. 
 
Guidance 
- 
INCREASED full-year 2026 guidance for the second straight quarter, with revenue range UPDATED to $85-87B (up $2-3B), 
representing 32% projected annual growth, non-GAAP performance margin INCREASED to 49-50.5% (+200 bps), signaling 
underlying operating leverage, and non-GAAP EPS RAISED to $35.50-36.50 (+$2.78 midpoint), reflecting strong H1 2026 
performance. Management signaled a shift in capital allocation toward increased business development, characterized by larger 
and more frequent deals such as the recent infectious disease platform acquisitions and the $2.8 billion IPR&D charge related to 
Centessa. 
 
Rating actions and target price changes 
The investment community largely responded with target price increases and bullish upward revisions to long-term forecasts. 
Consensus expectations have reset significantly higher, moving from a "supply-catching-up" story to a "category-expansion" thesis. 
3 
 
The primary drivers of the thesis are now the velocity of Medicare uptake, the global rollout of Foundayo (particularly its oral-at-scale 
potential), and pricing elasticity. Lilly is signaling it will trade price for volume to broaden its market reach before major patent cliffs in 
the 2030s. The risk/reward profile has evolved into a "durable growth" narrative with limited loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) risk for the next 
10 years. However, some analysts (HSBC) caution that TAM expectations of $150bn+ could be optimistic if pricing compresses more 
rapidly due to semaglutide generics and intensified competition later this decade. The Q2 print suggests that LLY is successfully 
leveraging its cardiometabolic leadership to fund massive expansion into new therapeutic areas and manufacturing scale, supporting 
a valuation premium that remains at the high end of the pharmaceutical sector.

Mounjaro is the injectable dual GLP-1/GIP for type 2 diabetes. Zepbound is the injectable dual GLP-1/GIP for obesity. Trulicity, the 
former diabetes cash cow that is being actively cannibalized by Mounjaro, is the injectable GLP-1 for type 2 diabetes that was never 
approved for weight loss. Verzenio is the non-GLP-1 blockbuster (breast cancer). Jardiance, Taltz and Humalog are legacy 
blockbusters (diabetes, psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis and insulin, respectively). 
 
Why we own 
Eli Lilly is the leading player in the incretin drug category, the GLP-1/GIP-based hormone therapies that have become the standard of 
care for type 2 diabetes and, increasingly, obesity. Its two flagship products, Mounjaro (diabetes) and Zepbound (obesity), are the 
same tirzepatide molecule sold under different labels, and together with the newer oral pill Foundayo, they now represent 2/3 of 
total company revenue. Lilly's business model is patent-protected chemistry, it develops, manufactures and sells therapeutics that 
reduce a chronic, enormous unmet need, and it gets paid through a mix of direct purchase, insurance reimbursement and PBM-
negotiated rebates. The remaining 1/3 of revenue comes from a diversified base of oncology, immunology, dermatology and 
neuroscience products, alongside a legacy diabetes/insulin franchise that is now shrinking as patients migrate to the newer incretins. 
J.P. Morgan projects the global incretin market will reach $200bn by 2030, up from a US patient base of about 10mn today, projected 
to reach 25-30mn by the end of the decade, a market still expanding on volume even as per-patient pricing comes down. Lilly's moat 
rests on manufacturing scale, clinical data depth and payer/physician relationships built over decades running the world's largest 
diabetes-care franchise. It has committed $23bn+ to US manufacturing capacity since 2020 (including a new $4.5bn "Medicine 
Foundry" in Indiana), a scale advantage that is difficult and slow for challengers to replicate given the complexity of peptide synthesis 
at volume. Its dual GLP-1/GIP mechanism has produced superior head-to-head efficacy data against Novo Nordisk's single-agonist 
semaglutide, and its next-generation pipeline, the oral small-molecule orforglipron (Foundayo) and the triple-agonist retatrutide, 
which management has described as approaching bariatric-surgery-level weight loss in trial data, is designed to extend that lead 
rather than cede it as the category matures. This remains fundamentally a two-company race with Novo Nordisk, and high clinical-
trial, regulatory and manufacturing barriers keep it that way for now, though pricing power is already eroding (this is an entirely 
volume-over-price growth story at this point). With a leading and defensible position in a massive addressable market, Lilly should 
remain a core position in PFOE.

lines.text: Eli Lilly delivered a substantial "beat-and-raise" performance in its Q2 2026 earnings, reporting 48% revenue growth driven by
unprecedented demand for its incretin portfolio. Total revenue of $22.97bn exceeded consensus expectations by 11%, with
outperformance primarily fueled by the cardiometabolic health segment, which reached $18.35bn in revenue for the quarter.
Mounjaro and Zepbound grew 91% and 46% year-over-year, respectively, beating consensus by 11% and 6%. While the company
significantly raised its full-year revenue and performance margin guidance, a large acquired IPR&D charge resulted in a slight
reduction to the reported EPS midpoint, which analysts largely viewed as a non-recurring accounting event that does not detract
from robust underlying fundamentals. The investment community has responded with aggressive upward revisions to long-term
forecasts, with some analysts now seeing $50 in EPS as achievable by 2027.
Broad-based revenue beat, with sales of $23.0bn growing 48% year-over-year, beating consensus and continuing the beat-and-
raise pattern of the prior several quarters. H1 2026 revenue reached $42.8 billion, up 51%. Incretin franchise momentum
continued as combined Mounjaro and Zepbound sales hit $14.9bn in the quarter (Mounjaro $9.9B, +91%, Zepbound $4.9B,
+46%), underscoring the incretin franchise's continued scale-up. Margins expanded with non-GAAP gross margin expanding to
86.3% (+130 bps y/y) on better production costs and favorable mix, partly offsetting price declines. Guidance was raised again,
with full-year revenue guidance raised to $85-87bn from $82-85bn previously, the second consecutive quarterly raise this year
(following the Q1 2026 raise). Pipeline products are scaling meaningfully, with newer launches including Ebglyss (+131% to
$201M), Kisunla (from $49M to $167M) and Jaypirca (+56% to $192M), diversifying growth beyond the incretins.
EPS was diluted by deal charges. GAAP EPS growth (+26%) lagged revenue growth (+48%) and non-GAAP EPS growth (+33%),
reflecting $3.03/share of acquired IPR&D charges tied to the Orna, Ajax, Centessa and Kelonia deals plus a $703M asset-
impairment/restructuring charge. Tax rate stepped up, as the reported effective tax rate rose to 23.3% from 16.5% a year ago
(non-GAAP rate to 22.2% from 16.5%), largely because IPR&D charges are mostly non-deductible, a drag that recurs with each
bolt-on acquisition. Pricing declined across both regions, and growth was “entirely from volume,” per the release. US net pricing
fell roughly 3% (about 9% excluding one-time rebate adjustments) and international pricing fell approximately 36%, mainly from
Mounjaro's addition to China's National Reimbursement Drug List (NRDL). Non-GAAP EPS guidance ceiling was actually lowered
to $35.50-36.50 from $35.50-37.00 even as revenue guidance rose, because the $2.78/share of operational upside was more
than offset by the $3.03/share of new IPR&D charges. While the operational trend is favorable, further bolt-on M&A could
repeat this pattern in future quarters. Oral GLP-1 launch is off to a slow start. Foundayo (oral orforglipron) launch in the US was
described by management as slower than anticipated despite heavy promotional spend, though new-patient share had recently
Rest of world had most impact with 136% constant currency growth, followed by China at 93%. Europe grew 55%, US 33%, and
Japan 30%. International incretin market expanded 74% YoY with Lilly maintaining 55% global market share leadership. The US
remains the larger profit pool (37% volume growth at a much smaller price decline), while ex-US growth is increasingly a volume
story funded by steep price concessions, most visibly in China, where NRDL inclusion traded price for a much larger addressable
Within Mounjaro, US revenue was $4.8B (+45%) and international revenue $5.2B (+172%). International now contributes more
than half of Mounjaro sales, a mix shift toward the lower-price, higher-volume international book. Zepbound remains US-only at
this stage ($4.9B, +44% domestically), so its growth is a purer read on US obesity-market share versus compounded/generic
competition and payer access. On the oral GLP-1 franchise, Foundayo (oral orforglipron) was submitted to the FDA for type 2
diabetes during the quarter and generated its first meaningful revenue post-launch, though management flagged a slower-than-
expected US ramp. Oncology, Immunology, and Neuroscience collectively grew 121% YoY. Legacy products (Trulicity, Verzenio,
Jardiance, Taltz, Humalog/Humulin, Cyramza, Alimta, Olumiant, Emgality, Cymbalta) were not broken out individually in the
release as growth continues to be dominated by the incretin and newer-launch portfolio.
Pricing/rebate pressure and growth impact – Realized price is falling across both US and international books (down 9% and 36%,
respectively, on the metrics disclosed). The release and call both frame current growth as “entirely from volume.” As it relates to
formulary/channel mix, the Zepbound “medical exception” channel is expected to shrink as CVS Caremark returns the product to
standard formulary status, which should pressure realized price per prescription even as volumes hold up. Continued
acceleration of price erosion is flagged by outside analysts as the most likely mechanism to break the bull thesis. Management
guided to slower H2 2026 growth on tougher comparisons, one-time rebate adjustments unwinding, and seasonal effects
(European summer vacation impact on Q3 volumes, diabetes seasonality in Q4).
Emerging generic competition – Generic/compounded semaglutide competition is emerging in markets such as India and Brazil.
While Mounjaro is still growing in those markets, it is a reminder that incretin pricing power is not uniform globally.
Oral GLP-1 launch execution and retatrutide regulatory timeline – Foundayo's US launch trajectory has been slower than the
company initially anticipated, an early signal worth monitoring given how central the oral GLP-1 opportunity is to the long-term
thesis. Retatrutide's regulatory pathway is the subject of active discussion with the FDA. Management now expects a BLA
submission in Q1 2027 rather than sooner, pushing out a key pipeline catalyst.
M&A/IPR&D charges – The company disclosed $2.8B of acquired IPR&D charges in the quarter (Orna, Ajax, Centessa, Kelonia)
plus $703M of asset impairment/restructuring, versus a combined $154M a year ago, a direct drag on GAAP and non-GAAP EPS
and, via non-deductibility, on the effective tax rate.
INCREASED full-year 2026 guidance for the second straight quarter, with revenue range UPDATED to $85-87B (up $2-3B),

and more frequent deals such as the recent infectious disease platform acquisitions and the $2.8 billion IPR&D charge related to

lines.text: The investment community largely responded with target price increases and bullish upward revisions to long-term forecasts.
Consensus expectations have reset significantly higher, moving from a "supply-catching-up" story to a "category-expansion" thesis.
The primary drivers of the thesis are now the velocity of Medicare uptake, the global rollout of Foundayo (particularly its oral-at-scale
potential), and pricing elasticity. Lilly is signaling it will trade price for volume to broaden its market reach before major patent cliffs in
the 2030s. The risk/reward profile has evolved into a "durable growth" narrative with limited loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) risk for the next
10 years. However, some analysts (HSBC) caution that TAM expectations of $150bn+ could be optimistic if pricing compresses more
rapidly due to semaglutide generics and intensified competition later this decade. The Q2 print suggests that LLY is successfully
leveraging its cardiometabolic leadership to fund massive expansion into new therapeutic areas and manufacturing scale, supporting
a valuation premium that remains at the high end of the pharmaceutical sector.

Nu Holdings Ltd. (NU-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
   
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE  
Nu Holdings delivered stellar Q2 2026 performance, beating consensus estimates on revenue, profit, and margin metrics. They 
surpassed $4bn in net revenue and $1bn in net income for the first time while maintaining a record 33% ROE. The efficiency ratio 
stood at 19.5% for the quarter, compared to 17.6% in Q1 2026, though management noted the Q1 figure benefited from temporary 
expense timing. 15-to-90-day delinquencies improved 16bps to 4.8%. The 90-plus delinquency ratio increased to 6.9%, which 
management attributed to the natural migration of seasonal cohorts from Q1. Provisioning expenses decreased sequentially to 
$1.7bn, a reversal from the spike seen in the previous quarter. Management's tone was confident, focusing on long-term NPV per 
client rather than short-term P&L optimization. They signaled a shift from mass-market acquisition to "Super Core" segmentation and 
an "all-in" AI transformation, even as the investment community remains divided on near-term asset quality risks and the costs of 
global expansion. All said, the print prompted a 9%+ jump in share price and a wave of price-target increases from sell-side analysts.  
 
Headline results 
Positives 
- 
First-ever $1B net-income quarter, with net income reaching $1.06bn, up 49% YoY and 17% QoQ on a constant currency basis. 
Margin inflected, with risk-adjusted net interest margin climbing 290bps sequentially to a record 12.4% from 9.5% in Q1, which 
management framed as the first clear evidence that credit-cost normalization is under way alongside continued monetization 
gains. Monetization is climbing, with monthly ARPAC (average revenue per active customer) rising to $17.10, up from $12.50 a 
year earlier, helped by product cross-sell and the new premium Croma tier. Revenue mix is diversifying, with credit contributing 
41% of gross profit, float income 34%, and fee-based revenue 25%, reducing reliance on any single income stream. Credit quality 
improved at the front end. The earlier-stage 15-90 day NPL ratio improved 16bps to 4.8%, and cost of credit fell 9% quarter-over-
quarter despite continued loan growth. The customer base reached 139M (+118M Brazil, +5M Colombia, +16M Mexico). The 
activity rate hit 83.5% sequentially, Brazil exceeded 86%. Mexico banking license approval completed digital bank 
transformation, unlocking payroll deposits and expanded credit offerings.  
Negatives 
- 
Management noted macro caution in Brazil requiring vigilance on consumer credit. The efficiency ratio rose to 19.5% from 17.6% 
in Q1 as operating expenses jumped 20% QoQ to $806mn on real-estate and marketing expense timing plus continued 
international (US, Mexico) build-out costs. Later-stage delinquencies still rising, as the 90+ day NPL ratio increased 35bps to 
6.9%. Management characterized the move as seasonal migration rather than deterioration, but CFO Rob Livingston 
acknowledged the broader NPL trend has trended “upwards” over the past two years as the portfolio mix has shifted toward 
higher-risk, higher-yield products. Cost of credit is still elevated. At $1.7bn, cost of credit ran 61% above the year-ago quarter, 
reflecting both loan-book growth and the deliberate push into higher-risk lending segments. Mexican deposits declined slightly

quarter-over-quarter, which management attributed to an intentional deposit-optimization strategy rather than customer 
attrition. The Desenrola government program (Brazilian federal debt-renegotiation program designed to let over-indebted 
consumers settle defaulted debts with banks and fintechs at steep, government-brokered discounts, essentially a policy tool for 
working down system-wide consumer NPLs rather than leaving banks to charge them off individually) impacted cost of credit by 
5%. Management emphasized vigilance on consumer credit trends despite strong underlying portfolio quality and maintained 
conservative underwriting assumptions. 
 
Geographic highlights 
- 
In Brazil, they have primary banking relationships for 60% of mass market customers, monthly activity rate topped 86% for the 
first time, ARPAC rose from $13 to $17 and mature 7-8 year cohorts are running mid-$20s and higher. Desenrola renegotiation 
program benefited 1.8mn customers. New local banking license secured. In Mexico, ARPAC of $12.30 compares with Brazil's 
$5.60 at the same stage of penetration (they broke even after 6 years, faster than Brazil's 8-year timeline). New banking license 
was approved, enabling payroll deposits, expanded credit, and higher deposit insurance. Loan-to-deposit ratio is only 35%, 
leaving room to lend more aggressively. Mexico’s 16mn customers represents 16.5% adult penetration, matching Brazil’s 2020 
levels. Colombia was described by management as “significantly overperforming” with substantial untapped opportunity, 
continuing steady net customer additions. In the US, management flagged that building credit-bureau-level confidence in the US 
market comparable to Latin America and will take an estimated 12-30 months, a near-term drag on group efficiency ratios. 
 
Segment highlights 
- 
Nu's small-business banking product now serves 6.8mn customers in Brazil, making Nu the country's largest bank by business-
customer count. Croma, the newly launched premium subscription tier aimed at affluent “super core” customers, is part of the 
broader ARPAC-expansion strategy. The NuFormer AI platform now handles 60%+ of Brazilian customer-support conversations 
and is being expanded into underwriting and credit-decisioning workflows across markets. Total deposits reached $45.3bn (+18% 
YoY, +6% QoQ in constant currency) while cost of deposits held at 88% of interbank rates, an improvement of 3pp YoY. 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Rising later-stage (90+ day) delinquencies, up 35 bps sequentially to 6.9%, tied to a multi-year mix shift toward higher-risk, 
higher-yield credit products. Deliberate expansion into higher-risk credit segments increases sensitivity to any macro 
deterioration in Brazil or Mexico, even though management says it sees no broad-based consumer weakness today. 
- 
Operating expenses up 20% QoQ, pushing the efficiency ratio to 19.5% from 17.6% in Q1. Part of the increase (real 
estate/marketing timing) is expected to reverse, but international expansion costs are structural. 
- 
US market entry remains a multi-year, low-visibility investment. Management estimates 12-30 months to build the credit-bureau 
data and underwriting confidence it enjoys in Latin America. 
- 
Mexico deposit base contracted slightly on an intentional funding-cost optimization strategy, a reminder that Mexico's build-out 
is still early and can move non-linearly. 
 
Guidance 
- 
Nu does not publish formal quarterly revenue or EPS guidance, but management updated its key operating targets on the call. 
On risk-adjusted NIM, management said the Q2 level of 12.4% is sustainable “for the foreseeable future,” though CFO Rob 
Livingston cautioned this is the expected running range rather than a hard floor. Efficiency ratio was reiterated at approximately 
20% for full-year 2026, with management noting Q2's better-than-trend 19.5% print benefited from favorable expense timing 
that is not expected to persist at the same magnitude. On ARPAC ceiling, CEO David Vélez said Nu sees “significant upside” in 
ARPAC expansion but does not expect to reach incumbent-bank levels of $40-45, given Nu's structurally lower-fee model. 
Growth drivers were reaffirmed as management pointed to three priorities for the balance of 2026 and into 2027, including 
continued Brazilian customer growth (1mn net adds per month), ARPAC expansion via product segmentation (including Croma), 
continued scaling in Mexico following the new banking license. 
 
Rating actions and target price changes 
Sentiment heading into the print had cooled after a soft Q1 report, and the Q2 beat reversed that tone. Shares rose 9%+ following

Why we own 
Nu is the largest digital bank in Latin America, operating under the Nubank brand across Brazil, Mexico and Colombia. They have 
139mn customers with 118mn in Brazil, where it now touches well over half the adult population, 16mn in Mexico, where 
management says it has become the country's largest digital bank, and 5+mn in Colombia, its earliest-stage market. The product set 
spans the full retail-banking stack, from deposit accounts, credit cards, personal and secured lending to insurance, investing, and, 
more recently, Nu Global, a multicurrency account live in 35+ countries offering yield, fee-free FX transfers and crypto trading. Nu's 
business model is a licensed, deposit-funded bank that gathers low-cost deposits (cost of deposits running at 88% of interbank rates), 
extends credit against them, and gets paid through net interest margin, interchange and fees. The moat is a cost-to-serve structure 
that legacy banks in the region cannot replicate without cannibalizing their own branch networks. Nu's cost to serve per active 
customer in Brazil (currently $1/month) runs 85% lower than incumbents. That structural gap sits on top of a physical-footprint 
difference. Nu runs on zero branches and 8,000 employees in Brazil versus Itaú's 16,000+ branches/ATMs and Bradesco's 82,000+ 
headcount. Nu's NuFormer AI foundation model now powers credit decisioning, customer service and growth targeting across the 
full customer base, and management notes that customers where Nu is the primary banking relationship show delinquency of half 
the portfolio average. The data advantage compounds through underwriting, with the flywheel functioning as a genuine risk-
management edge, not just a marketing one. Nu sizes the serviceable addressable market, or the revenue potential of retail financial 
services in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia, measured as interest income plus service fees minus funding costs, at $213bn+ in 2024. 
Capital allocation is a real point of differentiation versus both fintech peers still burning cash to grow and incumbent banks funding 
growth with dilutive capital raises. This is self-funded compounding, which is a materially cleaner capital story than most high-growth 
financials. With Brazil still under-monetized relative to its penetration, Mexico repeating the early Brazil trajectory against a well-
documented unbanked base (World Bank's 2025 Global Findex report names Mexico as one of just eight countries holding over half 
the world's roughly 1.3bn unbanked adults), Colombia providing a third, earlier-stage leg, and an AI-driven underwriting edge that's 
showing up in the delinquency data rather than just the marketing deck, Nu should remain a core position in PFOE.

lines.text: Nu Holdings delivered stellar Q2 2026 performance, beating consensus estimates on revenue, profit, and margin metrics. They
surpassed $4bn in net revenue and $1bn in net income for the first time while maintaining a record 33% ROE. The efficiency ratio
stood at 19.5% for the quarter, compared to 17.6% in Q1 2026, though management noted the Q1 figure benefited from temporary
expense timing. 15-to-90-day delinquencies improved 16bps to 4.8%. The 90-plus delinquency ratio increased to 6.9%, which
management attributed to the natural migration of seasonal cohorts from Q1. Provisioning expenses decreased sequentially to
$1.7bn, a reversal from the spike seen in the previous quarter. Management's tone was confident, focusing on long-term NPV per
client rather than short-term P&L optimization. They signaled a shift from mass-market acquisition to "Super Core" segmentation and
an "all-in" AI transformation, even as the investment community remains divided on near-term asset quality risks and the costs of
global expansion. All said, the print prompted a 9%+ jump in share price and a wave of price-target increases from sell-side analysts.
First-ever $1B net-income quarter, with net income reaching $1.06bn, up 49% YoY and 17% QoQ on a constant currency basis.
Margin inflected, with risk-adjusted net interest margin climbing 290bps sequentially to a record 12.4% from 9.5% in Q1, which
management framed as the first clear evidence that credit-cost normalization is under way alongside continued monetization
gains. Monetization is climbing, with monthly ARPAC (average revenue per active customer) rising to $17.10, up from $12.50 a
year earlier, helped by product cross-sell and the new premium Croma tier. Revenue mix is diversifying, with credit contributing
41% of gross profit, float income 34%, and fee-based revenue 25%, reducing reliance on any single income stream. Credit quality
improved at the front end. The earlier-stage 15-90 day NPL ratio improved 16bps to 4.8%, and cost of credit fell 9% quarter-over-
quarter despite continued loan growth. The customer base reached 139M (+118M Brazil, +5M Colombia, +16M Mexico). The
activity rate hit 83.5% sequentially, Brazil exceeded 86%. Mexico banking license approval completed digital bank
transformation, unlocking payroll deposits and expanded credit offerings.
Management noted macro caution in Brazil requiring vigilance on consumer credit. The efficiency ratio rose to 19.5% from 17.6%
in Q1 as operating expenses jumped 20% QoQ to $806mn on real-estate and marketing expense timing plus continued
international (US, Mexico) build-out costs. Later-stage delinquencies still rising, as the 90+ day NPL ratio increased 35bps to
6.9%. Management characterized the move as seasonal migration rather than deterioration, but CFO Rob Livingston
acknowledged the broader NPL trend has trended “upwards” over the past two years as the portfolio mix has shifted toward
higher-risk, higher-yield products. Cost of credit is still elevated. At $1.7bn, cost of credit ran 61% above the year-ago quarter,
reflecting both loan-book growth and the deliberate push into higher-risk lending segments. Mexican deposits declined slightly
quarter-over-quarter, which management attributed to an intentional deposit-optimization strategy rather than customer
attrition. The Desenrola government program (Brazilian federal debt-renegotiation program designed to let over-indebted
consumers settle defaulted debts with banks and fintechs at steep, government-brokered discounts, essentially a policy tool for
working down system-wide consumer NPLs rather than leaving banks to charge them off individually) impacted cost of credit by
5%. Management emphasized vigilance on consumer credit trends despite strong underlying portfolio quality and maintained
In Brazil, they have primary banking relationships for 60% of mass market customers, monthly activity rate topped 86% for the
first time, ARPAC rose from $13 to $17 and mature 7-8 year cohorts are running mid-$20s and higher. Desenrola renegotiation
program benefited 1.8mn customers. New local banking license secured. In Mexico, ARPAC of $12.30 compares with Brazil's
$5.60 at the same stage of penetration (they broke even after 6 years, faster than Brazil's 8-year timeline). New banking license
was approved, enabling payroll deposits, expanded credit, and higher deposit insurance. Loan-to-deposit ratio is only 35%,
leaving room to lend more aggressively. Mexico’s 16mn customers represents 16.5% adult penetration, matching Brazil’s 2020
levels. Colombia was described by management as “significantly overperforming” with substantial untapped opportunity,
continuing steady net customer additions. In the US, management flagged that building credit-bureau-level confidence in the US
market comparable to Latin America and will take an estimated 12-30 months, a near-term drag on group efficiency ratios.
Nu's small-business banking product now serves 6.8mn customers in Brazil, making Nu the country's largest bank by business-
customer count. Croma, the newly launched premium subscription tier aimed at affluent “super core” customers, is part of the
broader ARPAC-expansion strategy. The NuFormer AI platform now handles 60%+ of Brazilian customer-support conversations
and is being expanded into underwriting and credit-decisioning workflows across markets. Total deposits reached $45.3bn (+18%
YoY, +6% QoQ in constant currency) while cost of deposits held at 88% of interbank rates, an improvement of 3pp YoY.
Rising later-stage (90+ day) delinquencies, up 35 bps sequentially to 6.9%, tied to a multi-year mix shift toward higher-risk,
higher-yield credit products. Deliberate expansion into higher-risk credit segments increases sensitivity to any macro
deterioration in Brazil or Mexico, even though management says it sees no broad-based consumer weakness today.
Operating expenses up 20% QoQ, pushing the efficiency ratio to 19.5% from 17.6% in Q1. Part of the increase (real
estate/marketing timing) is expected to reverse, but international expansion costs are structural.
US market entry remains a multi-year, low-visibility investment. Management estimates 12-30 months to build the credit-bureau
data and underwriting confidence it enjoys in Latin America.
Mexico deposit base contracted slightly on an intentional funding-cost optimization strategy, a reminder that Mexico's build-out
is still early and can move non-linearly.
Nu does not publish formal quarterly revenue or EPS guidance, but management updated its key operating targets on the call.
On risk-adjusted NIM, management said the Q2 level of 12.4% is sustainable “for the foreseeable future,” though CFO Rob
Livingston cautioned this is the expected running range rather than a hard floor. Efficiency ratio was reiterated at approximately
20% for full-year 2026, with management noting Q2's better-than-trend 19.5% print benefited from favorable expense timing
that is not expected to persist at the same magnitude. On ARPAC ceiling, CEO David Vélez said Nu sees “significant upside” in
ARPAC expansion but does not expect to reach incumbent-bank levels of $40-45, given Nu's structurally lower-fee model.
Growth drivers were reaffirmed as management pointed to three priorities for the balance of 2026 and into 2027, including
continued Brazilian customer growth (1mn net adds per month), ARPAC expansion via product segmentation (including Croma),
continued scaling in Mexico following the new banking license.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN 1% POSITION IN IDVZ 
 
Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte (OMA) reported solid Q2 2026 results, characterized by resilient margins and strong non-
aeronautical revenue growth that offset a slight miss in aeronautical income. While it is a challenging operating environment for 
Mexican airports, OMA still delivered positive growth across traffic, revenue, and EBITDA during the period. It was the only major 
operator in the sector to do this. 
 
OMA reported a beat on both the top and bottom lines relative to the average analyst projections. Total revenue reached MXN 3,622 
mm, which was 2.5% higher than the consensus estimate of MXN 3,532 mm. 
 
 
 
Investment thesis: OMA operates 13 airports in northern and central Mexico under a concession running to 2048, anchored by 
Monterrey (~half of traffic), Mexico's industrial capital. It is the purest listed play on nearshoring: its catchment covers the 
manufacturing corridor (Nuevo León, Chihuahua, Tamaulipas) where US-bound supply-chain relocation drives business travel, cargo, 
and industrial real estate demand. OMA uniquely monetizes the latter through its industrial park and OMA Carga logistics businesses, 
diversifying beyond passenger fees. The regulated dual-till model provides inflation-linked tariff visibility via five-year Master 
Development Programs, while unregulated commercial revenue (still underpenetrated versus ASUR/GAP) offers a self-help margin 
lever. The business converts EBITDA to cash at industry-leading margins (~75%+), carries modest leverage, and returns essentially all 
free cash flow through dividends and buybacks. 
 
Q2 2026 Financial and Operational Summary 
OMA's financial performance was bolstered by disciplined cost control and successful commercial initiatives. 
 
• 
Adjusted EBITDA grew 6.2% year-over-year to MXN 2.72 bn, with margins expanding by 60 basis points to 75.2%  
• 
Net income reached MXN 1.47 bn, a 10.2% increase compared to Q2 2025 
• 
Total revenues (excluding construction) rose 5.4% to MXN 3.62 bn  
o 
This growth was primarily driven by a 9.8% surge in non-aeronautical revenues, supported by high-performing

lines.text: Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte (OMA) reported solid Q2 2026 results, characterized by resilient margins and strong non-
aeronautical revenue growth that offset a slight miss in aeronautical income. While it is a challenging operating environment for
Mexican airports, OMA still delivered positive growth across traffic, revenue, and EBITDA during the period. It was the only major
operator in the sector to do this.
OMA reported a beat on both the top and bottom lines relative to the average analyst projections. Total revenue reached MXN 3,622
mm, which was 2.5% higher than the consensus estimate of MXN 3,532 mm.
Investment thesis: OMA operates 13 airports in northern and central Mexico under a concession running to 2048, anchored by
Monterrey (~half of traffic), Mexico's industrial capital. It is the purest listed play on nearshoring: its catchment covers the
manufacturing corridor (Nuevo León, Chihuahua, Tamaulipas) where US-bound supply-chain relocation drives business travel, cargo,
and industrial real estate demand. OMA uniquely monetizes the latter through its industrial park and OMA Carga logistics businesses,
diversifying beyond passenger fees. The regulated dual-till model provides inflation-linked tariff visibility via five-year Master
Development Programs, while unregulated commercial revenue (still underpenetrated versus ASUR/GAP) offers a self-help margin
lever. The business converts EBITDA to cash at industry-leading margins (~75%+), carries modest leverage, and returns essentially all
free cash flow through dividends and buybacks.
OMA's financial performance was bolstered by disciplined cost control and successful commercial initiatives.
Adjusted EBITDA grew 6.2% year-over-year to MXN 2.72 bn, with margins expanding by 60 basis points to 75.2%
Net income reached MXN 1.47 bn, a 10.2% increase compared to Q2 2025
Total revenues (excluding construction) rose 5.4% to MXN 3.62 bn
This growth was primarily driven by a 9.8% surge in non-aeronautical revenues, supported by high-performing
commercial categories such as VIP lounges (+15.8%), restaurants (+11.3%), and parking (+8.8%)
Passenger traffic increased 0.4% during 2Q26, as compared to 2Q25, reaching 7.2 mm passengers
86.1% of total traffic was domestic and 13.9% was international
Domestic passenger traffic grew 0.6%, as compared to 2Q25, while international traffic decreased by 1.2%
Airports with the largest passenger traffic growth in volume terms as compared to 2Q25, were:
San Luis Potosí (+22.6%), on its AIFA, Houston, Cancún, San Antonio and Guadalajara routes

RECOMMENDATION: Consider size reduction in IDVZ to ~3%.  
 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: ORA is a global telecom leader serving ~300mm customers, including 262mm mobile and 22mm fixed broadband customers across 26 countries, 
with roughly 127K employees worldwide. Think of it as France's version of AT&T or Verizon, but with a large, fast-growing footprint in Africa where it also operates a major mobile 
banking business. Orange is France's incumbent telephone company, privatized from its origin as a gov monopoly. It runs mobile networks, home internet (including fiber), TV 
services, and business tech services across Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.  
5 segments: France, Europe, Africa & Middle East, Orange Business, and TOTEM (its tower infrastructure company) 
France (~40% of rev): Mature market, modest growth, but improving profitability. Fiber rollout is the key near-term driver. 
Europe (~18% of rev): Spain, Poland, Belgium, Romania, & others. Spain recently merged with MásMóvil into a JV called MASORANGE, which simplifies competition there. 
Africa & Middle East (~21% of rev): Growth engines are Mobile data (+15.7%), Fixed broadband (+20.6%), Orange Money (+23.5%), and B2B across all activities (+14.1%).  
Orange Business (~17% of rev): The enterprise/B2B segment, currently in a recovery plan. IT and Integration services, including double-digit growth in Orange Cyberdefense 
(+15.3%) and Digital services, are partially offsetting the structural decline in legacy fixed voice and data activities. sec 
TOTEM: The passive tower infrastructure company, generating stable revenues from hosting mobile operators' equipment. 
Orange Money: mobile banking platform that as of 2025 hosts 37mm active users across 17 countries in the Middle East and Africa. Generates nearly €900mm in annual 
revenue. 
 
INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Fiber: Fiber-to-the-home coverage has reached 62.9mm households,14.4mm active 
customers, customers who migrate to fiber tend to pay more and churn less. 
African growth: Africa has low internet and banking penetration, favorable 
demographics, and Orange Money is well-positioned as digital infrastructure. 
European telecoms sector: Falling interest rates, a recognition that European 
telecoms have hit peak capex as fiber rollouts mature, and consolidation. 
French telco consolidation: In Oct 2025, Orange & Bouygues & Free made a joint bid 
for rival SFR. The proposal was rejected, but markets are pricing in that a deal gets 
done. France has 4 mobile operators making it one of the most fragmented markets in 
Europe. Consolidation = price increases, and reduced infra duplication. 
Defensive income: Telecom is among the most stable cash-flow businesses globally. 
People don't cancel their mobile plans in recessions. 
Capital discipline: Net debt/EBITDA of 1.88 is conservative for a telecom 
TOTEM: The tower company has significant asset value that may not be fully reflected 
in Orange's market cap. A sale or IPO of TOTEM could be a catalyst. 
Orange Money: Another imbedded asset. Generated ~€900mm in 2024, growing at 
roughly 20% annually. ORA does not disclose Orange Money’s profitability (M-Pesa in 
Kenya operates at EBITDA margins above 50%). Orange Money's profit is bundled 
inside Africa & Middle East's ~€3 billion annual EBITDAaL 
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: 
Government ownership: The French state holds a 23% stake, maintaining significant 
influence over strategic decisions. ORA is sometimes managed with political objectives 
in mind (employment levels, pricing) rather than purely shareholder value.  
Intense competition: European telecom markets are fragmented and compete on 
price. ORA’s CEO has argued publicly \Europe needs far fewer mobile operators to 
justify infrastructure investment. 
Capital intensity: Fiber rollout, 5G spectrum purchases, and network maintenance 
require large, ongoing capex limiting FCF. 
Orange Business recovery risk: Enterprise segment is in a multiyear turnaround. If IT 
service growth doesn't offset legacy voice/data declines fast enough, it remains a drag. 
F/X risk: ~30% of rev from Africa, exposing ORA to African currency devaluations.  
Regulatory risk: EU and French regulators can cap pricing, mandate network sharing, 
or block deals. The MASORANGE Spanish JV required lengthy regulatory approval.

lines.text: RECOMMENDATION: Consider size reduction in IDVZ to ~3%.
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: ORA is a global telecom leader serving ~300mm customers, including 262mm mobile and 22mm fixed broadband customers across 26 countries,
with roughly 127K employees worldwide. Think of it as France's version of AT&T or Verizon, but with a large, fast-growing footprint in Africa where it also operates a major mobile
banking business. Orange is France's incumbent telephone company, privatized from its origin as a gov monopoly. It runs mobile networks, home internet (including fiber), TV
services, and business tech services across Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.
5 segments: France, Europe, Africa & Middle East, Orange Business, and TOTEM (its tower infrastructure company)
France (~40% of rev): Mature market, modest growth, but improving profitability. Fiber rollout is the key near-term driver.
Europe (~18% of rev): Spain, Poland, Belgium, Romania, & others. Spain recently merged with MásMóvil into a JV called MASORANGE, which simplifies competition there.
Africa & Middle East (~21% of rev): Growth engines are Mobile data (+15.7%), Fixed broadband (+20.6%), Orange Money (+23.5%), and B2B across all activities (+14.1%).
Orange Business (~17% of rev): The enterprise/B2B segment, currently in a recovery plan. IT and Integration services, including double-digit growth in Orange Cyberdefense
(+15.3%) and Digital services, are partially offsetting the structural decline in legacy fixed voice and data activities. sec
TOTEM: The passive tower infrastructure company, generating stable revenues from hosting mobile operators' equipment.
Orange Money: mobile banking platform that as of 2025 hosts 37mm active users across 17 countries in the Middle East and Africa. Generates nearly €900mm in annual
Fiber: Fiber-to-the-home coverage has reached 62.9mm households,14.4mm active
customers, customers who migrate to fiber tend to pay more and churn less.
African growth: Africa has low internet and banking penetration, favorable
demographics, and Orange Money is well-positioned as digital infrastructure.
European telecoms sector: Falling interest rates, a recognition that European
telecoms have hit peak capex as fiber rollouts mature, and consolidation.
French telco consolidation: In Oct 2025, Orange & Bouygues & Free made a joint bid
for rival SFR. The proposal was rejected, but markets are pricing in that a deal gets
done. France has 4 mobile operators making it one of the most fragmented markets in
Europe. Consolidation = price increases, and reduced infra duplication.
Defensive income: Telecom is among the most stable cash-flow businesses globally.
People don't cancel their mobile plans in recessions.
Capital discipline: Net debt/EBITDA of 1.88 is conservative for a telecom
TOTEM: The tower company has significant asset value that may not be fully reflected
in Orange's market cap. A sale or IPO of TOTEM could be a catalyst.
Orange Money: Another imbedded asset. Generated ~€900mm in 2024, growing at
roughly 20% annually. ORA does not disclose Orange Money’s profitability (M-Pesa in
Kenya operates at EBITDA margins above 50%). Orange Money's profit is bundled
inside Africa & Middle East's ~€3 billion annual EBITDAaL
Government ownership: The French state holds a 23% stake, maintaining significant
influence over strategic decisions. ORA is sometimes managed with political objectives
in mind (employment levels, pricing) rather than purely shareholder value.
Intense competition: European telecom markets are fragmented and compete on
price. ORA’s CEO has argued publicly \Europe needs far fewer mobile operators to
Capital intensity: Fiber rollout, 5G spectrum purchases, and network maintenance
require large, ongoing capex limiting FCF.
Orange Business recovery risk: Enterprise segment is in a multiyear turnaround. If IT
service growth doesn't offset legacy voice/data declines fast enough, it remains a drag.
F/X risk: ~30% of rev from Africa, exposing ORA to African currency devaluations.
Regulatory risk: EU and French regulators can cap pricing, mandate network sharing,
or block deals. The MASORANGE Spanish JV required lengthy regulatory approval.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN 3% POSITION IN IDVZ 
 
ORA remains a core consistent earning holding with strong FCF and a nice div yield. It has been a great performer for us and we have 
trimmed twice. 
 
Orange reported record performance for the H1 2026, driven by exceptional growth in Africa & Middle East and a stabilization of the 
French domestic market. Following these results, the company raised its full-year guidance for both EBITDAaL and organic cash 
flow, reflecting the successful consolidation of MasOrange in Spain and strong organic momentum. 
 
H1 2026 Financial Performance 
• 
Group Revenue: Reached €20.95 bn, representing a 3.5% year-on-year (YoY) increase. 
• 
EBITDAaL: Grew 5% to €6.13 bn, with a margin expansion of 0.4 points to 29.3%. 
• 
Organic Cash Flow: Surged 29.8% YoY to €2.17 bn, significantly ahead of consensus estimates. 
• 
Adjusted Net Income: Rose 11.8% on a historical basis to €1.35 bn. 
• 
Net Debt: Stood at €35.7 bn, equivalent to a 2.4x leverage ratio, following the consolidation of the MasOrange joint venture 
in Spain. 
 
Regional Highlights and Strategic Initiatives 
The company’s growth was underpinned by a diverse regional performance and new infrastructure projects. 
 
• 
Africa & Middle East (MEA) 
o 
This region remained the primary growth engine, with revenue up 15% and EBITDAaL up 16.1%. 
o 
Growth was fueled by a 25% increase in mobile data traffic and a 20.7% rise in active Orange Money customers to 
52 million. 
• 
France 
o 
The domestic market showed "sound" performance, with retail services (excluding PSTN) growth accelerating to 
1.3%. 
o 
The segment saw healthy commercial momentum with 84,000 mobile net adds and 62,000 broadband net adds. 
• 
Spain (MasOrange) 
o 
Spain saw a stabilization of service revenues as of June 2026, though the market remains highly competitive. 
• 
Data Center Joint Venture 
o 
Orange announced a partnership with Morrison to create a sovereign data center platform, targeting a 10x capacity 
increase to 400MW. The project involves a €3 bn investment, with Orange contributing existing assets rather than 
cash. 
 
Updated 2026 Guidance 
Supported by the strong H1 performance and the integration of MasOrange, Orange upgraded its full-year outlook. 
o 
EBITDAaL Growth: Now expected to exceed 4% (up from the previous guidance of >3%). 
o 
Organic Cash Flow: Raised to approximately €4.3 billion (up from ~€4.0 billion). 
o 
Dividend: Confirmed a dividend floor of €0.79 per share for 2026.

Broker Commentary 
Analysts generally reacted positively to the "beat and raise" quarter, though opinions on long-term valuation varied. 
• 
UBS reiterated a Buy rating and named Orange their sector top pick, highlighting a unique combination of double-digit cash 
flow growth and material optionality from potential French M&A consolidation. 
• 
JPMorgan maintained an Overweight rating, noting that the results served as a reminder of the company's operational 
resilience following a recent stock pullback. 
• 
Berenberg reiterated a Buy rating, raising cash flow forecasts for the next four years and noting that encouraging trends in 
France were helping to offset "less impressive" initial data from the Spanish consolidation. 
• 
Kepler Cheuvreux kept a Buy rating, pointing out that the market has not yet factored in the potential structural benefits of 
French market consolidation. 
• 
ESN (CIC CIB) maintained a Neutral rating, expressing confidence in the H2 trajectory while noting that the share price had 
already welcomed the guidance revision. 
• 
Santander reiterated a Neutral rating, suggesting the sound outlook from the company’s strategic plan was already priced into 
the stock valuation. 
• 
CFRA Research maintained a 3-star Hold recommendation, citing a challenging European regulatory environment and risks 
associated with M&A integration and high leverage.

QXO, Inc. (QXO-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
 
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE  
QXO's latest second-quarter 2026 results demonstrated early traction in its multi-year transformation strategy, characterized by a 
modest beat on revenue and EBITDA despite a persistently challenging macro environment. QXO reported total revenue of $3.25bn 
for Q2, representing 70.27% year-over-year growth, primarily driven by the first-time inclusion of Kodiak Building Partners. The 
company achieved adjusted EBITDA of $272mn, which outperformed consensus estimates of $253mn. The investment community 
remains generally positive on the long-term consolidation thesis led by Brad Jacobs, though analysts have recently tempered near-
term expectations and lowered price targets to reflect broader housing demand headwinds and higher market multiples. 
 
Headline results 
Positives 
- 
Revenue nearly doubled and beat consensus. Net sales of $3.25B grew 70.3% y/y, ahead of the $3.19B consensus estimate. H1 
2026 net sales reached $4.98B vs. $1.92B in H1 2025. Kodiak Building Partners (acquired April 1, 2026) contributed $595M of the 
quarter's sales. Adjusted EBITDA of $272M vs. $205M in Q2 2025 was up 33% and ahead of expectations. This provides evidence 
that stacking three acquisitions (Beacon, Kodiak, and now TopBuild) hasn't broken profitability at the EBITDA line. Operating loss 
narrowed sharply with GAAP operating loss improving to -$42M from -$162M a year earlier (a $120M improvement) even as 
gross margin expanded 360bps to 24.7%. TopBuild closed on schedule and long-term targets held. The $17B TopBuild acquisition 
closed July 1, 2026 (just after quarter-end), making QXO the second-largest publicly traded building products distributor in North 
America. Management reiterated its target to more than double EBITDA by 2030 and reach $50B of revenue within the decade. 
Negatives 
- 
Adjusted EPS fell even as adjusted net income rose. Adjusted diluted EPS declined to $0.08 from $0.11 a year ago, despite 
adjusted net income rising to $130M from $109M. The $120M improvement in operating loss barely moved the GAAP net loss (-
$55M vs. -$59M, a $4M improvement), consistent with sharply higher interest expense on a balance sheet that already carries 
$6.0B of long-term debt, up from $3.1B a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA margin compressed, declining to 8.4% from 10.7% a year 
earlier, as newly consolidated Kodiak revenue diluted the blended margin mix even as the dollar figure grew. Operating cash flow 
was negative. H1 2026 operating cash flow was -$146M, on top of roughly $2.0B of H1 acquisition spending (chiefly Kodiak). 
Core operations consumed cash before a dollar of deal spending is counted. H1 GAAP loss was far wider than the Q2 print alone 
suggests. H1 2026 net loss totaled -$282M vs. -$50M in H1 2025, reflecting a -$227M Q1 2026 loss concentrated around deal 
costs, a reminder that quarter-to-quarter GAAP results are still noisy around each acquisition close. Sell-side estimates kept 
falling even after the beat.

Geographic highlights 
- 
No regional color provided at this stage. 
 
Segment highlights 
- 
Not an apples-to-apples year-over-year comparison, as Q2 2025 revenue was entirely Beacon (residential roofing, non-
residential roofing, and complementary products). Kodiak's $595M (added April 1, 2026) sits inside “complementary building 
products” in the Q2 2026 figures, and TopBuild (closed July 1, 2026) isn't in the Q2 2026 numbers at all. Complementary building 
products is already QXO's second-largest bucket. At 37.9% of sales, ahead of non-residential roofing, this underscores how 
quickly Kodiak's specialty distribution lines have shifted the revenue mix in a single quarter. Software & services remains 
negligible at 0.4% of sales, so the “technology-enabled distributor” positioning Jacobs has emphasized hasn't yet shown up as a 
distinct, monetized revenue line. The segment table will look different again next quarter. TopBuild's insulation distribution and 
installation businesses (a multibillion-dollar standalone revenue base historically) will be consolidated for the first time in Q3 
2026 and should become one of the largest segments in the mix. 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Demand cyclicality, acknowledged by management itself – QXO's own risk disclosures flag “cyclicality and dependence on 
general economic conditions,” “seasonality and weather-related challenges,” “labor and supply shortages,” and “construction 
demand softness or shifts.” In CEO Brad Jacobs's Q2 commentary, “our results reflect current market conditions”, stopped short 
of specifics. Outside analysts have pointed to weak non-residential construction activity (not anything specific to QXO's 
execution) as the main pressure on near-term earnings power. 
- 
Leverage from stacking deals – Roughly $3B of new senior notes were raised to help fund TopBuild, pushing long-term debt to 
about $6.0B by quarter-end, before TopBuild's July 1 close, meaning the balance sheet carried a full quarter of that leverage 
without a full quarter of the acquired earnings behind it. 
- 
Negative operating cash flow – H1 2026 operating cash flow was -$146M, a genuine cash-generation headwind independent of 
the $2.0B spent on acquisitions. 
- 
Thin near-term visibility – QXO issues no formal quarterly or full-year revenue/EPS guidance. All forward commentary is multi-
year target language, which limits how precisely results can be held to account quarter to quarter. 
- 
Heavy, persistent short interest and a battered stock – Short interest has reportedly exceeded 18% of the float (currently 11%), 
and the stock is down 40%+ over the last six months, consistent with the market pricing meaningful execution risk across three 
simultaneous integrations (Beacon, Kodiak, TopBuild). 
 
Guidance 
- 
QXO does not issue traditional quarterly or full-year sales/EPS guidance ranges. Management instead communicates multi-year 
targets, most recently set out when the TopBuild acquisition was announced in April 2026, and updates them on earnings calls.

limit large-scale M&A in the immediate quarters, risk-reward profile is viewed as asymmetrically positive by many analysts who 
believe current trading levels do not yet reflect the full potential of the Jacobs playbook in a consolidated building products market. 
Analysts have revised near-term forecasts lower to account for a more conservative residential demand environment and higher 
SG&A investments required for technology rollouts. Stephens lowered its FY 2026 adjusted EBITDA estimate to $1.25bn from 
$1.30bn and its target price to $20 from $26. KeyBanc reiterated its Overweight rating but lowered its price target to $28 from $32, 
citing lower market multiples and persistent macro weakness impacting the Kodiak segment. Loop Capital modestly lowered its 2H 
2026 forecast, adjusting its 2027 EBITDA estimate to $2.49bn from $2.57bn. William Blair Research maintained an Outperform rating, 
forecasting significant EBITDA growth to $2.52bn in 2027E as integration and digitization initiatives under new President Ken West 
begin to yield margin expansion. A tension worth noting is that the near-unanimous bullish rating consensus sits awkwardly next to 
the estimate-cut pattern. Keeping a Buy rating and an elevated, multi-year-anchored price target while simultaneously marking down 
near-term numbers usually signals that analysts are underwriting the long-dated Jacobs track record and the 2030 targets rather than 
the trailing 12-month print, which is worth remembering given how far out (through 2030) the bull case requires you to look. 
 
Appendix 
 
 
 
 
Why we own 
QXO is Brad Jacobs' latest industry roll-up, this time targeting building products distribution, the network of businesses that moves 
roofing, insulation, siding, and other construction materials from manufacturers to contractors and jobsites. Following the Beacon 
Roofing (2025), Kodiak Building Partners (April 2026), and TopBuild (July 2026) acquisitions, QXO operates roughly 1,150 locations 
across all 50 states and seven Canadian provinces, more than 10,000 delivery vehicles, and 28,000 employees, generating combined 
annualized revenue of $18bn+. The company holds the no. 1 position in insulation and waterproofing distribution and no. 2 in 
roofing distribution, making it the second largest publicly traded building products distributor in North America. QXO doesn't 
manufacture anything. Like Jacobs' prior roll-ups (United Waste Systems, United Rentals, XPO/GXO/RXO), it owns the distribution and 
logistics layer connecting a concentrated set of manufacturers to a highly fragmented, relationship-driven base of contractors and 
builders. The building materials distribution market spans $800bn across North America and Europe combined (QXO's own stated 
North American TAM, where it currently operates, is $300bn), growing an estimated 5-9% annually through 2031, and remains 
extraordinarily fragmented. An estimated 10,000 distributors compete across North America alone, most of them small, family-run 
operations without QXO's scale, owned logistics fleet, or balance sheet. That fragmentation, combined with a purchasing process 
that is inherently relationship- and trust-based and hard to digitize or centralize quickly, is the same setup Jacobs has exploited three 
times before. Buy the scale advantages smaller competitors can't match (national account relationships, owned last-mile logistics, 
procurement leverage), then layer in technology (an integrated ERP, warehouse management, and pricing platform are targeted for 
2027) to extract efficiency the fragmented incumbents never had the capital to build. Management's stated long-term targets are to 
more than double EBITDA by 2030 and reach $50bn of revenue within the decade, a bar Jacobs has hit or exceeded in each prior roll-
up, albeit on a much longer timeline than the 2+ years QXO has operated so far. QXO is not yet the free-cash-flow generator we 
typically own, and QXO's negative cash generation is structural to a company still mid-build. Leverage roughly doubled over the past 
year to fund Kodiak and TopBuild, and the balance sheet will carry that debt through several more quarters of integration before any 
targeted margin expansion shows up. The bull case here isn't "proven moat generating cash today", it's a bet that Jacobs' repeatable 
playbook plays out a fourth time in a new but structurally similar industry. On current evidence, QXO belongs in PFOE as a higher-risk 
position underwritten on execution and the Jacobs track record, not yet as a demonstrated-quality, FCF-generative core holding.

lines.text: QXO's latest second-quarter 2026 results demonstrated early traction in its multi-year transformation strategy, characterized by a
modest beat on revenue and EBITDA despite a persistently challenging macro environment. QXO reported total revenue of $3.25bn
for Q2, representing 70.27% year-over-year growth, primarily driven by the first-time inclusion of Kodiak Building Partners. The
company achieved adjusted EBITDA of $272mn, which outperformed consensus estimates of $253mn. The investment community
remains generally positive on the long-term consolidation thesis led by Brad Jacobs, though analysts have recently tempered near-
term expectations and lowered price targets to reflect broader housing demand headwinds and higher market multiples.
Revenue nearly doubled and beat consensus. Net sales of $3.25B grew 70.3% y/y, ahead of the $3.19B consensus estimate. H1
2026 net sales reached $4.98B vs. $1.92B in H1 2025. Kodiak Building Partners (acquired April 1, 2026) contributed $595M of the
quarter's sales. Adjusted EBITDA of $272M vs. $205M in Q2 2025 was up 33% and ahead of expectations. This provides evidence
that stacking three acquisitions (Beacon, Kodiak, and now TopBuild) hasn't broken profitability at the EBITDA line. Operating loss
narrowed sharply with GAAP operating loss improving to -$42M from -$162M a year earlier (a $120M improvement) even as
gross margin expanded 360bps to 24.7%. TopBuild closed on schedule and long-term targets held. The $17B TopBuild acquisition
closed July 1, 2026 (just after quarter-end), making QXO the second-largest publicly traded building products distributor in North
America. Management reiterated its target to more than double EBITDA by 2030 and reach $50B of revenue within the decade.
Adjusted EPS fell even as adjusted net income rose. Adjusted diluted EPS declined to $0.08 from $0.11 a year ago, despite
adjusted net income rising to $130M from $109M. The $120M improvement in operating loss barely moved the GAAP net loss (-

paragraphs.text: SANOFI [SAN FP] Research Note
RECOMMENDATION: BUY

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: French pure-play biopharma company headquartered in Paris, founded in 1973. Engages in the R&D, manufacturing, and marketing of pharma products, principally in the prescription market. Describes itself as an "R&D driven, AI-powered biopharma company." It applies its deep understanding of the immune system to invent medicines and vaccines across six therapeutic areas: Immunology and Inflammation, Oncology, Rare Diseases, Rare Blood Disorders, and Vaccines.

Largest product is Dupixent (dupilumab), a biologic injection developed with Regeneron that treats a range of inflammatory conditions — eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, and more. In 2025, Sanofi Dupixent sales were €15.7 bn in, ~33.6% of total sales of €46.7 bn that year. Sanofi expects Dupixent to reach around €22 bn in annual sales by 2030. Primary patent covering Dupixent’s composition expires around 2031.

Sold 50% controlling stake in its consumer Healthcare division (OTC products like cold medicines and vitamins) in Oct 2024 to CD&R providing Sanofi with ~€10 bn in net cash proceeds. Sanofi remains a significant shareholder.
3 biopharma franchises:
Specialty Care (high-value drugs like Dupixent, rare disease treatments, oncology, multiple sclerosis) ~45% of rev
General Medicines (older established products, including diabetes drugs like Lantus and Toujeo) ~37% of rev
Vaccines (through its Sanofi Pasteur subsidiary, the world's largest vaccine producer) ~18% of rev
INVESTMENT THESIS:
Dupixent is a generational drug: It works across an unusually wide range of conditions and is still growing fast. Expected to reach ~€22 bn in sales by 2030.

No near-term patent issues: Sanofi has already gone over its near-term cliff (Aubagio), has nothing material expiring for the rest of this decade, and its big cliff — Dupixent — is a 2030s problem. That gives management roughly 5–7 years to build the next generation of the portfolio.
FCF generation: By the time Dupixent starts to lose patent protection SAN will have generated ~60% of it’s current market cap in FCF

Vaccines franchise: Vaccine division posted 13.5% growth in 2024, exceeding €8 bn in sales. Beyfortus, its RSV preventative antibody co-developed with AstraZeneca, rapidly achieved blockbuster status with €1.7 bn in reported sales in its first full launch cycle.
Clean balance sheet and shareholder returns: Net Debt/EBITDA below 1.0x. Executed a €5 bn share buyback program in 2025. Has raised its div for 30 consecutive years.
Strategic focus and cost discipline: Targeting savings of up to €2 bn from 2024 to the end of 2025, of which most will be reallocated to fund innovation and growth drivers.
Rich pipeline: Robust pipeline of 82 clinical-stage projects as of mid-2025, including 30 in late-stage development or under regulatory review.
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:
The thesis hinges on whether the current pipeline can produce the next wave of multi-billion-dollar drugs before Dupixent's exclusivity erodes.

Dupixent concentration: At ~30% of total sales and growing, Sanofi is dangerously reliant on one drug. Dupixent's eventual exposure to biosimilar competition represents a revenue risk that cannot be offset by incremental growth alone. Regeneron and Sanofi hold patents expiring between 2027 and 2032 in key jurisdictions.

Pipeline setbacks: In 2025, Sanofi's pipeline suffered several setbacks: the anti-OX40L antibody amlitelimab failed a Phase 2 asthma trial, oral TNF inhibitor balinatunfib missed its midstage psoriasis study goal. This is partly why the board replaced the CEO.
Vaccine policy headwinds: Faced rising pressure on vaccine business, espin the U.S. Vaccine sales will be "slightly negative" in 2026, partly due to US policy changes under Trump.
Currency risk: Sanofi reports in euros but earns a large chunk of revenue in USD

Pricing pressure: Drug pricing reform in the US (via the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare negotiation provisions and potential executive actions) can compress the revenue Sanofi earns on its drugs in its most profitable market.
R&D execution risk: Spending heavily on R&D. If pipeline doesn't deliver, earnings could be squeezed without the payoff of new blockbusters.
Acquisition integration: The Blueprint Medicines acquisition alone cost up to $9.5bn Large acquisitions always carry the risk of overpaying or failing to integrate effectively.
Management change: Recent CEO change raises some questions about leadership and execution.

Management/Board: There was a significant and very recent leadership change. Paul Hudson, CEO since 2019, was ousted in Feb 2026 and abruptly replaced after a massive research spending boost failed to deliver rapid results, appointing its first-ever female leader, Belén Garijo.

Who is Belén Garijo? Garijo has served as CEO and Chair of the Executive Board of Merck KGaA since 2021. Her appointment marks a return to Sanofi, where she previously spent 15 years — including leading the integration of Genzyme following its acquisition, serving as VP of Pharmaceutical Operations for Europe and Canada, and sitting on Sanofi's Executive Committee. Earlier in her career, she worked in R&D at Abbott Laboratories.
Sanofi stated that Garijo's priority will be to "strengthen the productivity, governance, and innovation capacity of R&D."
In short, the board is asking her to bring more discipline and rigor to the R&D engine that Hudson built up but struggled to deliver results from.
Sanofi shares fell nearly 6% on the announcement of the CEO change, with some analysts pointing to Garijo's relatively low profile.
