COMPANY DESCRIPTION: French pure-play biopharma company headquartered in Paris, founded in 1973. Engages in the R&D, manufacturing, and marketing of pharma products, principally in the prescription market. Describes itself as an "R&D driven, AI-powered biopharma company." It applies its deep understanding of the immune system to invent medicines and vaccines across six therapeutic areas: Immunology and Inflammation, Oncology, Rare Diseases, Rare Blood Disorders, and Vaccines. Largest product is Dupixent (dupilumab), a biologic injection developed with Regeneron that treats a range of inflammatory conditions — eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, and more. In 2025, Sanofi Dupixent sales were €15.7 bn in, ~33.6% of total sales of €46.7 bn that year. Sanofi expects Dupixent to reach around €22 bn in annual sales by 2030. Primary patent covering Dupixent’s composition expires around 2031. Sold 50% controlling stake in its consumer Healthcare division (OTC products like cold medicines and vitamins) in Oct 2024 to CD&R providing Sanofi with ~€10 bn in net cash proceeds. Sanofi remains a significant shareholder. 3 biopharma franchises: Specialty Care (high-value drugs like Dupixent, rare disease treatments, oncology, multiple sclerosis) ~45% of rev General Medicines (older established products, including diabetes drugs like Lantus and Toujeo) ~37% of rev Vaccines (through its Sanofi Pasteur subsidiary, the world's largest vaccine producer) ~18% of rev

INVESTMENT THESIS: Dupixent is a generational drug: It works across an unusually wide range of conditions and is still growing fast. Expected to reach ~€22 bn in sales by 2030.  No near-term patent issues: Sanofi has already gone over its near-term cliff (Aubagio), has nothing material expiring for the rest of this decade, and its big cliff — Dupixent — is a 2030s problem. That gives management roughly 5–7 years to build the next generation of the portfolio. FCF generation: By the time Dupixent starts to lose patent protection SAN will have generated ~60% of it’s current market cap in FCF Vaccines franchise: Vaccine division posted 13.5% growth in 2024, exceeding €8 bn in sales. Beyfortus, its RSV preventative antibody co-developed with AstraZeneca, rapidly achieved blockbuster status with €1.7 bn in reported sales in its first full launch cycle.  Clean balance sheet and shareholder returns: Net Debt/EBITDA below 1.0x. Executed a €5 bn share buyback program in 2025. Has raised its div for 30 consecutive years. Strategic focus and cost discipline: Targeting savings of up to €2 bn from 2024 to the end of 2025, of which most will be reallocated to fund innovation and growth drivers.  Rich pipeline: Robust pipeline of 82 clinical-stage projects as of mid-2025, including 30 in late-stage development or under regulatory review.

RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: The thesis hinges on whether the current pipeline can produce the next wave of multi-billion-dollar drugs before Dupixent's exclusivity erodes.  Dupixent concentration: At ~30% of total sales and growing, Sanofi is dangerously reliant on one drug. Dupixent's eventual exposure to biosimilar competition represents a revenue risk that cannot be offset by incremental growth alone. Regeneron and Sanofi hold patents expiring between 2027 and 2032 in key jurisdictions.  Pipeline setbacks: In 2025, Sanofi's pipeline suffered several setbacks: the anti-OX40L antibody amlitelimab failed a Phase 2 asthma trial, oral TNF inhibitor balinatunfib missed its midstage psoriasis study goal. This is partly why the board replaced the CEO. Vaccine policy headwinds: Faced rising pressure on vaccine business, espin the U.S. Vaccine sales will be "slightly negative" in 2026, partly due to US policy changes under Trump.  Currency risk: Sanofi reports in euros but earns a large chunk of revenue in USD Pricing pressure: Drug pricing reform in the US (via the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare negotiation provisions and potential executive actions) can compress the revenue Sanofi earns on its drugs in its most profitable market. R&D execution risk: Spending heavily on R&D. If pipeline doesn't deliver, earnings could be squeezed without the payoff of new blockbusters. Acquisition integration: The Blueprint Medicines acquisition alone cost up to $9.5bn Large acquisitions always carry the risk of overpaying or failing to integrate effectively. Management change: Recent CEO change raises some questions about leadership and execution.

RECOMMENDATION: MAITAIN 3.00% POSITION IN IDVZ 
 
Sanofi delivered a strong financial performance in Q2 2026, beating expectations on both the top and bottom lines, yet the stock 
suffered a sharp decline as investors weighed robust current results against long-term pipeline concerns and potential M&A risks. 
 
The core question for Sanofi is what happens when their key product Dupixent 15.7 bn euros in rev in 2025, up to 19.7 in 2026) in the 
2030s when they lose exclusivity, but there is a ton of FCF to be generated and deployed between now and then and opportunities to 
delay the loss of exclusivity. With a 5%+ div yield and ~10% FCF margins, the risk is to the upside, hence it’s slightly above average 
sizing. 
 
Q2 2026 Financial Performance Summary 
Sanofi reported significant year-over-year growth for the quarter ending June 30, 2026, driven by the continued dominance of its 
immunology blockbuster and successful new product launches. 
 
• 
Revenue: Net sales reached €11.6 bn, representing a 17.8% increase at constant exchange rates (CER) 
 
• 
Earnings: Business EPS rose 33.3% to €2.09, driven by strong operational leverage and cost discipline 
 
• 
Profitability: The business operating margin expanded by 3.8 percentage points to 28.4%, aided by a high business gross 
margin of 81.2% 
 
• 
Dupixent Performance: Sales for the flagship drug exceeded €5 bn in a single quarter for the first time, growing 37.6% 
 
• 
Product Launches: The pharma launch portfolio grew by over 60%, contributing €1.53 bn to total sales, led by products like 
ALTUVIIIO and Ayvakit 
 
• 
Vaccines: Sales in this segment declined 4.7% to €1.15 bn, due to high prior-year comparisons for influenza vaccines, despite 
strong growth in Beyfortus (+54.2%) 
 
Guidance and Strategic Outlook 
 
Following the strong H1 results, management upgraded their full-year outlook and adjusted long-term sales ambitions 
 
• 
2026 Guidance Upgrade: Sanofi now expects FY2026 sales growth of around 10% CER (up from high-single digits) and 
anticipates Business EPS to grow slightly faster than sales. 
 
• 
2030 Ambition Adjustments: The 2030 sales target for Dupixent was raised to ~€25 billion (from €22 billion). Conversely, 
the 2030 Vaccines outlook was lowered to ~€9 billion (from €10 billion) due to currency impacts and market dynamics.

• 
R&D Transformation: New CEO Belén Garijo López emphasized a "fast-track" R&D transformation focused on scientific 
rigor, leading to the discontinuation of several programs, including itepekimab and balinatunfib, to refocus resources. 
 
Broker Commentary 
Brokers largely acknowledged the quality of the operational beat but expressed caution regarding the company's long-term 
replacement strategy for Dupixent. 
 
• 
UBS noted the strong Q2 beat but lowered its price target to €78 (from €88), reflecting concerns that recent pipeline 
terminations exacerbate the "Replacement Power gap" needed to offset Dupixent's eventual loss of exclusivity starting in 
2031. 
• 
Kepler Cheuvreux highlighted that while the headline beat was substantial, a portion of the Dupixent performance was driven 
by a €200 million favorable gross-to-net adjustment in the US, suggesting the underlying beat was smaller than it appeared. 
• 
Deutsche Bank maintained a Buy rating but observed that market sentiment was dampened by the lack of "strategic 
fireworks" from the new CEO and a "drip-feed" of negative R&D news. 
• 
JPMorgan downgraded the credit rating to Neutral from Overweight, citing rising M&A risk as management indicated a 
willingness to pursue larger, late-stage or commercial-stage acquisitions to bolster the pipeline. 
• 
Bernstein Research argued that Sanofi remains the cheapest stock in the global large-cap pharma peer group, suggesting the 
current low valuation implies the market is not yet giving credit for the company's long-term cash generation potential. 
• 
ESN Partnerships noted that while Q2 figures were strong, the market feared profitability dilution from an aggressive stance 
on potentially expensive late-stage M&A. 
• 
Leerink Partners raised its 2026 and 2027 EPS estimates following the results, maintaining an Outperform rating and stating 
that shares are undervalued at approximately 8x 2027E EPS.

RECOMMENDATION: ~1% position in IDVZ 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Founded in 1972 by 5 former IBM engineers in Germany to integrate all aspects of a company's ops into one cohesive software package (Enterprise 
Resource Planning software). Separate, siloed systems for finance, accounting, HR, payroll, manufacturing, procurement, inventory, supply chain, sales, customer service didn't 
talk to each other well. SAP's ERP software helps them streamline all of those core business processes with a unified view. When a purchase order is raised in procurement, the 
finance system knows about it automatically. When inventory ships, the supply chain and accounting systems update in real time. SAP is the operational backbone of a large 
enterprise. SAP also sells software for CRM, HR management (SuccessFactors), procurement (Ariba), spend management (Concur), and increasingly AI-powered analytics and 
automation tools. SAP is used by businesses across every industry (manufacturers, retailers, utilities, financial services, healthcare). With a share of predictable revenue (cloud + 
support) of 86%, SAP's business model is considered highly resilient. 
Operating segments: Applications, Technology & Support (ATS): The core generating rev from cloud subscriptions and from the sale of software licenses and support offerings. 
Core Services: Professional consulting and premium support services to support SAP’s product portfolio. 
Rev streams: 
Cloud subscriptions: Fastest-growing, largest piece. Customers pay recurring subscription fees to use SAP software hosted in the cloud (SAP's own data centers or 
hyperscalers). Cloud service rev reached €5.96 bn in Q1 2026, +19% y-o-y, or 27% in constant f/x. Actively migrating large installed base of on-premise customers to the cloud.  
Software licenses & support: The legacy model: customers bought a perpetual license to run SAP software on their own servers, then paid annual maintenance/support fees 
(~20% of the license cost/yr). This is declining but still a cash cow. Rev from software licenses and support fell 12% y-o-y in Q1 2026 to €2.59 bn as customers migrate to cloud.  
Professional services / consulting: SAP implementations are famously complex and expensive, requiring substantial consulting work. SAP earns fees from helping customers 
implement, customize, and run their software, though much of this is also done by a large ecosystem of third-party partners (Accenture, Deloitte, IBM, etc.). 
 
INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Unmatched Switching Costs/Moat: SAP's systems are deeply embedded in corporate 
workflows, creating enormous switching costs and a durable moat, with 98%+ 
customer retention, which underpins predictable, resilient recurring revenues.  
Dominant Enterprise AI Platform potential: Already the system of record for half the 
world's GDP in business transactions. AI needs trusted, clean, auditable business data 
to be useful. SAP has that data. 
Cloud Migration: SAP is moving its ~300K+ global customers to the cloud. Cloud 
subscriptions generate more rev per customer and are recurring. Cloud revup 26% YoY 
and cloud ERP growing 33% YoY, while its cloud backlog has increased nearly 30% to 
€18 billion, providing clear visibility for future growth. 
Margin Expansion Ahead: Cloud software has better economics than on-premise 
software. As transition occurs margins are expanding, and FCF is rebounding. SAP 
generated €8.2 bn in free cash flow in 2025 and guided to ~€10 bn in 2026, while 
launching a €10 bn share repurchase program.  
AI as a New Monetization Layer: Uniquely positioned to embed AI agents that 
automate workflows across finance, supply chain, and HR. AI allows SAP to charge 
more per user over time, a true ARPU (average revenue per user) expansion story on top 
of an already growing customer base 
KEY RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: 
Cloud Execution Risk: SAP is migrating its massive installed base from legacy on-
premises software to cloud subscriptions. This is harder in practice than it sounds. If a 
meaningful percentage of the installed base delays migration or explores alternatives, 
the cloud revenue growth trajectory and the margin expansion story both slow down. 
AI Disruption: AI agents automate workflows that previously required human users 
changing the economics of per-seat software pricing. There is a structural AI disruption 
risk: could AI-native vendors eventually displace SAP from the core ERP layer entirely?  
Regulatory / Antitrust Risk: The European Commission launched an antitrust probe 
into SAP in Sep 2025, citing concerns about the company's practices in software 
support services. If the EU mandates greater flexibility to switch to 3rd-party providers 
it would erode the profitable maintenance rev stream.  
Competition Risk: Oracle is the most direct peer and is pushing its own cloud ERP 
suite, competing for the same migration deals. Workday has taken meaningful share in 
HR and finance software among large enterprises. Cloud-native startups are targeting 
mid-market and specific verticals with lighter, cheaper ERP alternatives 
Macro: In a recession enterprises may defer cloud migrations, reduce headcount 
(which affects seat-based licensing), or delay new SAP implementations.

Management/Board: Christian Klein is the CEO and Chairman of SAP's Executive Board. 
 
• Klein started working for SAP as a 15-year-old student, literally carrying heavy CRT monitors around the building as part of a school-based

companies. SAP was his partner company throughout his studies. 
• Klein held various positions across SAP including CFO of SAP SuccessFactors (2011–2012), Chief Controlling Officer (2014), and Chief 
Operating Officer (2016). He joined the Executive Board in 2018 as head of the Intelligent Enterprise Group, responsible for the development 
and delivery of SAP's core applications including S/4HANA and the Digital Supply Chain portfolio. 
• On October 11, 2019, he was named Co-CEO alongside Jennifer Morgan, before being appointed sole CEO on April 20, 2020, after Morgan 
departed in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. In May 2025, SAP's Supervisory Board extended Klein's contract to five years, running 
through April 2030, citing his instrumental role in the company's transformation journey. 
• Klein is credited with engineering the cloud transition, the single most important strategic shift in SAP's modern history, and delivering on the 
financial targets he set. In January 2024, he launched a company-wide restructuring program to enhance scalability and drive AI-focused 
efficiencies, setting targets of ~€10B non-IFRS operating profit and ~€8B free cash flow for 2025, both of which SAP hit.

IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE 
3 AI-driven downside scenarios (not mutually exclusive) 
 
Scenario 1: The Pricing Model Disruption (Most Likely Near-Term Pain) 
• 
SAP built its business on per-seat licensing which means you pay for every employee who touches the system.  
• 
AI agents don't have seats. As agentic AI automates workflows that humans previously performed (processing invoices, running procurement approvals, 
generating financial reports), the number of human users declines and SAP's traditional pricing model loses relevance. 
• 
SAP's response is to shift to consumption-based pricing charging for AI usage rather than users. 
• 
This transition creates a revenue recognition gap.  
• 
During the switchover period, SAP is losing seat revenue faster than it can replace it with consumption revenue.  
• 
Consumption revenue is harder to forecast than subscription revenue 
• 
SaaS predictability was rewarded with a premium multiple, which has compress if/when revenue becomes less predictable 
• 
CEO Klein has called this dynamic "short-term pain." The January 2026 selloff (stock down 15% in one day) was substantially driven by this concern, not by any 
deterioration in the underlying business. 
• 
If consumption revenue ramps slower than seat revenue declines, SAP could face a multi-year period of cloud revenue deceleration even as it invests heavily in 
AI infrastructure. Margins could compress. 
 
Scenario 2: SAP Gets Bypassed at the Agent Layer (Medium-Term Structural Risk) 
• 
AI agents need two things, 1) instructions (from an LLM) and 2) data (from enterprise systems).  
• 
SAP has the data but if third-party AI platforms build robust connectors into SAP's data layer, they become the interface through which enterprises interact with 
their operational data. SAP becomes the back-end database, while the AI layer, where the value and the relationship with the customer resides, belongs to 
someone else.\ 
• 
In this scenario: SAP retains its data and system-of-record role (the moat holds) but cannot monetize the AI workflow layer because customers are buying AI 
from Microsoft or Google 
• 
SAP's addressable market for AI revenue is effectively zero. It's a data plumbing provider rather than an AI platform 
• 
Revenue growth stalls as the cloud migration benefit is captured but the AI uplift never materializes 
• 
SAP's June 2026 API lockdown, blocking third-party AI agents from calling SAP APIs outside SAP-endorsed pathways, is its aggressive defensive move against 
this scenario. Whether this works or backfires is the critical strategic question. It could entrench Joule as the only viable agent interface. Or it could trigger 
customer revolt, regulatory intervention (on top of the already-active EU antitrust probe), and accelerate defection to alternative ERP vendors who take a more 
open approach. 
 
Scenario 3: General-Purpose AI Makes ERP Itself Redundant (Long-Term / Low Probability But Non-Zero) 
• 
ERP systems exist to enforce consistent business processes across a large organization ensuring that when a purchase order is raised in Munich, the finance 
system in New York knows about it with the right data structure, the right approval workflow, and the right accounting treatment. ERP is essentially a set of very 
complex rules applied consistently across millions of transactions. 
 
 
 
 
 
2026-03-09 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
7 
 
• 
If AI models become capable enough to understand business context, apply judgment, and handle exceptions intelligently, without requiring rigid, pre-
programmed process structures, then the need for the underlying ERP layer could theoretically diminish. 
• 
An AI agent that is smart enough might route, reconcile, and audit transactions without needing SAP's 7.3 million data fields and 120+ mission-critical process 
templates. 
• 
This is currently a low-probability scenario: 
o 
SAP's 50-year accumulated business process knowledge is genuinely hard to replicate 
o 
Regulatory compliance (financial reporting, tax, payroll law) requires auditability that current AI cannot reliably provide 
o 
Enterprise risk tolerance for AI errors in payroll and financial close is extremely low 
o 
Agentic AI accuracy at 85–90% is insufficient for monetary workflows 
• 
Why it is not zero probability 
o 
AI capabilities are advancing faster than predicted 
o 
New cloud-native companies are building AI-first from scratch, without the constraint of legacy ERP thinking 
o 
In 10–15 years, if foundation models can reliably handle compliance and auditability, the structural need for a separate ERP layer becomes genuinely 
questionable

The Dominant Platform Scenario  
Step 1: Cloud migration completes, Joule becomes ubiquitous 
• 
SAP's 300,000+ customer base migrates to cloud 
• 
Joule gets embedded into every application they use, finance, procurement, HR, supply chain, sales. 
• 
Because Joule is included in cloud subscriptions at no extra license cost (RISE with SAP includes Joule), customers adopt it by default rather than making an 
active purchasing decision. Adoption grew ninefold in 2025.  
• 
By the time the migration cycle is substantially complete (~2027–2028), Joule is simply the interface through which employees interact with enterprise software, 
the way Google became the default interface for information retrieval. 
 
Step 2: Business Data Cloud becomes the enterprise data foundation 
• 
SAP's Business Data Cloud, built in partnership with Databricks, connects SAP's transactional data with external data sources, non-SAP systems, third-party 
analytics tools, unstructured data. 
• 
In the dominant platform scenario, this becomes the canonical enterprise data layer, the place where AI agents go to get the ground truth about a business. 
• 
SAP's unique advantage here is not just the volume of data but its structure and business context.  
• 
SAP knows that a transaction in module FI-AP is an accounts payable posting, that it relates to vendor master record XYZ, that it requires two-way invoice 
matching, and that it has specific tax treatment under 17 different country-specific regulations.  
• 
No general-purpose AI model trained on internet data has this level of enterprise process knowledge. 
 
Step 3: Joule becomes the enterprise agent orchestration layer 
• 
Joule evolves from a copilot (answers questions, surfaces information) into the operating system for AI agents across the enterprise. 
• 
SAP's API lockdown (blocking third-party agents from calling SAP APIs directly) is the strategic move that forces this: if you want an AI agent to interact with SAP 
data, it must go through Joule. 
• 
Joule becomes the identity provider, the permission governor, the audit trail keeper, and the orchestration hub for all enterprise AI workflows. Microsoft Copilot, 
Salesforce Agentforce, and custom enterprise AI systems all become applications running within the Joule ecosystem rather than competitors to it. 
 
Step 4: Consumption pricing creates a new revenue flywheel 
• 
With Joule as the agent layer and Business Data Cloud as the data foundation, SAP moves to consumption-based pricing tied to AI usage. 
• 
Every automated procurement approval, every AI-generated financial report, every supply chain reoptimization event generates a billable consumption unit. 
• 
The addressable revenue per customer expands dramatically, instead of charging per human seat, SAP is charging per business outcome, of which there are 
orders of magnitude more than there are human users.  
• 
Klein himself has said that less than 40% of SAP's cloud revenue was already seat-based, the infrastructure for non-seat pricing already exists. 
• 
In the bull case, this consumption layer adds billions in incremental revenue on top of the existing subscription base without requiring a single new customer. 
 
Step 5: SAP's moat deepens rather than erodes 
• 
AI makes switching costs higher, not lower 
 
 
 
 
 
2026-03-09 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
9 
 
• 
The more a customer's AI agents are trained on SAP-structured data, the more SAP process logic is baked into their workflows, and the more Joule-specific 
integrations are deployed across their operations, the harder it becomes to leave. 
• 
AI locks customers in at the workflow and data layer, not just the application layer. SAP transforms from a system that is hard to replace because of technical 
migration costs into a system that is hard to replace because the intelligence layer of the enterprise is built on top of it.

lines.text: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Founded in 1972 by 5 former IBM engineers in Germany to integrate all aspects of a company's ops into one cohesive software package (Enterprise
Resource Planning software). Separate, siloed systems for finance, accounting, HR, payroll, manufacturing, procurement, inventory, supply chain, sales, customer service didn't
talk to each other well. SAP's ERP software helps them streamline all of those core business processes with a unified view. When a purchase order is raised in procurement, the
finance system knows about it automatically. When inventory ships, the supply chain and accounting systems update in real time. SAP is the operational backbone of a large
enterprise. SAP also sells software for CRM, HR management (SuccessFactors), procurement (Ariba), spend management (Concur), and increasingly AI-powered analytics and
automation tools. SAP is used by businesses across every industry (manufacturers, retailers, utilities, financial services, healthcare). With a share of predictable revenue (cloud +
support) of 86%, SAP's business model is considered highly resilient.
Operating segments: Applications, Technology & Support (ATS): The core generating rev from cloud subscriptions and from the sale of software licenses and support offerings.
Core Services: Professional consulting and premium support services to support SAP’s product portfolio.
Cloud subscriptions: Fastest-growing, largest piece. Customers pay recurring subscription fees to use SAP software hosted in the cloud (SAP's own data centers or
hyperscalers). Cloud service rev reached €5.96 bn in Q1 2026, +19% y-o-y, or 27% in constant f/x. Actively migrating large installed base of on-premise customers to the cloud.
Software licenses & support: The legacy model: customers bought a perpetual license to run SAP software on their own servers, then paid annual maintenance/support fees
(~20% of the license cost/yr). This is declining but still a cash cow. Rev from software licenses and support fell 12% y-o-y in Q1 2026 to €2.59 bn as customers migrate to cloud.
Professional services / consulting: SAP implementations are famously complex and expensive, requiring substantial consulting work. SAP earns fees from helping customers
implement, customize, and run their software, though much of this is also done by a large ecosystem of third-party partners (Accenture, Deloitte, IBM, etc.).
Unmatched Switching Costs/Moat: SAP's systems are deeply embedded in corporate
workflows, creating enormous switching costs and a durable moat, with 98%+
customer retention, which underpins predictable, resilient recurring revenues.
Dominant Enterprise AI Platform potential: Already the system of record for half the
world's GDP in business transactions. AI needs trusted, clean, auditable business data
to be useful. SAP has that data.
Cloud Migration: SAP is moving its ~300K+ global customers to the cloud. Cloud
subscriptions generate more rev per customer and are recurring. Cloud revup 26% YoY
and cloud ERP growing 33% YoY, while its cloud backlog has increased nearly 30% to
€18 billion, providing clear visibility for future growth.
Margin Expansion Ahead: Cloud software has better economics than on-premise
software. As transition occurs margins are expanding, and FCF is rebounding. SAP
generated €8.2 bn in free cash flow in 2025 and guided to ~€10 bn in 2026, while
launching a €10 bn share repurchase program.
AI as a New Monetization Layer: Uniquely positioned to embed AI agents that
lines.lead_prefix: AI as a New Monetization Layer:

lines.text: automate workflows across finance, supply chain, and HR. AI allows SAP to charge
more per user over time, a true ARPU (average revenue per user) expansion story on top
of an already growing customer base
Cloud Execution Risk: SAP is migrating its massive installed base from legacy on-
premises software to cloud subscriptions. This is harder in practice than it sounds. If a
meaningful percentage of the installed base delays migration or explores alternatives,
the cloud revenue growth trajectory and the margin expansion story both slow down.
AI Disruption: AI agents automate workflows that previously required human users
changing the economics of per-seat software pricing. There is a structural AI disruption
risk: could AI-native vendors eventually displace SAP from the core ERP layer entirely?
Regulatory / Antitrust Risk: The European Commission launched an antitrust probe
into SAP in Sep 2025, citing concerns about the company's practices in software
support services. If the EU mandates greater flexibility to switch to 3rd-party providers
it would erode the profitable maintenance rev stream.
Competition Risk: Oracle is the most direct peer and is pushing its own cloud ERP
suite, competing for the same migration deals. Workday has taken meaningful share in
HR and finance software among large enterprises. Cloud-native startups are targeting
mid-market and specific verticals with lighter, cheaper ERP alternatives
Macro: In a recession enterprises may defer cloud migrations, reduce headcount
(which affects seat-based licensing), or delay new SAP implementations.
With a share of predictable revenue (cloud + support) of 86%, SAP's business model is highly resilient in uncertain times. This is particularly attractive in volatile macro environments
— enterprise customers don't cancel their ERP subscriptions when the economy softens; the software is too mission-critical. sec
SAP's net cash position and steadily growing dividend further strengthen its financial profile. The €10 bn buyback program announced for 2026 is meaningful at its market cap — it
signals management confidence and directly supports per-share earnings growth.
German Governance Discount: SAP is structured under German corporate law, with a two-tier board system (management board + supervisory board), which limits the speed and
directness of shareholder influence compared to US companies.
FX / Currency Risk: SAP reports in euros but generates a truly global revenue base — the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and EMEA each contribute meaningfully.
Management/Board: Christian Klein is the CEO and Chairman of SAP's Executive Board.
•Klein started working for SAP as a 15-year-old student, literally carrying heavy CRT monitors around the building as part of a school-based
internship, and became sole CEO in 2020 at only 39 years of age.
•He holds a diploma in International Business Administration from the Baden-Württemberg Cooperative State University (DHBW) in Mannheim,
Germany, an institution known for its dual education system that combines academic study with practical work experience in partner
companies. SAP was his partner company throughout his studies.
•Klein held various positions across SAP including CFO of SAP SuccessFactors (2011–2012), Chief Controlling Officer (2014), and Chief
Operating Officer (2016). He joined the Executive Board in 2018 as head of the Intelligent Enterprise Group, responsible for the development
and delivery of SAP's core applications including S/4HANA and the Digital Supply Chain portfolio.
•On October 11, 2019, he was named Co-CEO alongside Jennifer Morgan, before being appointed sole CEO on April 20, 2020, after Morgan
departed in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. In May 2025, SAP's Supervisory Board extended Klein's contract to five years, running
through April 2030, citing his instrumental role in the company's transformation journey.
•Klein is credited with engineering the cloud transition, the single most important strategic shift in SAP's modern history, and delivering on the
financial targets he set. In January 2024, he launched a company-wide restructuring program to enhance scalability and drive AI-focused
efficiencies, setting targets of ~€10B non-IFRS operating profit and ~€8B free cash flow for 2025, both of which SAP hit.
•His five-point growth plan for 2026, articulated on the Q4 2025 earnings call, is centered on: converting on-premise customers to cloud (at a 2–
3x revenue multiplier), expanding within existing customers via cross-selling across the full suite, growing the mid-market, and monetizing
Business AI and the Business Data Cloud. He noted that in Q4 2025 alone, almost two-thirds of deals exceeding €1M involved four or more
•Not everyone is a fan. Some industry observers have argued that Klein and the SAP Executive Board lack compelling AI and cloud storytelling,
that despite solid financials, SAP struggles to articulate an empathetic, forward-looking vision that resonates with investors and customers the
way rival executives do. This critique has some merit: SAP's 2026 stock selloff happened not because the business deteriorated, but partly
because Klein failed to paint a sufficiently exciting forward picture during earnings, leading to multiple compression despite continued
•Klein is a credible, technically grounded CEO with deep institutional knowledge. Arguably no one alive understands the mechanics of SAP
better. His execution track record on the cloud transition is strong, and the board clearly has confidence in him.
Scenario 1: The Pricing Model Disruption (Most Likely Near-Term Pain)
lines.lead_prefix: Scenario 1: The Pricing Model Disruption (Most Likely Near-Term Pain)

lines.text: SAP built its business on per-seat licensing which means you pay for every employee who touches the system.
AI agents don't have seats. As agentic AI automates workflows that humans previously performed (processing invoices, running procurement approvals,
generating financial reports), the number of human users declines and SAP's traditional pricing model loses relevance.
SAP's response is to shift to consumption-based pricing charging for AI usage rather than users.
This transition creates a revenue recognition gap.
During the switchover period, SAP is losing seat revenue faster than it can replace it with consumption revenue.
Consumption revenue is harder to forecast than subscription revenue
SaaS predictability was rewarded with a premium multiple, which has compress if/when revenue becomes less predictable
CEO Klein has called this dynamic "short-term pain." The January 2026 selloff (stock down 15% in one day) was substantially driven by this concern, not by any
If consumption revenue ramps slower than seat revenue declines, SAP could face a multi-year period of cloud revenue deceleration even as it invests heavily in
Scenario 2: SAP Gets Bypassed at the Agent Layer (Medium-Term Structural Risk)
lines.lead_prefix: Scenario 2: SAP Gets Bypassed at the Agent Layer (Medium-Term Structural Risk)

lines.text: AI agents need two things, 1) instructions (from an LLM) and 2) data (from enterprise systems).
SAP has the data but if third-party AI platforms build robust connectors into SAP's data layer, they become the interface through which enterprises interact with
their operational data. SAP becomes the back-end database, while the AI layer, where the value and the relationship with the customer resides, belongs to
In this scenario: SAP retains its data and system-of-record role (the moat holds) but cannot monetize the AI workflow layer because customers are buying AI
SAP's addressable market for AI revenue is effectively zero. It's a data plumbing provider rather than an AI platform
Revenue growth stalls as the cloud migration benefit is captured but the AI uplift never materializes
SAP's June 2026 API lockdown, blocking third-party AI agents from calling SAP APIs outside SAP-endorsed pathways, is its aggressive defensive move against
this scenario. Whether this works or backfires is the critical strategic question. It could entrench Joule as the only viable agent interface. Or it could trigger
customer revolt, regulatory intervention (on top of the already-active EU antitrust probe), and accelerate defection to alternative ERP vendors who take a more
Scenario 3: General-Purpose AI Makes ERP Itself Redundant (Long-Term / Low Probability But Non-Zero)
lines.lead_prefix: Scenario 3: General-Purpose AI Makes ERP Itself Redundant (Long-Term / Low Probability But Non-Zero)

lines.text: ERP systems exist to enforce consistent business processes across a large organization ensuring that when a purchase order is raised in Munich, the finance
system in New York knows about it with the right data structure, the right approval workflow, and the right accounting treatment. ERP is essentially a set of very
complex rules applied consistently across millions of transactions.
If AI models become capable enough to understand business context, apply judgment, and handle exceptions intelligently, without requiring rigid, pre-
programmed process structures, then the need for the underlying ERP layer could theoretically diminish.
An AI agent that is smart enough might route, reconcile, and audit transactions without needing SAP's 7.3 million data fields and 120+ mission-critical process
This is currently a low-probability scenario:
SAP's 50-year accumulated business process knowledge is genuinely hard to replicate
Regulatory compliance (financial reporting, tax, payroll law) requires auditability that current AI cannot reliably provide
Enterprise risk tolerance for AI errors in payroll and financial close is extremely low
Agentic AI accuracy at 85–90% is insufficient for monetary workflows
Why it is not zero probability
AI capabilities are advancing faster than predicted
New cloud-native companies are building AI-first from scratch, without the constraint of legacy ERP thinking
In 10–15 years, if foundation models can reliably handle compliance and auditability, the structural need for a separate ERP layer becomes genuinely
Step 1: Cloud migration completes, Joule becomes ubiquitous
lines.lead_prefix: Step 1: Cloud migration completes, Joule becomes ubiquitous

lines.text: SAP's 300,000+ customer base migrates to cloud
Joule gets embedded into every application they use, finance, procurement, HR, supply chain, sales.
Because Joule is included in cloud subscriptions at no extra license cost (RISE with SAP includes Joule), customers adopt it by default rather than making an
active purchasing decision. Adoption grew ninefold in 2025.
By the time the migration cycle is substantially complete (~2027–2028), Joule is simply the interface through which employees interact with enterprise software,
the way Google became the default interface for information retrieval.
Step 2: Business Data Cloud becomes the enterprise data foundation
lines.lead_prefix: Step 2: Business Data Cloud becomes the enterprise data foundation

lines.text: SAP's Business Data Cloud, built in partnership with Databricks, connects SAP's transactional data with external data sources, non-SAP systems, third-party
In the dominant platform scenario, this becomes the canonical enterprise data layer, the place where AI agents go to get the ground truth about a business.
SAP's unique advantage here is not just the volume of data but its structure and business context.
SAP knows that a transaction in module FI-AP is an accounts payable posting, that it relates to vendor master record XYZ, that it requires two-way invoice
matching, and that it has specific tax treatment under 17 different country-specific regulations.
No general-purpose AI model trained on internet data has this level of enterprise process knowledge.
Step 3: Joule becomes the enterprise agent orchestration layer
lines.lead_prefix: Step 3: Joule becomes the enterprise agent orchestration layer

lines.text: Joule evolves from a copilot (answers questions, surfaces information) into the operating system for AI agents across the enterprise.
SAP's API lockdown (blocking third-party agents from calling SAP APIs directly) is the strategic move that forces this: if you want an AI agent to interact with SAP
data, it must go through Joule.
Joule becomes the identity provider, the permission governor, the audit trail keeper, and the orchestration hub for all enterprise AI workflows. Microsoft Copilot,
Salesforce Agentforce, and custom enterprise AI systems all become applications running within the Joule ecosystem rather than competitors to it.
Step 4: Consumption pricing creates a new revenue flywheel
lines.lead_prefix: Step 4: Consumption pricing creates a new revenue flywheel

lines.text: With Joule as the agent layer and Business Data Cloud as the data foundation, SAP moves to consumption-based pricing tied to AI usage.
Every automated procurement approval, every AI-generated financial report, every supply chain reoptimization event generates a billable consumption unit.
The addressable revenue per customer expands dramatically, instead of charging per human seat, SAP is charging per business outcome, of which there are
orders of magnitude more than there are human users.
Klein himself has said that less than 40% of SAP's cloud revenue was already seat-based, the infrastructure for non-seat pricing already exists.
In the bull case, this consumption layer adds billions in incremental revenue on top of the existing subscription base without requiring a single new customer.
Step 5: SAP's moat deepens rather than erodes
lines.lead_prefix: Step 5: SAP's moat deepens rather than erodes

lines.text: AI makes switching costs higher, not lower
The more a customer's AI agents are trained on SAP-structured data, the more SAP process logic is baked into their workflows, and the more Joule-specific
integrations are deployed across their operations, the harder it becomes to leave.
AI locks customers in at the workflow and data layer, not just the application layer. SAP transforms from a system that is hard to replace because of technical
migration costs into a system that is hard to replace because the intelligence layer of the enterprise is built on top of it.

RECOMMENDATION: PASS risk reward doesn’t justify current valuation 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: SHOP provides the infrastructure to run a retail business. A merchant, anyone from a garage entrepreneur to a large company, pays a monthly 
subscription for an online storefront, then uses Shopify's tools to manage inventory, process payments, ship orders, borrow working capital, run marketing, and sell offline through 
point-of-sale hardware. The pitch is "everything you need to sell, in one system." Think of SHOP as an arms dealer to independent commerce vs AMZN which is a marketplace 
that competes with its own sellers.  
SHOP hosts ~2.86mm live storefronts across 175+ countries and powers more than 14% of all US e-commerce by GMV (gross merchandise volume). 
The majority of rev is now GMV-linked and consumer-spending-sensitive, not recurring SaaS.  
Two segments: 
Subscription Solutions (~24% of FY2025 rev): Recurring monthly fees 
Merchant Solutions (~76%): Take-rate rev that scales with merchant sales: payment processing, currency conversion, and other merchant services. Shopify Payments is the 
engine, plus shipping, Shopify Capital lending, and installments.  
Geography by merchant base: United States 44%, EMEA 31%, Asia Pacific/Australia/China 16%, with the remainder in Canada and Latin America. US is largest market. Europe 
is the fastest-growing (+49% in Q3 2025 and reached 21% of overall revenue, up from under 18% two years earlier).  
 
INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Category-defining platform with structural share gains: ~14% of US e-commerce 
and growing, with e-commerce itself still gaining share of retail. Four consecutive 
quarters of 30%+ revenue and GMV growth at $11B+ scale 
Take-rate expansion flywheel: attach rates on Payments, Capital, installments, tax, 
and audiences keep rising, so revenue grows faster than GMV. Shop Pay GMV surged 
62% YoY in Q4 2025 and Merchant Solutions grew 35%. 
Moving upmarket successfully: Plus is ~34% of MRR; enterprise wins (Carrier, Meta, 
JB Hi-Fi) validate the platform beyond SMB, lengthening the runway and reducing 
churn-prone small-merchant mix. 
Best-positioned platform for agentic commerce: Shopify co-developed the Universal 
Commerce Protocol with Google, now open to any developer, and management claims 
it's the only platform powering selling inside ChatGPT, Copilot, and Google from one 
system of record.  
Operating leverage is real: opex as a % of rev fell from 45% in 2023 to 37% in 2025 
even while investing in AI, international, and enterprise sales; FCF margins in the mid-
to-high teens. 
International optionality: Europe compounding ~50%; offline/POS and B2B are large, 
earlier-stage vectors. 
Valuation reset: down ~30%+ from the October 2025 high while fundamentals 
accelerated, the multiple compressed, not the business. 
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: 
Opex re-acceleration: the Q1 2026 selloff was driven by operating expense guidance 
coming in above expectations, not revenue concerns. The margin-expansion narrative is 
the thing bulls paid for; management spending it away on AI/enterprise investment is 
the live bear case. 
Consumer/macro sensitivity: ~76% of rev is GMV-linked. A discretionary spending 
downturn hits Shopify harder than a pure SaaS company. Tariff regimes also directly 
hurt its cross-border and dropshipping merchant base. 
AI disintermediation (two-sided): If AI agents commoditize storefronts or route 
discovery through a handful of chat platforms, brand-owned stores could lose traffic; 
also "vibe-coded" custom storefronts lower the barrier to leaving. 
Credit risk scaling quietly: the loans and merchant cash advance balance grew from 
$1.22B to $1.78B in 2025 (+46%) with Q4 transaction and loan losses of $114M, still 
50% higher year-over-year. SMB lending books look great until they don't.  
Key-man and governance: Founder super-voting share; Lütke's ~40% voting control 
means minority shareholders are along for the ride; his outspokenness (politics, AI 
mandates) is a periodic headline risk. 
Competition: Amazon (Buy with Prime), Commerce.com/BigCommerce at the low 
end, Salesforce at the high end, and Amazon and MercadoLibre continuing to take 
commerce share in developing and emerging markets.

MANAGEMENT 
• Tobi Lütke, co-founder and CEO since inception.  
• German-Canadian, born 1980, a programmer who emigrated from Germany, tried to sell snowboards online in 2004, found the e-commerce 
software terrible, and built his own on Ruby on Rails (he was part of the core Rails framework team and created open-source libraries like 
Active Merchant).  
• No university degree; German programming apprenticeship.  
• He's a genuine technologist-founder, still writes code, and holds a special "founder share" (approved by shareholders in 2022) giving him 
~40% voting power 
• Harley Finkelstein, the President, is the public commercial face. 
• Notably, Lütke also races in the IMSA SportsCar Championship in LMP2, which tells you something about his risk appetite.  
• Jeff Hoffmeister (ex-Morgan Stanley banker) is CFO.

Opex re-acceleration: the Q1 2026 selloff was driven by operating expense guidance
coming in above expectations, not revenue concerns. The margin-expansion narrative is
the thing bulls paid for; management spending it away on AI/enterprise investment is
Consumer/macro sensitivity: ~76% of rev is GMV-linked. A discretionary spending
downturn hits Shopify harder than a pure SaaS company. Tariff regimes also directly
hurt its cross-border and dropshipping merchant base.
AI disintermediation (two-sided): If AI agents commoditize storefronts or route
discovery through a handful of chat platforms, brand-owned stores could lose traffic;
also "vibe-coded" custom storefronts lower the barrier to leaving.
Credit risk scaling quietly: the loans and merchant cash advance balance grew from
$1.22B to $1.78B in 2025 (+46%) with Q4 transaction and loan losses of $114M, still
50% higher year-over-year. SMB lending books look great until they don't.
Key-man and governance: Founder super-voting share; Lütke's ~40% voting control
means minority shareholders are along for the ride; his outspokenness (politics, AI
mandates) is a periodic headline risk.
Competition: Amazon (Buy with Prime), Commerce.com/BigCommerce at the low
end, Salesforce at the high end, and Amazon and MercadoLibre continuing to take
commerce share in developing and emerging markets.
•Tobi Lütke, co-founder and CEO since inception.
•German-Canadian, born 1980, a programmer who emigrated from Germany, tried to sell snowboards online in 2004, found the e-commerce
software terrible, and built his own on Ruby on Rails (he was part of the core Rails framework team and created open-source libraries like
•He's a genuine technologist-founder, still writes code, and holds a special "founder share" (approved by shareholders in 2022) giving him
•Harley Finkelstein, the President, is the public commercial face.
•Notably, Lütke also races in the IMSA SportsCar Championship in LMP2, which tells you something about his risk appetite.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN POSITION 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Spotify is an audio-streaming platform that operates a two-sided network, with artists on one side and fans on the other. Their 750mn+ monthly 
active users (MAUs) have access to 100mn+ tracks, 7mn+ podcasts and 500,000+ audiobooks in more than 180 markets worldwide. As the most popular global audio 
streaming service, Spotify monetizes through both subscriptions and advertising. The ad-supported service serves as a funnel, driving a significant portion of total gross added 
premium subscribers. Their 290mn paid subscribers represent 39% of total MAUs. Subscriber plans range from $6.99/month for students to $21.99/month for premium family. 
Premium subscriptions generate 90% of sales (34% gross margin) with ad-supported sales representing 10% of revenues (18% gross margin). The business is geographically 
diversified, with 38% of total sales from the US and 62% OUS. 
 
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect mid-teens sales growth driven by growth in new users, raising price on existing users, and creating new revenue 
streams in verticals like podcasts and audiobooks (ads and monetization of other services). With margin expansion, EPS growth should be mid- to high-teens. 
INVESTMENT THESIS: After turning GAAP profitable in 2024, underlying fundamentals 
are strong with sales growing mid- to high-teens annually, gross margin improving to 
32%, operating margin improving to 13%, FCF margin reaching 17% (they’ve been FCF 
positive for a decade) and net cash on the balance sheet. 
 
Attractive industry trends, large and growing market opportunity: Radio remains a 
large medium for audio consumption and the shift to streaming is still early days. As 
disposable incomes continue to rise, particularly in emerging markets, streaming 
subscription services become more affordable/attainable. Spotify has 751mn MAUs 
and they target 1bn by 2030 (6% annual growth). Adjusting for limitations like internet 
connectivity and payment enabled smartphones in certain markets, the addressable 
footprint is 3bn+. They target 1bn paid subscribers beyond 2030 for the industry 
collectively, and they should continue to take their fair share. €5 monthly average 
revenue per user (ARPU) equates to €60bn TAM on the subscription side. Today, audio 
captures a disproportionately small share of ad spend relative to time spent, and that 
gap should close over time. Ad opportunity is estimated at an additional $10-15bn.  
 
Strong competitive positioning and durable moat: Spotify is the largest audio 
streaming platform by a wide margin, with roughly 1/3 share of music subscribers 
globally. Tencent Music is second, with just under half the subscriber base of Spotify. 
Apple is estimated to have low-teens share, and Amazon and YouTube are estimated 
to have just under 10% share each. Spotify benefits from strong network effects. A 
more engaged community of listeners creates more demand and opportunity for 
artists and podcasters to make a living in their creative work, and the more content 
created, the more there is for users to discover (the virtuous cycle). They also benefit 
from huge scale advantages (massive amounts of data enhances discovery, 
personalization and demand creation), ubiquity, global presence and a strong brand.  
RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Pre-mortem: A handful of labels own the supply (music catalog), meaning they have 
perpetual leverage and Spotify's margins are structurally capped. If the opportunity in 
new verticals and ads never materialize, and because growth in emerging markets is 
lower quality (lower ARPU, higher churn), Spotify is likely to disappoint on growth and 
profitability targets. Any deterioration in subscriber growth or failure to deliver on 
margin expansion will lead to stock de-rating (price risk).  
 
Execution risk: Spotify operates in a highly competitive market with well-resourced 
peers. In a world where one of the only scarce resources is attention, all the big media 
platforms are competitors. Consumers spend time and attention not just on audio, 
but also video, gaming and social media. Maintaining (ideally growing) engagement 
and time spent on the platform, and minimizing churn, is critical given the arguably 
minimal switching costs on both sides of the network (listeners and creators).  
 
Artificial intelligence (AI) risk: This should be a sustaining technology for Spotify since 
they already have the right business model in place (subscriptions and ads), but 
discovery could migrate to other AI interfaces over time. 
 
Ownership: Co-founder Daniel Ek owns 14% of shares outstanding and 29% of the 
voting rights (he exercises voting power over 8% of shares held by Tencent). Co-
founder Martin Lorentzon owns 9% of shares outstanding and 41% of the voting 
rights. Largest institutional investor is Baillie Gifford (4%). 
 
 
 
 
 
3_12_2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
 
 
Management and capital allocation: Co-founder Daniel Ek was instrumental in reviving the global music industry, shifting from a transaction-based model to access-based 
through mobile and on-demand. He transitioned from CEO to Chairman at the end of 2025. New co-CEOs Gustav Soderstrom (product and tech expertise) and Alex Norstrom 
(business and commercial expertise) have worked closely with Ek for more than a decade. Capital allocation priorities include reinvesting back into the business for future 
growth, mostly through internal R&D but also through acquisitions and returning excess capital to shareholders through opportunistic shares repurchases. Since 2013, Spotify 
has spent north of €9bn in R&D on a cumulative basis. They’ve spent just over €1bn in acquisitions over the same time frame, mostly strategic both for content (to drive listeners 
to the platform) and technology (to build infrastructure for creators and advertisers). Share buybacks have not been enough to offset dilution from stock-based compensation 
but repurchases have accelerated recently (Spotify repurchased $510mn in 2025 with total remaining authorization $1.4bn).

lines.text: Upside assumptions: mid-teens sales growth, operating margin
expansion to 20%, elimination of tax benefit in three years, no
Base assumptions: low-teens sales growth, operating margin
expansion to 17%, elimination of tax benefit in three years, no
operating margin flat, accelerated elimination of tax benefit, no
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Spotify is an audio-streaming platform that operates a two-sided network, with artists on one side and fans on the other. Their 750mn+ monthly
active users (MAUs) have access to 100mn+ tracks, 7mn+ podcasts and 500,000+ audiobooks in more than 180 markets worldwide. As the most popular global audio
streaming service, Spotify monetizes through both subscriptions and advertising. The ad-supported service serves as a funnel, driving a significant portion of total gross added
premium subscribers. Their 290mn paid subscribers represent 39% of total MAUs. Subscriber plans range from $6.99/month for students to $21.99/month for premium family.
Premium subscriptions generate 90% of sales (34% gross margin) with ad-supported sales representing 10% of revenues (18% gross margin). The business is geographically
diversified, with 38% of total sales from the US and 62% OUS.
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect mid-teens sales growth driven by growth in new users, raising price on existing users, and creating new revenue
lines.lead_prefix: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return

lines.text: streams in verticals like podcasts and audiobooks (ads and monetization of other services). With margin expansion, EPS growth should be mid- to high-teens.
INVESTMENT THESIS: After turning GAAP profitable in 2024, underlying fundamentals
are strong with sales growing mid- to high-teens annually, gross margin improving to
32%, operating margin improving to 13%, FCF margin reaching 17% (they’ve been FCF
positive for a decade) and net cash on the balance sheet.
Attractive industry trends, large and growing market opportunity: Radio remains a
lines.lead_prefix: Attractive industry trends, large and growing market opportunity

lines.text: large medium for audio consumption and the shift to streaming is still early days. As
disposable incomes continue to rise, particularly in emerging markets, streaming
subscription services become more affordable/attainable. Spotify has 751mn MAUs
and they target 1bn by 2030 (6% annual growth). Adjusting for limitations like internet
connectivity and payment enabled smartphones in certain markets, the addressable
footprint is 3bn+. They target 1bn paid subscribers beyond 2030 for the industry
collectively, and they should continue to take their fair share. €5 monthly average
revenue per user (ARPU) equates to €60bn TAM on the subscription side. Today, audio
captures a disproportionately small share of ad spend relative to time spent, and that
gap should close over time. Ad opportunity is estimated at an additional $10-15bn.
Strong competitive positioning and durable moat: Spotify is the largest audio
lines.lead_prefix: Strong competitive positioning and durable moat:

lines.text: streaming platform by a wide margin, with roughly 1/3 share of music subscribers
globally. Tencent Music is second, with just under half the subscriber base of Spotify.
Apple is estimated to have low-teens share, and Amazon and YouTube are estimated
to have just under 10% share each.Spotify benefits from strong network effects. A
more engaged community of listeners creates more demand and opportunity for
artists and podcasters to make a living in their creative work, and the more content
created, the more there is for users to discover (the virtuous cycle). They also benefit
from huge scale advantages (massive amounts of data enhances discovery,
personalization and demand creation), ubiquity, global presence and a strong brand.
Pre-mortem: A handful of labels own the supply (music catalog), meaning they have
perpetual leverage and Spotify's margins are structurally capped. If the opportunity in
new verticals and ads never materialize, and because growth in emerging markets is
lower quality (lower ARPU, higher churn), Spotify is likely to disappoint on growth and
profitability targets. Any deterioration in subscriber growth or failure to deliver on
margin expansion will lead to stock de-rating (price risk).
Execution risk: Spotify operates in a highly competitive market with well-resourced
peers. In a world where one of the only scarce resources is attention, all the big media
platforms are competitors. Consumers spend time and attention not just on audio,
but also video, gaming and social media. Maintaining (ideally growing) engagement
and time spent on the platform, and minimizing churn, is critical given the arguably
minimal switching costs on both sides of the network (listeners and creators).
Artificial intelligence (AI) risk: This should be a sustaining technology for Spotify since
they already have the right business model in place (subscriptions and ads), but
discovery could migrate to other AI interfaces over time.
Ownership: Co-founder Daniel Ek owns 14% of shares outstanding and 29% of the
voting rights (he exercises voting power over 8% of shares held by Tencent). Co-
founder Martin Lorentzon owns 9% of shares outstanding and 41% of the voting
rights. Largest institutional investor is Baillie Gifford (4%).
Management and capital allocation: Co-founder Daniel Ek was instrumental in reviving the global music industry, shifting from a transaction-based model to access-based
through mobile and on-demand. He transitioned from CEO to Chairman at the end of 2025. New co-CEOs Gustav Soderstrom (product and tech expertise) and Alex Norstrom
(business and commercial expertise) have worked closely with Ek for more than a decade. Capital allocation priorities include reinvesting back into the business for future
growth, mostly through internal R&D but also through acquisitions and returning excess capital to shareholders through opportunistic shares repurchases. Since 2013, Spotify

Spotify Technology SA (SPOT-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
 
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE 
Spotify delivered an accelerating top line and record profitability in Q2 2026, crossing 300mn Premium subscribers for the first time 
(versus 299mn guide), even as EPS and MAU net adds fell modestly short of Street expectations and guidance. The EPS miss and 
softer Q3 guidance on MAUs and operating income drove shares down 1.7% on the print date. Record profitability and a major 
subscriber milestone, though, appears to have shifted the narrative from a pure user-growth story to one of disciplined monetization 
and operational efficiency. Management's deliberate reset of emerging market growth levers is largely viewed as a strategic pivot 
toward higher-quality, convertible users rather than a sign of market saturation. Scaling of new verticals like Audiobooks+ and the 
deployment of AI-driven efficiency tools are now emerging as primary catalysts for the next phase of margin expansion. 
 
Headline results 
- 
Positive: Crossed 300mn Premium subscribers for the first time, with net adds of 7mn beating the 6mn guide. Gross margin hit 
an all-time high of 33.4%, up ~193 bps year-over-year, driven by Premium mix, marketing efficiency and cost discipline. Returned 
to a sizeable GAAP net profit of €545mn, reversing an €86mn net loss in the prior-year quarter. Operating income of €655mn 
(+61% YoY) and free cash flow of €797mn both represented record levels for a second quarter, lifting cash to €9.4bn. Premium 
ARPU rose 7.4% YoY on prior price increases, with management noting stable churn, a sign of continued pricing power. 
- 
Negative: EPS of $2.61 missed consensus of $2.76 by roughly 5%, and revenue landed marginally below expectations despite the 
YoY acceleration. MAU net adds of 16mn came in slightly below the 17mn guide, the first sign of the deliberate deceleration to 
come. Ad-supported sales growth of just 1% reported (3% cc) remained the weakest line item in the P&L, with direct sales 
advertising continuing to decline. Guidance for Q3 pointed to a further slowdown in user growth and profit that undershot Wall 
Street's expectations, which was the primary driver of the post-earnings share-price decline.  
 
Geographic highlights 
- 
N. America and Rest of World outperformed on Premium subscriber growth in Q2, helping drive the beat on net adds relative to 
the guide. Developed markets showed early signs of slowing expansion given high penetration, a dynamic management called 
out as a contributor to more conservative forward MAU guidance. Emerging markets (India, Indonesia) remain the primary 
source of MAU growth, but management is now deliberately introducing friction (reduced ad load, pared-back free-tier features) 
to shift the mix toward monetization rather than pure user acquisition.

Segment highlights 
- 
Premium revenue +15% YoY (+16% cc) to €4.33bn, with subscriber growth of 9% and ARPU growth of 7.4% both contributing. 
Automated/programmatic ad channels grew to ~40% of ad revenue, up from ~30% in the prior quarter, partially offsetting 
continued softness in direct sales, which management said is now “stabilizing.” Management guided that advertising should 
inflect toward double-digit growth in 2H 2026 as programmatic mix continues to build. 
- 
New verticals/bets: Audiobooks+ (the a-la-carte/add-on audiobook offering) surpassed $100mn in annualized recurring revenue, 
pointed to as validation of a “power law” monetization strategy where a subset of highly engaged users pay for incremental 
features. Early traction on reserved concert ticketing (launched with Live Nation in the US in June). ~100,000 tickets reserved to 
date, with some tour allocations selling out and Live Nation upsizing inventory mid-run. Confirmed AI licensing arrangements 
with UMG and Merlin (representing ~30,000 independent labels) to support AI-assisted covers/remix products, while noting 
Spotify does not need every major label on board before launching (drawing a parallel to their own early catalog gaps). 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Elevated near-term operating expense – management flagged “temporarily elevated” op ex in Q2 and Q3 from marketing and AI-
related investment, totaling €200mn of incremental spend for the full year, expected to moderate in Q4 as marketing spend 
concentrates earlier in the year). 
- 
Slowing growth in mature markets – N. America and Europe are highly penetrated, limiting the runway for MAU growth from 
those regions going forward. 
- 
Deliberate MAU friction in emerging markets – reduced ad load and free-tier features in markets like India and Indonesia will 
weigh on headline user growth even as it supports monetization. 
- 
Persistently weak advertising growth – at just 1% reported growth, the ad-supported segment continues to lag the core 
subscription business, with a hoped-for 2H inflection not yet visible in the numbers.

Why we own 
Spotify is an audio-streaming platform that operates a two-sided network, with artists on one side and fans on the other. Their nearly 
800mn monthly active users (MAUs), including 300mn+ paid subscribers, have access to 100mn+ tracks, 7mn+ podcasts and 
700,000+ audiobooks in more than 180 markets worldwide. Spotify monetizes through subscriptions and advertising, with the ad-
supported service serving as a funnel, driving a significant portion of total gross added premium subscribers. Management targets 
1bn users by 2030 (and 1bn paid subscribers over a longer time horizon) with a total addressable footprint of 3bn+. In dollars, TAM is 
in the tens (or even hundreds) of billions. As the most popular global audio streaming service, with scale advantages and strong 
network effects, Spotify benefits from the continued shift in audio consumption to streaming, as well as the shift in ad dollars to 
digital platforms with better returns on investment than traditional media. Audio captures a disproportionately small share of ad 
spend relative to time spent, that gap should close over time, and Spotify is well-positioned to capitalize on the opportunity. It should 
remain a core position.

paragraphs.text: SINGAPORE TELECOMMUNICATIONS [LOCAL: ST SP / ADR] Research Note
RECOMMENDATION:
Interesting exposure for IDVZ. Exposure to Asia telecom industry including India which is hard to buy directly.

COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Asia's largest telecom conglomerate, headquartered in Singapore and listed on the Singapore Exchange. With roots stretching back to Singapore's first telephone exchange in 1879, Singtel today operates as a diversified communications and digital infrastructure group spanning consumer connectivity, enterprise IT services, and data centers across Asia-Pacific and beyond. In Singapore, Singtel controls ~82% of the fixed-line market, 47% of mobile, and 43% of broadband. In Australia, it wholly owns Optus, Australia’s 2nd-largest mobile and broadband provider. Combined these are the backbone of the group's direct rev, generating around S$10–11bn annually.

Singtel also has strategic stakes in some of Asia's largest mobile operators: Bharti Airtel (India, ~27.5% stake), with the Mittal family, through their holding company Bharti Telecom Limited, holding ~40.5% of Bharti Airtel's shares. Telkomsel (Indonesia’s largest mobile operator) Singtel owns 30.1%, with Telkom Indonesia holding the majority 69.9%. AIS (Thailand), Singtel holds a 23% stake in AIS directly, and also owns 9% of a JV b/w Intouch Holdings and Gulf Energy Development, which owns 40.4% and is AIS's controlling shareholder. Globe Telecom (the Philippines). Singtel owns ~47% of Globe Telecom. It is classified as an associate rather than a subsidiary for accounting purposes.
Singtel has indirect exposure to over 800mm mobile subs, and their combined profit contributions account for roughly two-thirds of group operating profit.

Singtel is actively building two growth engines. NCS, its IT services arm, provides cloud, cybersecurity, and digital transformation services to governments and enterprises across the region. Nxera, its data center business, is rapidly expanding capacity to meet the surging demand for AI and cloud infrastructure across Asia-Pacific.

Majority-owned by Temasek, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund (50.5% ownership), Singtel is one of the largest companies on the Singapore Exchange by market cap. Targets a 70–90% payout ratio, \making it a widely-held stock among income-oriented investors in the region.

4 reporting segments: Optus (its fully-owned Australian telco, covering mobile, fixed, satellite, cloud, and cybersecurity); Singapore Consumer (mobile, broadband, TV, and digital services for consumers in Singapore); Group Enterprise (ICT, cloud, cybersecurity, and managed services for businesses globally); and NCS (IT services, consulting, and cybersecurity in Singapore, Australia, and the broader region). Plus, Singtel also reports the profit contributions from its regional associates (Airtel, AIS, Telkomsel, Globe) separately, which is arguably the most watched part of the business.
INVESTMENT THESIS:

Dividend compounder with growth optionality:  Solid FCF supported by its leading position in Singapore and as the 2nd-largest service provider in Australia. Committed to a 70–90% dividend payout ratio.

Asian telecom growth: Singtel is the No.1 integrated telco in Singapore, owns the No.2 mobile player in Australia, and holds significant stakes in telecom associates in India, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Thailand.
27.5% ownership in Bharti Airtel: Indian telco growing topline at 15-20% and EPS at 40-60%,
Data center re-rating story: The market is increasingly viewing Singtel as more than a stodgy telco given investments in data center capacity.
Temasek backing: Majority-owned by Temasek, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund, which provides a backstop of stability and access to capital markets that pure commercial telcos don't always enjoy.
Singapore dollar is a relatively stable currency, reducing a key risk of international investing
Singapore has no dividend withholding tax for foreign investors, an advantage over, Japanese or European holdings where withholding can bite 15–30%
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS:
Legal overhang: Optus 2022 data breach exposed nearly 10mm Australians' data. Commissioner has filed a lawsuit against Optus.
F/X: Significant earnings come from outside Singapore. Strong SP$ erodes profits.
Domestic competition: Competition exists with established players StarHub, and M1 remains with smaller players like TPG Telecom and Circles.Life vying for share

Lack of control: ST doesn't control Airtel, Telkomsel, or Globe. Political instability, f/x devaluations (as seen with the Nigerian Naira affecting Airtel Africa), or competitive pressures in any of those markets hurts earnings

Execution risk on data centers: Nxera is a big bet that requires significant capital, land, power, and customers. Data center construction timelines and costs can balloon, and there is competition from hyperscalers like AWS and Microsoft.

Regulatory risk: As a dominant operator in Singapore and Australia, Singtel faces ongoing regulatory scrutiny on pricing, network quality, and competition. It was fined by Singapore's IMDA for network reliability issues in late 2025.
High capex: Total capex guidance is around S$2.8bn annually limiting FCFd flexibility.
Management/Board 80

CEO: Yuen Kuan Moon, 54, has been Group CEO of Singtel since January 1, 2021. Prior to that, he was CEO of Consumer Singapore from 2012, leading the integrated mobile, broadband, and TV business, and served as Group Chief Digital Officer from 2018 — a role created to drive the company's digital transformation strategy. He has been with Singtel since joining in 1993. He holds a degree from Stanford University's Graduate School of Business.

Under his watch, Singtel has established 5G leadership and reinvigorated its core business while developing new growth engines by turning NCS into a regional tech services provider and forming a regional data center business. He has also unlocked the latent value of Singtel's assets to recycle capital into higher-growth areas.

Company lifer. He knows the business inside out, but he also comes from a consumer telco background rather than a capital markets or infrastructure background, which is where much of the future value creation is expected to come from.
Asdsa
Common Stock Comparison
SOME OF THE PART ANALYSIS
CASE STUDY The Nigerian Naira Crisis and Its Impact on Airtel Africa and Singtel
Background: A Broken FX System
For decades, Nigeria maintained an artificially controlled official exchange rate that bore little resemblance to the naira's true market value
A thriving parallel black market traded at dramatically weaker levels — by the eve of the 2023 reforms, the official CBN rate was ~N467/$ while the parallel market traded closer to N750/$
Nigeria's FX supply depends overwhelmingly on oil export revs so the currency is always vulnerable to oil price swings and production shortfalls
Years of falling oil output, mounting debt, and rapid money supply growth created an overvaluation estimated at as much as 250% by 2021
Foreign multinationals were effectively trapped — earning naira locally but unable to convert and repatriate profits at a fair rate
2023 Breaking Point
Newly elected President Bola Tinubu came to power in May 2023 promising painful but necessary economic reforms
On June 14, 2023, the CBN collapsed the old system of multiple rate windows into a single market-determined rate unifying all FX market segments
The naira immediately fell ~36% on the official market in one day — one of the largest single-day f/x moves anywhere in the world in recent memory
The naira continued falling throughout 2023 and 2024, from ~N469/$ before the reforms to ~N1,601/$ by Oct 2024 and ending 2024 at ~N1,535/$
Total collapse: roughly 70% against the dollar in ~18 months
Inflation ended 2024 at ~35%, compounded by the simultaneous removal of a long-standing fuel subsidy that had been costing the gov ~$10bn annually
The Direct Impact on Airtel Africa
Nigeria had been Airtel Africa's single largest market, making the company acutely exposed to the naira's collapse
Airtel earns Nigerian revs in naira but reports in USD — so even a growing local business can look terrible in reported numbers when the currency collapses
In H1 2024 rev grew 38% in constant f/x terms, rev, the underlying business was healthy, but Airtel Nigeria's dollar rev fell 44% year-on-year, from $878mm to $489mm
For the full year to Mar 2025, Nigeria's reported dollar revs declined 30.4% to just over $1bn, even as constant f/x growth came in at 36.4%
Beyond translation losses, Airtel had $231mm in exceptional derivative and FX losses before tax in the half-year to Sep 2024, resulting in a $151mm hit to after tax profit
Group EBITDA margins compressed from 49.6% to 45.8%, further hurt by rising fuel costs across African markets
The Knock-On to Singtel
Singtel owns ~27.5% of Bharti Airtel, which consolidates Airtel Africa's results

3-step chain: Nigeria devalues → Airtel Africa's reported profits collapse → Bharti Airtel's earnings are lower → Singtel receives a smaller profit contribution and dividend from one of its most important strategic assets
Aftermath
In Jan2025, Nigeria's communications regulator approved tariff increases of up to 50% for telecom operators, allowing Airtel Nigeria to begin recovering margin
The underlying Nigerian demand story remains intact — over 200 mm people, rising smartphone penetration, and growing appetite for mobile data (long-term tailwinds)
A freely floating, market-determined naira — if sustained — should make Nigeria a more attractive destination for foreign investment over time, ultimately benefiting Airtel's long-term prospects
