COMPANY DESCRIPTION: French energy giant & one of the world's seven "supermajor" oil companies. Total finds oil and gas in the ground, pumps it out, ships it, refines it into 
gasoline and chemicals, sells it at gas stations, and increasingly generates and sells electricity from renewables and natural gas. Has customers in ~130 countries. Founded in 
1924, and rebranded from "Total" to "TotalEnergies" in 2021 to signal a pivot toward being a broader energy company. 100,000+ employees as of 2025. 
Exploration & Production (E&P): The core engine. Finds and extracts oil and gas. Produced ~2.5mm barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d) in 2025. Generated $15bn in 
operating income and $15bn in cash flow in 2025. Operating costs are notably low at under $5/boe, making it competitive even in lower-price environments. 
Integrated LNG: Covers the entire LNG chain, production, liquefaction, shipping, and global trading. Sold 44mm tons of LNG in 2025. $4.9bn in adjusted net operating income 
and $5bn in Cash flow. TotalEnergies is one of the world's largest LNG players, with a 50% production growth target in this segment from 2024–2030. 
Integrated Power: The "new" business: electricity generation from renewables (solar, wind, hydro) and flexible gas-fired plants. Net electricity generation grew ~17% year-over-
year to 48 TWh in 2025. Gross renewable installed capacity reached 34 GW by end of 2025, targeting 100+ TWh of annual net production by 2030. $2bn of cash flow in 2025. 
Refining & Chemicals: Operates 14 refineries globally with ~1.8mm barrels/day capacity. Produces petrochemicals (olefins, aromatics, polymers, fertilizers). This is the largest 
segment by external sales (over $87 bn in 2025) but a relatively thin-margin business vulnerable to refining spreads. $3.5bn in cash flow in 2025 
Marketing & Services: ~13,000 service stations, lubricants, and B2B energy distribution. High volumes but modest margins. 2nd-largest by external sales (~$78 bn in 2025). 
$2.8bn in cash flow in 2025 
Geographical breakdown of sales:  France: ~23%, Europe (ex-France): ~18.5% (total Europe ~41.5%), Africa: ~10.2%, North America: ~8.4%, Rest of World: ~16.9% 
 
INVESTMENT THESIS: 
Low-cost, high-quality upstream portfolio: Sub-$5/boe operating costs are among 
the lowest in the industry, giving TTE profitability even in $60 oil environments 
Best-in-class LNG franchise: positioned for a secular LNG demand boom, especially 
in Asia and Europe post-Ukraine 
Energy transition credibility: unlike BP and Shell, which have zigzagged on 
renewables, TTE has maintained a consistent dual-pillar plan (oil & gas + electricity) 
Production growth: targeting ~3–4% annual production growth through 2030, driven by 
already-sanctioned projects (a rarity among majors) 
Generous shareholder returns: $7.5bn in share buybacks in 2025 alone, plus 
dividends, consistent div growth (sustained raises each year) 
Valuation discount: TTE has historically traded at a discount to US majors (Exxon, 
Chevron) and to its intrinsic value, partly due to being French-listed 
RISKS AND CONSDIERATIONS: 
Oil prices: Oil prices ($60 or below) reduces c/f, pressures the div, makes buybacks 
unsustainable. Targets maintaining divs at $40 oil 
Geopolitical Risk: Significant operations in Africa (Angola, Nigeria, Libya, Congo, 
Uganda), the Middle East (Qatar, Iraq), and had exposure to Russia (Novatek, Arctic 
LNG 2 — now largely unwound but still leaving reputational damage 
ESG / Legal / Reputational Risk: A French court case alleges greenwashing over 
carbon-neutrality claims The East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) project in 
Uganda has drawn criticism over human rights and environmental concerns. Risk of 
ESG-driven investor divestment 
Energy Transition Risk: TTE walks a tightrope: too much oil & gas for green investors, 
not enough renewables for traditional ESG mandates.  
Currency Risk (for U.S. investors): Divis and earnings are reported in euros. A stronger 
dollar reduces the USD-denominated div, which matters for U.S.-based investors. 
Governance / French State Influence: Subject to French regulatory and political 
pressures, and the combined Chairman/CEO role (Pouyanné holds both) is a 
governance concern for some institutional investors. 
Refining Margin Compression: Refining & Chemicals is under structural pressure from 
global overcapacity. Q1 2025 results showed earnings declining partly due to softer 
refining margins.

CEO Patrick Pouyanné: A graduate of École Polytechnique and a Chief Engineer of France's Corps des Mines, Pouyanné held various administrative 
positions in the French Ministry of Industry and cabinet roles from 1989 to 1996, including technical advisor to Prime Minister Édouard Balladur. He 
joined TotalEnergies' Exploration & Production division in January 1997. Following the death of CEO Christophe de Margerie in a plane crash in October 
2014, Pouyanné was appointed CEO and became Chairman and CEO as of December 2015.  
 
Pouyanné has led the business through turbulent times including the decarbonization commitments in the Paris Agreement, the COVID-19 pandemic, 
and the war in Ukraine. His decade-long track record has been operationally strong, and his commitment to the dual-pillar strategy has been notably 
more consistent than BP's or Shell's. Among oil and gas majors, TotalEnergies stands alone in its plans to shift a fifth of its business to renewable-led 
integrated power by 2030 — a tightrope walk that's "not enough oil and gas" for traditional investors nor "enough renewables" for green ones.

paragraphs.text: RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN 3.25% POSITION IN IDVZ
Top 3 position in the fund providing an above average dividend yield. Benefiting from oil price increases due to the war in Iran.

TotalEnergies reported its Q2 2026 earnings on July 23, 2026, delivering results that were in-line. The company demonstrated solid operational execution despite Middle East disruptions, with management emphasizing a strategic focus on deleveraging and net debt reduction using windfall cash flow.

In a high commodity price environment, TTE posted adjusted net income of $6.0 bn and CFFO of $9.8 bn, up almost 15% quarter-on-quarter, with the CEO attributing the price backdrop to the Middle East conflict. Adjusted net income was up 67% year-over-year, the best quarter in nearly three years. Adj EPS of $2.68 beat consensus of $2.66, and revenue of $57.1 billion topped the estimated $55.13 bn. Brent averaged $104/b in Q2 versus $81/b in Q1, with the crude market softening in June amid the Middle East ceasefire; TTF averaged $15.6/Mbtu and average LNG prices rose 20% to $10.2/Mbtu.
Q2 2026 Earnings and Financial Performance
TotalEnergies delivered a quarter marked by consistent execution and disciplined capital allocation.
Q2 2026 EPS came in as "in-line" with expectations, reflecting a stable operating environment.
Deleveraging and Debt Priority: A primary message from the Q2 report was management's commitment to prioritizing net debt reduction using windfall cash flow.
Analyst Estimates: Wall Street analysts had estimated quarterly earnings of USD 2.94 per share for Q2 2026.
Future Outlook: While Q2 was solid, analysts project a potential 23% decrease in quarterly earnings to USD 2.27 per share by Q2 2027.
Production
Hydrocarbon production was 2,395 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day in Q2 2026, down 4% year‑on‑year, due to the following:
+4% from project start‑up and ramp‑up of projects, including Mero‑3, Mero‑4 and Lapa SW in Brazil,
Anchor and Ballymore in the United States, Begonia and Clov Phase 3 in Angola and Mabruk in Libya,
+3% due to improved plant availability,
-1% due to pricing effect,
-2% due to the natural decline of fields,
-8% due to the impact of the conflict in the Middle East.
Excluding the impact of the conflict in the Middle East, production was up more than 4% year-on-year, driven by the ramp-up and start-up of new projects and improved facility availability.
Capital Returns and Investments

TTE is prioritizing deleveraging — gearing down to 13% — and raised the second interim dividend 5.9% to €0.90/share. Net debt fell $3.3 billion, net investments were $3.4 billion in Q2 ($7.9 billion H1, consistent with the $15 billion annual guidance), and ROACE was 13.9% for the trailing twelve months. Buybacks were $1.5 billion in Q2 with another $1.5 billion authorized for Q3 — notable that they held the buyback flat rather than scaling it up with the windfall, consistent with the debt-paydown priority.
The company continues to provide robust returns to shareholders while maintaining its low-carbon investment strategy.
Dividends: The Board declared a 5.9% increase in the interim dividend to EUR 0.90 per share.
Share Buybacks: Share buyback guidance for 2026 is set between USD 3 billion and USD 6 billion.
Capital Expenditure: TotalEnergies maintained its 2026 net investment guidance at USD 15 billion, which includes USD 3 billion earmarked for low-carbon energies.
Broker Commentary and Analysis
Brokers maintained varied outlooks following the July 23 report, balancing the company's strong cash generation against potential cyclical downturns.

JPMorgan (pre-print reaction to the July trading update, which set the tone): called the results "fundamentally solid" but didn't expect the outlook to drive the earnings upgrades seen at Shell and BP, flagging softer LNG/gas trading versus the British majors; shares slid ~2% on that update.

TD Cowen: raised its price target to $105 from $102 on July 24, kept Buy, and argued the weak gas trading — the main driver of the lower Q2 EPS — should reverse in Q3 if prices hold. The firm also noted the reiterated 40% payout ratio implies a buyback increase later this year.
Mizuho: initiated coverage ahead of the print with Outperform and a $103 target, citing the dual-engine hydrocarbons plus low-carbon strategy.
Piper Sandler was more cautious: assumed coverage with a Neutral rating and an $85 price target.

Wolfe Research (Market Overweight): reiterated an Outperform rating, citing "consistency pays" as a theme for the quarter. Highlighted visible Free Cash Flow (FCF) expansion through 2030, which they believe supports a dividend growth pace converging on their USD 106 price target. Management's focus on utilizing windfall cash for debt reduction was viewed as a positive signal for long-term stability.

CFRA Research (Sell): CFRA maintained a 2-STARS (Sell) rating on the stock as of July 23, 2026, despite a target price of EUR 70. The "Sell" opinion is primarily driven by the stock's high correlation (roughly 67%) to crude oil price movements and the expectation of a downcycle in 2027. While Brent crude is forecast to average USD 95 per barrel in 2026, the analyst expressed concern over a projected 13.12% decline in fiscal year 2027 earnings to USD 9.48 per share. CFRA noted that the stock was trading at a demanding 2026 P/E of 9.1x, which represents a 26% premium to its five-year average.

UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (UNH-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
 
 
Recommendation: Maintain positions in PFOE and DIVZ  
UnitedHealth Group delivered a substantial "beat and raise" in its Q2 2026 results, reporting adjusted EPS of $6.38 against consensus 
expectations of approximately $4.90. This performance was primarily driven by a significant Medical Care Ratio (MCR) beat of 86.7%, 
which was roughly 180bps better than consensus forecasts, fueled by a faster-than-expected recovery in the Medicare Advantage 
(MA) business. While management raised its full-year EPS guidance to $19.50-$20.00 (from the previous floor of $18.25), it also 
introduced a more cautious medium-term outlook for the Commercial segment, citing "stubbornly high" cost trends and regulatory 
headwinds that will likely delay that segment's margin recovery until after 2027. 
 
Headline results 
Positives 
- 
Sharp earnings beat and guidance raise, as adjusted EPS of $6.38 beat consensus ($4.85-$4.91) by roughly 30%. GAAP diluted 
EPS of $6.04 was up 62% year-over-year. Medical cost trend inflected favorably, as the medical care ratio fell to 86.7% (from 
89.4% a year ago), a 270bps improvement and the lowest MCR in eight quarters, reflecting benefit redesign, repricing, and 
continued exits from unprofitable Medicare Advantage and ACA exchange plans. Operating leverage returned, as operating 
earnings rose 54% year-over-year to $8.0B and net margin expanded 180bps to 4.9%, with operating cash flow of $11.1B (1.9x 
net income) in the quarter. Guidance was raised for the second consecutive quarter. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance moved to 
$19.50-$20.00, up from "greater than $18.25" at Q1 2026. Management characterized the improvement as structural rather 
than temporary. Shares gained sharply on the print (reported premarket gains in the high-single digits, briefly touching 52-week 
highs) as both the beat and the raise exceeded buy-side expectations. 
Negatives 
- 
Top-line growth remains muted, with revenue growing just 0.4% year-over-year as the company continues to deliberately shed 
unprofitable Medicare Advantage, ACA exchange, and Medicaid membership. Membership attrition continued. 
UnitedHealthcare people served fell to 48.5M, down 525K sequentially. Medicare Advantage membership contracted 965K since 
2025 year-end. Commercial cost trend is still running hot. Management flagged commercial medical cost trend "modestly above 
11%", above plan, driven by No Surprises Act arbitration dynamics and provider coding intensity. Medicaid remains loss-making. 
Segment margins are still guided to -1% to -1.7% for full-year 2026, though management cited early signs of improvement. DOJ 
scrutiny is unresolved. The ongoing civil/criminal Department of Justice review of Medicare Advantage billing practices remains 
an overhang with no disclosed timeline to resolution.

Geographic highlights 
- 
UNH's book is now almost entirely US-domiciled, so geographic dynamics this quarter are best read as domestic market and 
state-level actions rather than international exposure. UNH has completed its multi-year retreat from Latin America (the sale of 
Brazil's Amil and the earlier Banmedica divestiture), leaving essentially no international or currency exposure, a contrast with 
more globally diversified healthcare peers. They fully exited Medicare Advantage (MA) PPO plans in 16 US markets for the 2026 
plan year (180K affected members), part of a broader 600K member national pullback announced in October 2025 as the 
company shifts its mix toward HMO products. UnitedHealthcare's Louisiana Medicaid managed-care contract was wound down 
over Q1-Q2 2026 (state-directed closeout effective March 31, 2026), reassigning roughly 280,000-330,000 members to other 
carriers, a meaningful piece of the segment's reported Medicaid membership decline. Management continues to describe 
Medicaid margin pressure as a function of state-by-state rate adequacy relative to member acuity, rather than a single-state or 
single-region issue. In Optum Health, western and southern regions showed the most impact with an approximately 10% 
reduction in hospitalizations from care transition initiatives. Rural areas demonstrated significant impact with Optum Health 
reaching nearly 90% of US counties and conducting approximately 2.5mn rural patient home visits annually. 
 
Segment highlights 
- 
UnitedHealthcare operating margin nearly doubled year-over-year (4.6% vs. 2.4%) on improved Medicare performance, even as 
commercial benefits remained cost-pressured. Medicare margins expected above 3% with enrollment decline limited to 1.1M. 
Optum Health continued to build momentum with improved care-management discipline, though the base of patients in value-
based arrangements declined year-over-year as the unit prioritizes profitability over enrollment growth. Optum Insight was 
modestly ahead of expectations, with management citing early AI-driven productivity gains as a contributor to the segment's 
26% operating margin, by far the highest in the portfolio. Optum Rx performance in line with plan. The PBM continues to shift 
clients toward 100%-rebate-pass-through and transparency-based contracts, with management citing over 95% of clients on the 
new model. 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
No Surprises Act / IDR dynamics and delayed commercial margin recovery – Management estimated the independent dispute 
resolution (IDR) process alone contributes roughly 50bps of incremental commercial cost trend, with arbiter awards to out-of-
network providers running near 11x Medicare reimbursement rates when providers prevail. Management pushed out its 
timeline for commercial margin recovery to "extending past 2027," later than previously communicated. 
- 
Elevated provider coding intensity – Cited alongside IDR as a driver of commercial medical cost trend running "modestly above 
11%", above management's original plan for the year. 
- 
Continued Medicaid losses and Medicare Advantage membership erosion – Elevated specialty pharmacy and behavioral health 
costs are keeping segment margins negative (-1% to -1.7%) despite early repricing and redesign efforts. MA enrollment is 
expected to decline roughly 1.1-1.4M members in 2026 from intense annual-enrollment-period competition compounded by 
UNH's own deliberate exits from underperforming plans. 
- 
Unresolved DOJ investigation – Civil and criminal DOJ inquiries into Medicare Advantage billing practices remain outstanding. 
Any eventual settlement or remediation requirement is a tail risk not reflected in current guidance. 
 
Guidance 
- 
UPDATED full year 2026 guidance, including adjusted EPS range INCREASED to $19.50-$20, UnitedHealthcare operating earnings 
INCREASED to at least $12B, Optum Health operating earnings INCREASED to at least $2.2B, share repurchases INCREASED to at 
least $5B from initial $2.5B guidance. 
 
Rating actions and target price changes 
The print triggered a broad wave of price-target increases. The investment community largely viewed the results as a "clearing of the 
bar" that re-established UNH's "blue chip" status, though concerns regarding Commercial trend and Medicaid rate lags tempered 
some enthusiasm. Analysts have generally raised 2026-2028 EPS estimates to align with management's new baseline, viewing the 
$19.50-$20.00 range as a durable jumping-off point for future growth.

Why we own 
UnitedHealth Group is the largest health insurer in the US and, through its Optum arm, one of the largest owners of physician 
practices, pharmacy benefit management and healthcare data in the country. UnitedHealthcare insures 50mn+ Americans across 
employer, Medicare and Medicaid plans, collecting premiums up front and paying out medical claims as care is consumed, keeping 
the spread between the two. Optum then reinserts UNH into most of the other dollars flowing through the system. Optum Rx is one 
of just three PBMs that process 80% of the nation's prescriptions, Optum Health employs or is affiliated with roughly 10% of all US 
physicians, making UNH the country's largest employer of doctors, and Optum Insight sells data, analytics and revenue-cycle 
software back to hospitals and other payers. UNH generates roughly three-quarters of consolidated revenue, but Optum, at 
structurally higher margins, contributes close to half of total operating profit, the reverse of a typical insurer's economics. US 
healthcare spending is a $5.6-5.7tn market growing 5% annually, one of the largest and most defensive spending pools in the 
economy. Within it, Medicare Advantage (UNH's single largest profit pool) now covers 35mn of 64mn Medicare-eligible seniors and 
keeps taking share from traditional fee-for-service Medicare, while the drug spend Optum Rx sits atop just crossed $1tn annually, 
growing 10-12% on GLP-1 demand alone. UNH's moat rests on scale (the largest MA book and physician network), decades of 
proprietary claims data feeding underwriting and care-management algorithms, and the switching costs of a fully integrated payer-
provider-PBM stack that's extremely hard to replicate. CVS's struggles trying to copy it are the proof. The 2024-2025 cost-trend 
blowout was real. The dividend hike (streak uninterrupted since 2010) was cut to its smallest in a decade and buyback pace slowed, a 
genuine signal of stress rather than a discretionary choice. But medical cost trend is now inflecting favorably, two consecutive 2026 
guidance raises suggest the repricing cycle is working, buybacks are ramping back toward $5bn+ for 2026, and 2027 Medicare 
Advantage base rates just came in well ahead of fears. With the core insurance engine repricing back to health and Optum's scale 
advantage still compounding underneath it, even as the vertically integrated model itself becomes a live regulatory target, UNH 
should remain a core position in PFOE and DIVZ.

physicians, making UNH the country's largest employer of doctors, and Optum Insight sells data, analytics and revenue-cycle
software back to hospitals and other payers. UNH generates roughly three-quarters of consolidated revenue, but Optum, at
structurally higher margins, contributes close to half of total operating profit, the reverse of a typical insurer's economics. US
healthcare spending is a $5.6-5.7tn market growing 5% annually, one of the largest and most defensive spending pools in the
economy. Within it, Medicare Advantage (UNH's single largest profit pool) now covers 35mn of 64mn Medicare-eligible seniors and
keeps taking share from traditional fee-for-service Medicare, while the drug spend Optum Rx sits atop just crossed $1tn annually,
growing 10-12% on GLP-1 demand alone. UNH's moat rests on scale (the largest MA book and physician network), decades of
proprietary claims data feeding underwriting and care-management algorithms, and the switching costs of a fully integrated payer-
provider-PBM stack that's extremely hard to replicate. CVS's struggles trying to copy it are the proof. The 2024-2025 cost-trend
blowout was real. The dividend hike (streak uninterrupted since 2010) was cut to its smallest in a decade and buyback pace slowed, a
genuine signal of stress rather than a discretionary choice. But medical cost trend is now inflecting favorably, two consecutive 2026
guidance raises suggest the repricing cycle is working, buybacks are ramping back toward $5bn+ for 2026, and 2027 Medicare
Advantage base rates just came in well ahead of fears. With the core insurance engine repricing back to health and Optum's scale
advantage still compounding underneath it, even as the vertically integrated model itself becomes a live regulatory target, UNH
should remain a core position in PFOE and DIVZ.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN POSITION (POTENTIAL ADD) 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: UMG is like the Disney of music. UMG is home to many of the world’s most iconic music labels, including Capitol Music Group, Motown Records and 
Def Jam Recordings. They help artists make music and build careers, and they own the rights to that music. Specifically, UMG deploys capital across a large portfolio of artists in 
the form of advances, which are recouped from royalty earnings over time. Once recouped, UMG continues to collect royalties in perpetuity, sharing a portion with the artist, 
generating a durable, compounding income stream from the underlying music rights. Recorded music sales (75% of total, 24.1% EBITDA margin) come from streaming royalties 
(largest and fastest-growing), digital downloads, physical sales (still meaningful, driven partly by vinyl's resurgence), and licensing music for use in film, TV, advertising, and 
video games. Music publishing sales (18% of total, 23.5% margin) come from royalties paid every time a song is performed, played on radio, streamed or used in TV, film or ads 
(regardless of which artist recorded it). Merchandising & other sales (7% of total, 2% margin) include touring-related revenues, fan experiences and artist services. UMG is 
consistently home to the world’s best-selling artists (seven to nine of top 10 in each of the last seven years), including Taylor Swift, Drake, Morgan Wallen and Lady Gaga. 
 
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect high-single-digit sales growth driven by subscriber growth and improved monetization from price increases and 
customer segmentation. With margin expansion, EPS growth should be low-double-digits. With the dividend, total shareholder return should be 2-3pp higher. 
INVESTMENT THESIS: Underlying fundamentals are strong with sales growing high-
single-digits annually, gross margin in the low-40s, EBITDA margin improving to mid-
20s, strong free cash flow and manageable leverage (under 1x net debt to EBITDA). 
 
Attractive industry trends, large and growing market opportunity: The labels grow 
on the back of growth in streaming, from growing users, increasing subscriber 
penetration and improving monetization through better tiering and price increases. 
Streaming has lowered barriers to entry, democratizing access to audio for listeners 
globally. As disposable incomes continue to rise, particularly in emerging markets, 
streaming subscription services become more affordable/attainable. Using Spotify’s 
target of 1bn paid subscribers for the industry collectively, €5 monthly average 
revenue per user (ARPU) equates to €60bn TAM on the subscription side. UMG’s 
share of the royalties paid from that pool of revenues will grow as the overall pool 
grows. They also benefit from the secular migration of ad spend from analog to digital 
channels and better monetization of ad-supported tiers.  
 
Strong competitive positioning and solid (but potentially narrowing) moat: With 
3.4mn+ music recordings, 5mn owned music titles, and 220+ artists/brands signed, 
UMG is the world's largest music company. Of the three major record labels (including 
Sony and Warner), UMG has a third of the total market, and arguably every up-and-
coming artist on the planet aspires to work with UMG for a chance to become the 
next Taylor Swift. UMG benefits from industry- leading IP and an unmatched catalog 
of songs and recordings, tremendous scale advantages, indirect network effects and 
strong relationships across the music industry ecosystem. Their ownership of decades 
of the most culturally significant music ever recorded is a durable asset, and their full 
suite of services (global distribution, marketing) gives artists their best opportunity to 
grow and expand their career in the music business.  
RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Pre-mortem: Better terms for artists, including 1) reversion clauses (after a defined 
period, master rights revert back to the artist), 2) higher royalty rates, and 3) licensing 
deals rather than label ownership, coupled with AI-generated content flooding the 
market erodes the value of the back catalog. “Streaming 2.0” (pricing and better 
monetization of the most engaged fans) is not enough to offset these structural 
headwinds.  
 
Artificial intelligence (AI) risk: While UMG is attempting to license copyright data to 
train AI models that generate music content and collect royalties on AI-generated 
music that was derived from their protected content, courts could rule that use of 
copyrighted material to train AI models constitutes fair use rather than infringement. 
Attempting to collect royalties on music generated from use of open-source AI tools 
(rather than commercial platforms) is not reasonably achievable. 
 
Ownership (governance risk): Vincent Bolloré, Vivendi and Tencent own 18.5%, 
13.4% and 11.5% of shares outstanding, respectively. They have a shareholder pact 
that coordinates their voting power, giving the bloc collectively outsized influence 
relative to economic ownership. Bolloré is a French billionaire who accumulated a 
stake in Vivendi (French media company) that used to own UMG. An ongoing French 
legal dispute centers on whether Vincent Bolloré exercises de facto control of Vivendi 
(threshold is 30%). If the court rules in favor of control, a mandatory tender offer for 
Vivendi shares would likely be required, potentially forcing asset sales to fund the 
obligation, which could include the Bolloré family's 18.5% stake in UMG. Adding to 
governance uncertainty, Pershing Square has reduced its stake from 10% at IPO to 
4.7%, and Bill Ackman has stepped down from the UMG board. 
 
 
 
 
 
3_19_2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
 
 
Management and capital allocation: Chairman and CEO Sir Lucian Grainge has spent his entire career in the music industry and has signed and worked with many worldwide 
stars, including ABBA, Jay Z, Elton John, Katy Perry, Queen, Rihanna, The Rolling Stones, Sam Smith, U2 and Amy Winehouse, among others. During the span of four decades, he 
has pioneered new approaches to the signing and development of the world’s most successful recording artists and songwriters. He also consistently champions the 
development of innovative business models and partnerships with a wide range of technology and media partners around the world. Capital allocation priorities include 
reinvesting for future growth (royalty advances grow frontline IP, these are required and core to their business), opportunistically pursuing M&A (third-party catalog 
investments), and returning excess capital to shareholders via dividends. There have been no share buybacks to date. From 2018 to 2024, they spent €1.7bn on royalty advances 
and €2.4bn on catalog investments, which includes Bob Dylan publishing, Sting publishing and Neil Diamond recorded music and publishing. Since 2018, they’ve also paid out 
€6.7bn in dividends.  
 
Special items: UMG is conservative in their calculation of free cash flow, given they deduct royalty advances (this is like content investment that most media companies 
capitalize and amortize over time) and strategic investments (in equity affiliates like Chord, a catalog acquisition vehicle, and Mavin, an Afrobeats label).

Downside assumptions: low-single-digit (3%) sales growth, no
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: UMG is like the Disney of music. UMG is home to many of the world’s most iconic music labels, including Capitol Music Group, Motown Records and
Def Jam Recordings. They help artists make music and build careers, and they own the rights to that music. Specifically, UMG deploys capital across a large portfolio of artists in
the form of advances, which are recouped from royalty earnings over time. Once recouped, UMG continues to collect royalties in perpetuity, sharing a portion with the artist,
generating a durable, compounding income stream from the underlying music rights. Recorded music sales (75% of total, 24.1% EBITDA margin) come from streaming royalties
(largest and fastest-growing), digital downloads, physical sales (still meaningful, driven partly by vinyl's resurgence), and licensing music for use in film, TV, advertising, and
video games. Music publishing sales (18% of total, 23.5% margin) come from royalties paid every time a song is performed, played on radio, streamed or used in TV, film or ads
(regardless of which artist recorded it). Merchandising & other sales (7% of total, 2% margin) include touring-related revenues, fan experiences and artist services. UMG is
consistently home to the world’s best-selling artists (seven to nine of top 10 in each of the last seven years), including Taylor Swift, Drake, Morgan Wallen and Lady Gaga.
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect high-single-digit sales growth driven by subscriber growth and improved monetization from price increases and
lines.lead_prefix: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return

lines.text: customer segmentation. With margin expansion, EPS growth should be low-double-digits. With the dividend, total shareholder return should be 2-3pp higher.
INVESTMENT THESIS: Underlying fundamentals are strong with sales growing high-
single-digits annually, gross margin in the low-40s, EBITDA margin improving to mid-
20s, strong free cash flow and manageable leverage (under 1x net debt to EBITDA).
Attractive industry trends, large and growing market opportunity: The labels grow
lines.lead_prefix: Attractive industry trends, large and growing market opportunity

lines.text: on the back of growth in streaming, from growing users, increasing subscriber
penetration and improving monetization through better tiering and price increases.
Streaming has lowered barriers to entry, democratizing access to audio for listeners
globally. As disposable incomes continue to rise, particularly in emerging markets,
streaming subscription services become more affordable/attainable. Using Spotify’s
target of 1bn paid subscribers for the industry collectively, €5 monthly average
revenue per user (ARPU) equates to €60bn TAM on the subscription side. UMG’s
share of the royalties paid from that pool of revenues will grow as the overall pool
grows. They also benefit from the secular migration of ad spend from analog to digital
channels and better monetization of ad-supported tiers.
Strong competitive positioning and solid (but potentially narrowing) moat: With
lines.lead_prefix: Strong competitive positioning and solid (but potentially narrowing) moat:

lines.text: 3.4mn+ music recordings, 5mn owned music titles, and 220+ artists/brands signed,
UMG is the world's largest music company. Of the three major record labels (including
Sony and Warner), UMG has a third of the total market, and arguably every up-and-
coming artist on the planet aspires to work with UMG for a chance to become the
next Taylor Swift. UMG benefits from industry- leading IP and an unmatched catalog
of songs and recordings, tremendous scale advantages, indirect network effects and
strong relationships across the music industry ecosystem. Their ownership of decades
of the most culturally significant music ever recorded is a durable asset, and their full
suite of services (global distribution, marketing) gives artists their best opportunity to
grow and expand their career in the music business.
Pre-mortem: Better terms for artists, including 1) reversion clauses (after a defined
period, master rights revert back to the artist), 2) higher royalty rates, and 3) licensing
deals rather than label ownership, coupled with AI-generated content flooding the
market erodes the value of the back catalog. “Streaming 2.0” (pricing and better
monetization of the most engaged fans) is not enough to offset these structural
Artificial intelligence (AI) risk: WhileUMG is attempting to license copyright data to
train AI models that generate music content and collect royalties on AI-generated
music that was derived from their protected content, courts could rule that use of
copyrighted material to train AI models constitutes fair use rather than infringement.
Attempting to collect royalties on music generated from use of open-source AI tools
(rather than commercial platforms) is not reasonably achievable.
Ownership (governance risk): Vincent Bolloré, Vivendi and Tencent own 18.5%,
13.4% and 11.5% of shares outstanding, respectively. They have a shareholder pact
that coordinates their voting power, giving the bloc collectively outsized influence
relative to economic ownership. Bolloré is a French billionaire who accumulated a
stake in Vivendi (French media company) that used to own UMG. An ongoing French
legal dispute centers on whether Vincent Bolloré exercises de facto control of Vivendi
(threshold is 30%). If the court rules in favor of control, a mandatory tender offer for
Vivendi shares would likely be required, potentially forcing asset sales to fund the
obligation, which could include the Bolloré family's 18.5% stake in UMG. Adding to
governance uncertainty, Pershing Square has reduced its stake from 10% at IPO to
4.7%, and Bill Ackman has stepped down from the UMG board.
Management and capital allocation: Chairman and CEOSir Lucian Grainge has spent his entire career in the music industry and has signed and worked with many worldwide
stars, including ABBA, Jay Z, Elton John, Katy Perry, Queen, Rihanna, The Rolling Stones, Sam Smith, U2 and Amy Winehouse, among others. During the span of four decades, he
has pioneered new approaches to the signing and development of the world’s most successful recording artists and songwriters. He also consistently champions the
development of innovative business models and partnerships with a wide range of technology and media partners around the world. Capital allocation priorities include
reinvesting for future growth (royalty advances grow frontline IP, these are required and core to their business), opportunistically pursuing M&A (third-party catalog
investments), and returning excess capital to shareholders via dividends. There have been no share buybacks to date. From 2018 to 2024, they spent €1.7bn on royalty advances
and €2.4bn on catalog investments, which includes Bob Dylan publishing, Sting publishing and Neil Diamond recorded music and publishing. Since 2018, they’ve also paid out
Special items: UMG is conservative in their calculation of free cash flow, given they deduct royalty advances (this is like content investment that most media companies
capitalize and amortize over time) and strategic investments (in equity affiliates like Chord, a catalog acquisition vehicle, and Mavin, an Afrobeats label).

Universal Music Group N.V. (UNVGY-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
 
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE and IDVZ 
Fundamentally, UMG's quarter was solid on the surface but soft underneath. Sales grew 13.3% YoY constant currency to €3.29bn on 
strong Recorded Music performance, vinyl/physical demand, and licensing. But stripping out the Spotify wholesale price hike, organic 
subscription growth decelerated to roughly 6.7% from 7.9% in Q1 (real volume growth closer to 3%), adjusted EBITDA margin 
contracted 2.2pp to 20.5%, and H1 free cash flow declined 85% to just €24mn while net debt rose 73%. The market reaction was 
severe and arguably outsized relative to the headline beat, with shares down 25% on the print date. This was the stock's largest one-
day drop since its 2021 listing, wiping out €8.8bn in market value. The selloff reflects investors reading through the revenue beat to 
the underlying story. Subscriber growth is masked by pricing rather than driven by volume and margins are under pressure from the 
Downtown acquisition and mix shift. That cash conversion is “deteriorating” is debatable given inherent lumpiness, but timing of the 
change in methodology is curious. These concerns have been serious enough to compress UMG's forward earnings multiple from a 
"quality compounder" premium to 14x, even though no major bank issued a formal downgrade in the quarter. At a 3.9% weight in 
PFOE and 2.4% in IDVZ, I recommend holding the position unless lower growth proves to be structural rather than transitory. 
 
Headline results 
- 
Positive: Revenue growth accelerated, with H1 revenue rising to €6.19bn, up 10.8% YoY at constant currency (+5.3% reported). 
Recorded Music was strong, as segment revenue rose 16.2% YoY to €2.52bn, with double-digit growth across subscription 
streaming, physical, and licensing. Streaming 2.0 pricing is working, as wholesale price increases (including the Spotify tier move 
to $12.99) added roughly 3.5pp of subscription revenue growth, validating UMG's pricing-led streaming strategy. Physical and 
licensing outperformed, with physical revenue growing 15.9% YoY on strong vinyl demand tied to releases from Olivia Rodrigo 
and Noah Kahan. Licensing & other revenue jumped 34.9% YoY. 
- 
Negative: Subscription growth decelerated, with underlying (organic ex-Downtown) subscription streaming growth slowing to 
6.7% in Q2 from 7.9% in Q1, with real volume/subscriber growth estimated at only 3.2pp once the Spotify price-hike benefit is 
stripped out. Margins compressed, with adjusted EBITDA margin declining to 20.5% from 22.7% a year ago, and H1 adjusted 
EBITDA margin declined to 21.1% (-1.6pp), driven by the Downtown consolidation, unfavorable revenue mix, higher central 
costs, and Merchandising losses. Free cash flow collapsed, with H1 free cash flow falling 85% YoY to just €24mn (from €163mn), 
while net financial debt rose 72.8% since year-end 2025 to €4.13bn.

-

market, revenue grew 20%+ YoY, led by premium subscription adoption. In India, management announced a new 72-hour 
premium windowing strategy for major releases, effective late August 2026, designed to convert ad-supported listeners to paid 
subscriptions in one of their highest-priority emerging markets. Following the Downtown Music Holdings acquisition, Virgin 
Music Group was positioned by management as the world's second-largest independent artist- and label-services operator, 
broadening UMG's reach outside its major-label core. 
 
Segment highlights 
- 
In recorded music, revenue reached €2.52bn, up 8.7% organically. Strength in physical sales (+15.9%) and licensing (+34.9%) 
helped offset the softer subscription volume. In music publishing, revenue grew 9.8% in constant currency, but only 2.7% when 
excluding the Downtown acquisition. The slowdown was attributed to ad-funded headwinds and a secular decline in radio and 
linear TV performance revenues. In merchandising & other, revenue declined 10.7% to €167mn, with the segment posting an 
adjusted EBITDA loss of €5mn. 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Decelerating organic subscriber growth – once Spotify's wholesale price increase is stripped out, underlying subscription growth 
is running near 3.2%, suggesting actual subscriber/volume momentum is softer than headline figures imply. 
- 
Ad-supported/short-form competition – consumer attention continues to shift from better-monetized on-demand and video 
services toward short-form platforms, structurally capping ad-supported streaming growth (1.7% organic in Q2). 
- 
Margin dilution from M&A and mix – the Downtown consolidation, a lower-margin mix at Virgin Music Group's artist- and label-
services business, and rising central costs all weighed on group profitability. 
- 
Cash generation and leverage – 85% drop in H1 free cash flow and 73% rise in net debt raise questions about near-term capacity 
to fund dividends and buybacks from organic cash flow. 
- 
Merchandising softness – timing-related A&R cost increases and sales declines pushed the segment to an adjusted EBITDA loss. 
- 
Elevated corporate costs – higher professional/legal fees were also cited as a drag on reported profitability during the quarter. 
 
Guidance 
- 
UPDATED Music Publishing outlook to mid-single-digit growth versus prior high single-digit expectations. Merchandising 
expected to improve in 2027 versus 2026. H2 free cash flow expected to be stronger than 1H. Spotify stake sale (€400 million) 
and an enlarged share buyback program signal continued willingness to return capital despite the FCF shortfall, alongside the 
€0.24/share interim dividend. Downtown expected to create increasing strategic and financial value with efficiency 
opportunities. Subscription sales expected to improve in H2 versus Q2 levels. €250mn run-rate savings program remains on 
schedule, though management admitted that 1H savings were largely reinvested into AI initiatives and IP protection.  
 
Broker rating and price target actions 
 
 
3 
 
Sell-side reaction was mixed rather than uniformly negative, but the results triggered a significant valuation re-rating. UMG's forward 
P/E compressed from roughly 18x pre-earnings to roughly 14x afterward, a re-rating of comparable magnitude to a multi-notch 
sentiment downgrade, even without a wave of formal rating changes. The sharp share-price reaction, wide analyst dispersion, and 
compressed multiple indicate sentiment has become notably more cautious and bifurcated, with the bull case resting on Streaming 
2.0 pricing power and H2 reacceleration, and the bear case centered on decelerating organic subscriber growth, margin pressure, 
and weak free cash flow conversion.

Why we own 
UMG is like the Disney of music, home to many of the world’s most iconic music labels, including Capitol Music Group, Motown 
Records and Def Jam Recordings. They help artists make music and build careers, and they own the rights to that music. UMG 
deploys capital across a large portfolio of artists in the form of advances, which are recouped from royalty earnings over time. Once 
recouped, UMG continues to collect royalties in perpetuity, sharing a portion with the artist, generating a durable, compounding 
income stream from the underlying music rights. They are home to the world’s best-selling artists (seven to nine of top 10 in each of 
the last seven years), including Taylor Swift, Drake, Morgan Wallen and Lady Gaga. As the world’s largest music company with 
industry-leading IP and an unmatched catalog of songs and recordings, tremendous scale advantages and strong relationships across 
the music industry ecosystem, UMG benefits from growth in audio streaming, including growing users and subscriber penetration, 
and improving monetization. They also benefit from the secular migration of ad spend from analog to digital channels and better 
monetization of ad-supported tiers. Trading at 14x forward consensus earnings, valuation is attractive assuming no sustained 
deceleration in growth profile. UMG should remain a core position unless we determine the long-term growth algorithm is 
structurally lower than originally expected.

Ad-supported/short-form competition – consumer attention continues to shift from better-monetized on-demand and video
services toward short-form platforms, structurally capping ad-supported streaming growth (1.7% organic in Q2).
Margin dilution from M&A and mix – the Downtown consolidation, a lower-margin mix at Virgin Music Group's artist- and label-
services business, and rising central costs all weighed on group profitability.
Cash generation and leverage – 85% drop in H1 free cash flow and 73% rise in net debt raise questions about near-term capacity
to fund dividends and buybacks from organic cash flow.
Merchandising softness – timing-related A&R cost increases and sales declines pushed the segment to an adjusted EBITDA loss.
Elevated corporate costs – higher professional/legal fees were also cited as a drag on reported profitability during the quarter.
UPDATED Music Publishing outlook to mid-single-digit growth versus prior high single-digit expectations. Merchandising
expected to improve in 2027 versus 2026. H2 free cash flow expected to be stronger than 1H. Spotify stake sale (€400 million)
and an enlarged share buyback program signal continued willingness to return capital despite the FCF shortfall, alongside the
€0.24/share interim dividend. Downtown expected to create increasing strategic and financial value with efficiency
opportunities. Subscription sales expected to improve in H2 versus Q2 levels. €250mn run-rate savings program remains on
schedule, though management admitted that 1H savings were largely reinvested into AI initiatives and IP protection.
Broker rating and price target actions

lines.text: Sell-side reaction was mixed rather than uniformly negative, but the results triggered a significant valuation re-rating. UMG's forward
P/E compressed from roughly 18x pre-earnings to roughly 14x afterward, a re-rating of comparable magnitude to a multi-notch
sentiment downgrade, even without a wave of formal rating changes. The sharp share-price reaction, wide analyst dispersion, and
compressed multiple indicate sentiment has become notably more cautious and bifurcated, with the bull case resting on Streaming
2.0 pricing power and H2 reacceleration, and the bear case centered on decelerating organic subscriber growth, margin pressure,
and weak free cash flow conversion.

lines.text: UMG is like the Disney of music, home to many of the world’s most iconic music labels, including Capitol Music Group, Motown
Records and Def Jam Recordings. They help artists make music and build careers, and they own the rights to that music. UMG
deploys capital across a large portfolio of artists in the form of advances, which are recouped from royalty earnings over time. Once
recouped, UMG continues to collect royalties in perpetuity, sharing a portion with the artist, generating a durable, compounding
income stream from the underlying music rights. They are home to the world’s best-selling artists (seven to nine of top 10 in each of
the last seven years), including Taylor Swift, Drake, Morgan Wallen and Lady Gaga. As the world’s largest music company with
industry-leading IP and an unmatched catalog of songs and recordings, tremendous scale advantages and strong relationships across
the music industry ecosystem, UMG benefits from growth in audio streaming, including growing users and subscriber penetration,

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN POSITION IN PFOE 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Visa is the largest processor of debit and credit transactions globally, operating as a "toll booth" for global commerce. They connect consumers, 
banks and merchants, making commerce safer, faster and more reliable for all parties. Specifically, the company facilitates authorization, clearing and settlement of payment 
transactions and delivers related products and services, including engagement solutions, risk and security services, and consulting and advisory solutions. They do not issue 
credit or lend money, but collect a small fee based on volume and number of transactions processed. The total monetary volume of all transactions processed through the 
network is $16.7tn annually and growing at a mid- to high-single-digit rate. The number of individual transactions routed through the network for authorization, clearing and 
settlement is 310bn+ annually, growing at a high-single-digit to low-double-digit rate. They’ve spent the last few decades building out the merchant acceptance network, 
which is north of 175mn (and when you include digital endpoints, it expands the network’s reach into the billions of individual accounts and real-time payment rails). The 
business is diversified across segments and geographies. 36% of sales are derived from data processing, 25% from international transactions, 32% from services, and the 
remaining 7% from other sources (advisory services, licensing fees and the like). From a regional standpoint, 39% of sales are generated in the US with 61% from international 
markets. There are 5bn+ Visa-branded cards in circulation (and growing at a mid- to high-single-digit clip). 
 
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect low-double-digit sales growth driven by mid-single-digit growth in personal consumer expenditure, low- to mid-
single-digit contribution from the continued shift of cash and check to digital forms of payment, growth in new flows, services, e-commerce, pricing and market share gains. 
With modest margin expansion and share buybacks, EPS should grow in the mid-teens range. With the dividend, total shareholder return should be slightly higher. 
INVESTMENT THESIS: Despite an ever-evolving payments landscape, most roads lead 
back to Visa and Mastercard payment rails. Fundamentals remain strong with sales 
growing low-double-digits, operating margin modestly expanding, solid free cash flow 
(margin 50%+) and manageable leverage (net debt to free cash flow < 1x). 
 
Multiple tailwinds driving growth in a large and attractive market: Visa sizes the 
opportunity at $240tn+ annually in global payment volumes. Core PCE represents 
$41tn of the TAM (excluding China), with an even larger opportunity in non-core 
commercial and new payment flows. These include $145tn in business-to-business 
payments and $55tn in peer-to-peer, business-to-consumer and government-to-
consumer payments. Services TAM is $520bn+ (in dollars, not payment flows). The 
largest services opportunities include advisory services, risk & security, issuing and 
acceptance solutions. Tailwinds driving growth include growth in global PCE (mid-
single-digits), the continued secular shift from cash and check to digital forms of 
payment (low- to mid-single-digits), acceptance growth and e-commerce. 
 
Duopoly in global payments with one of the most unassailable moats in existence: 
Outside of China, Visa (no. 1) and Mastercard (no. 2) operate a global duopoly. Visa 
benefits from global scale, strong network effects and a solid brand. They enable 
transactions for customers through the network in 200+ countries, and with 5bn+ Visa 
branded cards and 175mn+ points of acceptance, Visa products and infrastructure are 
truly ubiquitous. While Visa and Mastercard dominate carded payment flows in global 
PCE (excluding China), cash, check and ACH remain their largest competitor, with 
global PCE card penetration at 2/3 of total payments. 
RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Pre-mortem: The core consumer payments opportunity in most developed markets is 
saturated. While the runway remains long in emerging markets like Indonesia, India, 
Mexico and Africa, where card penetration is 10-40%, traditional card rails do not 
provide the same opportunity given the popularity of government-backed account-to-
account or closed-loop alternatives (like UPI in India and Pix in Brazil). Services are not 
enough to make up for the shortfall, leading to a meaningful deceleration in growth. 
As a result, the stock trades at a meaningful discount to historical levels. 
 
Disintermediation: Disintermediation through stablecoin, government mandated 
account-to-account rails or central bank digital currencies that would structurally 
bypass the card networks entirely is a tail risk that’s genuinely hard to stress test.  
 
Regulatory and litigation risk: Regulation related to payments, privacy, data or 
security has the potential to lead to less attractive economics in the future. Regulation 
around interchange rates can increase the cost of doing business and significantly 
impact volumes that flow through the network. Regulatory margin pressure has been 
real but gradual. Litigation with merchants and competitors is ongoing, and while Visa 
and Mastercard have navigated this well in the past, any future settlements could 
have significant financial impact. Litigation charges tend to be noisy but bounded. 
 
Ownership: Largest shareholders are Vanguard (8.6%), Blackrock (5.4%) and SSgA 
(4.9%). 
 
 
 
 
 
4_23_2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
Management and capital allocation: CEO Ryan McInerney, age 49, has been with Visa since 2013. Prior to the CEO role in 2023, he served as President of Visa’s global 
businesses. Before joining Visa, he served as CEO of consumer banking at JPMorgan Chase, and before that, he was a principal at McKinsey in the firm’s retail banking and 
payments practices. CFO Chris Suh, age 54, joined Visa in 2023 from Electronic Arts where he served as CFO. Prior to EA, he held senior finance roles at Microsoft for nearly two 
decades, most recently as CFO of the cloud and AI division. The most consistent thread in executive backgrounds prior to joining Visa is major financial institutions and strategy 
consulting (particularly JPMorgan and McKinsey), with big tech as a secondary feeder. In short, management is long-tenured and deeply domain specialized. Capital allocation 
priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business for future growth (organic and inorganic) and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share 
buybacks. Strategic M&A is disciplined and bolt-on in nature. Notable acquisitions include Visa Europe for $24bn in 2016, Earthport for $320mn in 2019 (cross-border payment 
capabilities), Tink for $2.2bn in 2022 (open banking), Currencycloud for $963mn in 2022 (cross-border payment capabilities), and Pismo for $1bn in 2024 (enabled connectivity 
for emerging payment rails like Pix in Brazil). Since the IPO in 2008, Visa has paid out $33.2bn in dividends and they’ve repurchased $138bn in shares outstanding. They’ve 
increased the dividend every year since March 2008 and current yield is 0.9%. 
 
Special items: Visa has a complex share structure as a result of the company’s origins as a member cooperative. Class A common stock is the public float that has ordinary voting 
rights (one vote per share). Class B common stock is held by US member banks. These shares were issued at the IPO at US financial institutions that were members of Visa USA 
before the reorganization in 2008. They are not publicly traded and carry transfer rights tied to litigation resolution. These shareholders retain exposure to pre-IPO interchange 
litigation. Each time Visa puts money into escrow to settle that litigation, it effectively reduces the Class A shares that Class B shareholders will eventually receive (so they bear 
the litigation cost, not public shareholders). Class C common stock is held by non-US member institutions with a conversion rate of four to one (one Class C converts into four 
Class A upon transfer). They also have preferred stock created specifically for the 2016 Visa Europe acquisition. These are convertible into Class A but the conversion rates on 
certain of these shares can also be reduced to offset liabilities from litigation relating to multilateral interchange fee rates in the Visa Europe territory.

continued shift of cash and check to digital payments, growth
in PCE, new flows and services, modest margin expansion
Base (consensus) assumptions: low-double-digit top line growth,
Downside assumptions: mid-single-digit top line growth,
COMPANY DESCRIPTION:Visa is the largest processor of debit and credit transactions globally, operating as a "toll booth" for global commerce. They connect consumers,
banks and merchants, making commerce safer, faster and more reliable for all parties. Specifically, the company facilitates authorization, clearing and settlement of payment
transactions and delivers related products and services, including engagement solutions, risk and security services, and consulting and advisory solutions. They do not issue
credit or lend money, but collect a small fee based on volume and number of transactions processed. The total monetary volume of all transactions processed through the
network is $16.7tn annually and growing at a mid- to high-single-digit rate. The number of individual transactions routed through the network for authorization, clearing and
settlement is 310bn+ annually, growing at a high-single-digit to low-double-digit rate. They’ve spent the last few decades building out the merchant acceptance network,
which is north of 175mn (and when you include digital endpoints, it expands the network’s reach into the billions of individual accounts and real-time payment rails). The
business is diversified across segments and geographies. 36% of sales are derived from data processing, 25% from international transactions, 32% from services, and the
remaining 7% from other sources (advisory services, licensing fees and the like). From a regional standpoint, 39% of sales are generated in the US with 61% from international
markets. There are 5bn+ Visa-branded cards in circulation (and growing at a mid- to high-single-digit clip).
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect low-double-digit sales growth driven by mid-single-digit growth in personal consumer expenditure, low- to mid-
lines.lead_prefix: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return

lines.text: single-digit contribution from the continued shift of cash and check to digital forms of payment, growth in new flows, services, e-commerce, pricing and market share gains.
With modest margin expansion and share buybacks, EPS should grow in the mid-teens range. With the dividend, total shareholder return should be slightly higher.
INVESTMENT THESIS: Despite an ever-evolving payments landscape, most roads lead
back to Visa and Mastercard payment rails. Fundamentals remain strong with sales
growing low-double-digits, operating margin modestly expanding, solid free cash flow
(margin 50%+) and manageable leverage (net debt to free cash flow < 1x).
Multiple tailwinds driving growth in a large and attractive market: Visa sizes the
lines.lead_prefix: Multiple tailwinds driving growth in a large and attractive market

lines.text: opportunity at $240tn+ annually in global payment volumes. Core PCE represents
$41tn of the TAM (excluding China), with an even larger opportunity in non-core
commercial and new payment flows. These include $145tn in business-to-business
payments and $55tn in peer-to-peer, business-to-consumer and government-to-
consumer payments. Services TAM is $520bn+ (in dollars, not payment flows). The
largest services opportunities include advisory services, risk & security, issuing and
acceptance solutions. Tailwinds driving growth include growth in global PCE (mid-
single-digits), the continued secular shift from cash and check to digital forms of
payment (low- to mid-single-digits), acceptance growth and e-commerce.
Duopoly in global payments with one of the most unassailable moats in existence:
lines.lead_prefix: Duopoly in global payments with one of the most unassailable moats in existence

lines.text: Outside of China, Visa (no. 1) and Mastercard (no. 2) operate a global duopoly. Visa
benefits from global scale, strong network effects and a solid brand. They enable
transactions for customers through the network in 200+ countries, and with 5bn+ Visa
branded cards and 175mn+ points of acceptance, Visa products and infrastructure are
truly ubiquitous. While Visa and Mastercard dominate carded payment flows in global
PCE (excluding China), cash, check and ACH remain their largest competitor, with
global PCE card penetration at 2/3 of total payments.
Pre-mortem:Thecoreconsumer payments opportunity in most developed markets is
saturated. While the runway remains long in emerging markets like Indonesia, India,
Mexico and Africa, where card penetration is 10-40%, traditional card rails do not
provide the same opportunity given the popularity of government-backed account-to-
account or closed-loop alternatives (like UPI in India and Pix in Brazil). Services are not
enough to make up for the shortfall, leading to a meaningful deceleration in growth.
As a result, the stock trades at a meaningful discount to historical levels.
Disintermediation: Disintermediation through stablecoin, government mandated
account-to-account rails or central bank digital currencies that would structurally
bypass the card networks entirely is a tail risk that’s genuinely hard to stress test.
Regulatory and litigation risk:Regulation related to payments, privacy, data or
security has the potential to lead to less attractive economics in the future. Regulation
around interchange rates can increase the cost of doing business and significantly
impact volumes that flow through the network. Regulatory margin pressure has been
real but gradual. Litigation with merchants and competitors is ongoing, and while Visa
and Mastercard have navigated this well in the past, any future settlements could
have significant financial impact. Litigation charges tend to be noisy but bounded.
Ownership:Largest shareholders are Vanguard (8.6%), Blackrock (5.4%) and SSgA
Management and capital allocation: CEO Ryan McInerney, age 49, has been with Visa since 2013. Prior to the CEO role in 2023, he served as President of Visa’s global
businesses. Before joining Visa, he served as CEO of consumer banking at JPMorgan Chase, and before that, he was a principal at McKinsey in the firm’s retail banking and
payments practices. CFO Chris Suh, age 54, joined Visa in 2023 from Electronic Arts where he served as CFO. Prior to EA, he held senior finance roles at Microsoft for nearly two
decades, most recently as CFO of the cloud and AI division. The most consistent thread in executive backgrounds prior to joining Visa is major financial institutions and strategy
consulting (particularly JPMorgan and McKinsey), with big tech as a secondary feeder. In short, management is long-tenured and deeply domain specialized. Capital allocation
priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business for future growth (organic and inorganic) and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share
buybacks. Strategic M&A is disciplined and bolt-on in nature. Notable acquisitions include Visa Europe for $24bn in 2016, Earthport for $320mn in 2019 (cross-border payment
capabilities), Tink for $2.2bn in 2022 (open banking), Currencycloud for $963mn in 2022 (cross-border payment capabilities), and Pismo for $1bn in 2024 (enabled connectivity
for emerging payment rails like Pix in Brazil). Since the IPO in 2008, Visa has paid out $33.2bn in dividends and they’ve repurchased $138bn in shares outstanding. They’ve
increased the dividend every year since March 2008 and current yield is 0.9%.
Special items: Visa has a complex share structure as a result of the company’s origins as a member cooperative. Class A common stock is the public float that has ordinary voting
rights (one vote per share). Class B common stock is held by US member banks. These shares were issued at the IPO at US financial institutions that were members of Visa USA
before the reorganization in 2008. They are not publicly traded and carry transfer rights tied to litigation resolution. These shareholders retain exposure to pre-IPO interchange
litigation. Each time Visa puts money into escrow to settle that litigation, it effectively reduces the Class A shares that Class B shareholders will eventually receive (so they bear
the litigation cost, not public shareholders). Class C common stock is held by non-US member institutions with a conversion rate of four to one (one Class C converts into four
Class A upon transfer). They also have preferred stock created specifically for the 2016 Visa Europe acquisition. These are convertible into Class A but the conversion rates on
certain of these shares can also be reduced to offset liabilities from litigation relating to multilateral interchange fee rates in the Visa Europe territory.
Source: Visa 10K. Total volume includes payments volume and cash volume (cash access transactions, balance access transactions, balance transfers and convenience checks).
Visa’s acquisition of Visa Europe in 2015 (inorganically) boosted their market share.
Value-added services are allocated across three of the four reported segments (service revenue, data processing revenue, and other revenue). Management began
disclosing VAS separately in their latest SEC filings and investor day materials.
Operating margin adjusted mostly for litigation provision and restructuring.

Visa Inc. (V-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE 
Visa's fiscal Q3 2026 beat expectations on both lines, with net revenue up 14% to $11.6B and non-GAAP EPS up 11% to $3.32, 
powered by record $4T in payments volume, 13% cross-border volume growth, and a standout 34% surge in Value-Added Services 
revenue (aided in part by one-time FIFA World Cup spending). The catch was profitability. Operating expenses grew faster than sales 
(17%, driven by severance costs and rising client incentives), and international transaction revenue grew 6% versus 12% cross-border 
volume growth (a yield/conversion gap that drew analyst scrutiny). Management raised full-year guidance modestly on revenue and 
EPS, and most sell-side firms responded by lifting price targets into the $400-450 range, though shares were roughly flat on the print. 
 
Headline results 
- 
Most positive comments: Strong Q3 results with 14% net revenue growth to $11.6B and 11% EPS growth, both exceeding 
expectations. Payments volume hit record $4 trillion (+10% YoY), processed transactions grew 10% to 72B, and value-added 
services surged 34% to $3.8B. Commercial solutions grew 17% and Visa Direct 21%, reflecting resilient consumer spending and 
successful product innovation. 
- 
Most negative comments: International transaction revenue grew only 6%, lagging 12% cross-border volume growth due to 
currency volatility lapping and mix headwinds. Op ex grew 17%, exceeding expectations from marketing and personnel costs. 
Severance charges totaled $563M from workforce reductions. Geopolitical conflict continued offsetting cross-border growth. 
Geographic highlights 
- 
US had the most significant impact, with payments volume up 10% YoY and card-present transactions up 20% in select host cities 
during FIFA. Europe showed strong credentials growth of 40M+ in 12 months, 70% faster than 2019-2024 annualized rates. 
LatAm benefited from FIFA with inbound cross-border growth exceeding 70% and 35% YoY in Mexico and Canada, respectively. 
Segment highlights 
- 
VAS had the most impact, growing 34% YoY to $3.8B, with all four portfolios (issuing solutions, acceptance solutions, 
risk/security, advisory/other) growing faster than historical rates. Commercial and money movement solutions revenue grew 
17% YoY (commercial payments volume up 13% YoY). Visa Direct transactions grew 21% YoY. Consumer payments benefited from 
strong volume growth (US payments volume up 10% YoY, cross-border volume up 12% YoY) and FIFA engagement.  
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Headwinds include: (1) currency volatility, with Q4 expected to be closer to Q1 levels; (2) lapping peak volatility from Q3 2025; 
(3) Middle East conflict as offsetting factor; (4) client incentive growth from renewals and new business; (5) timing of 
promotional shopping events and FIFA-related spend normalization. 
Guidance 
- 
UPDATED full-year 2026 net revenue growth guidance to low end of low-teens and EPS growth guidance to low end of mid-
teens. For Q4, Visa expects net revenue growth in high end of low-double-digits and EPS growth in low end of mid-teens.

Severance charges totaled $563M from workforce reductions. Geopolitical conflict continued offsetting cross-border growth.
US had the most significant impact, with payments volume up 10% YoY and card-present transactions up 20% in select host cities
during FIFA. Europe showed strong credentials growth of 40M+ in 12 months, 70% faster than 2019-2024 annualized rates.
LatAm benefited from FIFA with inbound cross-border growth exceeding 70% and 35% YoY in Mexico and Canada, respectively.
VAS had the most impact, growing 34% YoY to $3.8B, with all four portfolios (issuing solutions, acceptance solutions,
risk/security, advisory/other) growing faster than historical rates. Commercial and money movement solutions revenue grew
17% YoY (commercial payments volume up 13% YoY). Visa Direct transactions grew 21% YoY. Consumer payments benefited from
strong volume growth (US payments volume up 10% YoY, cross-border volume up 12% YoY) and FIFA engagement.
Headwinds include: (1) currency volatility, with Q4 expected to be closer to Q1 levels; (2) lapping peak volatility from Q3 2025;
(3) Middle East conflict as offsetting factor; (4) client incentive growth from renewals and new business; (5) timing of
promotional shopping events and FIFA-related spend normalization.
UPDATED full-year 2026 net revenue growth guidance to low end of low-teens and EPS growth guidance to low end of mid-
teens. For Q4, Visa expects net revenue growth in high end of low-double-digits and EPS growth in low end of mid-teens.
Visa is the largest processor of debit and credit transactions globally, operating as a "toll booth" for global commerce. With $240tn+
in addressable payment volumes, they benefit from growth in global personal consumer expenditure, the continued secular shift
from cash and check to digital forms of payment, merchant acceptance growth and e-commerce. Value-added services (1/3 of total
sales) are growing 2x faster than the core business, and they size this opportunity at $520bn+ (in sales, not payment flows). With
global scale, strong network effects and a ubiquitous brand, despite an ever-evolving and dynamic payments landscape (from digital
wallets and buy-now-pay-later to stablecoin and real-time payments), most roads lead back to Visa and Mastercard payment rails.
