RECOMMENDATION: CANDIDATE FOR PFOE 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Workday is a cloud-native enterprise application software company with roots in enterprise resource planning, or ERP. Specifically, they sell 
mission-critical products and services in human capital management, or HCM, and financial management systems, or FMS. As a software-as-a-service, or SaaS company, 
Workday sells subscriptions in-cloud (average terms not disclosed but minimum duration is three years) with major feature releases delivered twice a year, and weekly, 
smaller feature updates delivered with minimal downtime disruption. Feature releases are not subject to additional fees. The business mix is roughly 75% HCM and 25% 
financials, with the latter growing faster than the former (low-20s versus mid-teens over the last few years). From a geographic standpoint, the US represents 75% of total 
sales with the balance OUS. The company’s subscription backlog, or remaining performance obligations, which represents total contractual commitments for services that will 
be performed in the future, topped $27bn in the most recent period, up from less than $4bn in fiscal 2017. They currently serve 11,500 customers, including 65% of the 
Fortune 500 and have 80mn+ users generating 1.4tn transactions globally. Gross retention rate, which indicates stickiness of the existing customer base (and excludes upsell), 
consistently exceeds 95% with churn mostly due to M&A. Net retention (including upsell) is north of 100%. 
 
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect low-teens sales growth driven by growth in new customers or “logos” (going down market to medium enterprise 
and capitalizing on the larger opportunity OUS) as well as cross-sell and upsell to existing customers. With margin expansion and opportunistic share buybacks, EPS should 
grow mid-teens. There could be additional upside to total shareholder return if the multiple re-rates. 
INVESTMENT THESIS: Fundamentals are solid with sales growing low-teens, operating 
margin improvement, strong free cash flow and net cash on the balance sheet. 
 
Multiple favorable trends in a large and growing market: While no longer early days, 
ERP workload migration from on-premise to cloud remains a tailwind. A structural 
shift to unified, single platform systems of record benefits vendors like Workday 
compared with stitching together point solutions. AI is also (currently) a tailwind to 
growth. The opportunity is estimated at nearly $200bn, with > 50% of the regional 
opportunity in markets OUS and > 50% of the vertical opportunity in financials versus 
core HCM. The opportunity has expanded over time as Workday expands the product 
portfolio into non-core adjacencies like payroll, talent management (recruiting, 
reskilling), workforce planning and analytics in HCM and financial planning 
(budgeting, forecasting), procurement and spend management in FINS.  
 
Gold standard in HCM software (contender in FINS) with a historically strong moat: 
Workday offers the gold standard in HCM software, particularly for large enterprise. 
They’ve been named a leader in Gartner’s magic quadrant for cloud HCM suites for 
1,000+ employees for 10 consecutive years, competing mostly with Oracle and SAP. In 
financials, they have consistently gained market share and have also been recognized 
by Gartner as a magic quadrant leader (shorter duration than HCM). Workday 
benefits from high switching costs, scale and distribution advantages in a market still 
mid-migration (from on-premise to cloud), proprietary data feeding the AI layer, and a 
unified system of record. Customer captivity is evidenced by 95%+ gross retention 
revenue, as it’s painful to rip and replace mission-critical software. With HR and 
finance on one unified platform, AI agents get richer context with people and money 
data living in one graph as opposed to being stitched together across systems.  
RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Pre-mortem: Seat-based subscription pricing doesn’t hold, and Workday is too slow to 
respond (to a usage or consumption-based model). As they shift, agentic AI becomes 
good enough that large customers reduce headcount rather than augmenting existing 
staff. As agent use scales and becomes much larger as a percent of total business, 
inference costs grow faster than revenues (despite declining per token price). 
Operating margin expansion from headcount discipline is no longer able to offset 
gross margin declines. Optionality embedded in the depressed multiple doesn’t pay 
off, meaning the stock was closer to fairly priced than mispriced at initiation. 
 
Competition: While incumbents SAP and Oracle are bundling HCM with broader ERP 
suite offerings (and giving migration discounts to customers switching from on-prem 
to cloud), traditional competition is nothing new and Workday has been successful 
taking share over time. The newer competitive threat is cross-vertical encroachment. 
ServiceNow and Salesforce, who historically competed in other verticals (IT service 
management and CRM, respectively) are moving directly into HR. ServiceNow 
orchestrating workflows across various systems of record (HR, ERP, CRM) means 
Workday could be commoditized into the data plumbing underneath rather than the 
customer facing platform capturing the AI value. 
 
Ownership: Largest institutional shareholders include Vanguard (12.7%), Blackrock 
(7.9%) and Hotchkis & Wiley (5.3%). Workday has a dual class share structure with 
class A common stock carrying one vote per share and class B carrying 10 votes per 
share. While economic ownership is mostly institutional, co-founders Dave Duffield 
and Aneel Bhusri own 69% of total voting power.  
 
 
 
 
 
7_9_2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
Management and capital allocation: CEO Aneel Bhusri co-founded the business with Dave Duffield in 2005 and served as sole or co-CEO from 2009 to 2024. Before Workday, he 
held several leadership roles at PeopleSoft, including vice chair of the board and senior vice president responsible for prod uct strategy, business development, and 
marketing. PeopleSoft (acquired by Oracle in 2005) is an on-premise enterprise software company that provides HR, finance and other back office applications. Bhusri holds an 
MBA from Stanford and a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and economics from Brown University. Note that after stepping down as co-CEO in 2024, naming Carl 
Eschenbach sole CEO at the time, he returned earlier this year to “lead in the rapidly evolving AI era”. There was a gap between the official messaging and how it was received 
externally, though I personally view it as a net positive. Much of the rest of the management team has been freshly reassembled. Both the Chief Commercial Officer and 
President of Product and Technology have decades of experience at Google and SAP. CFO Zane Rowe was appointed in 2023 with ties to former CEO Carl Eschenbach, which 
makes him a bit of a continuity figure though his tenure is short. On capital allocation, priorities include reinvesting back into the business, strategic M&A and returning excess 
capital to shareholders through buybacks. While declining as a percent of total sales (currently high-20s), R&D remains a priority. Workday has spent $6.3bn on acquisitions over 
the last decade+. Notable deals include Adaptive Insights for $1.5bn in 2018 (enhanced financial planning, budgeting and forecasting), Scout RFP for $500mn in 2019 (cloud-
based procurement), Peakon for $700mn in 2021 (real-time visibility into employee experience) and VNDLY, also in 2021 (cloud-based external workforce and vendor 
management company). The earlier era of M&A helped the company build out the product suite, particularly in non-core financials, whereas the current era is focused on 
building out AI capabilities and functionality. Recent notable acquisitions include HiredScore (AI recruiting and talent matching), Evisort (contract intelligence for legal and 
procurement), Flowise (low-code AI agent building platform), Paradox (conversational AI for frontline/hourly worker recruiting) and Sana (AI native learning and agent platform). 
Sana was largest with a $1.1bn price tag. Over the last few years, Workday has repurchased $4.1bn+ in shares, offsetting share dilution from stock-based compensation. In 
September 2025, the board authorized an additional $4bn in repurchases. They’ve targeted a total of $5bn in repurchases through the end of fiscal 2027, which should more 
than offset SBC.  
 
Special items: SAP’s end of support for legacy ERP customers in 2027 should force a large install base to choose a cloud platform sooner than later (but they have been known to 
kick the can down the road with prior end of support announcements).

COMPANY DESCRIPTION:Workday is a cloud-native enterprise application software company with roots in enterprise resource planning, or ERP. Specifically, they sell
mission-critical products and services in human capital management, or HCM, and financial management systems, or FMS. As a software-as-a-service, or SaaS company,
Workday sells subscriptions in-cloud (average terms not disclosed but minimum duration is three years) with major feature releases delivered twice a year, and weekly,
smaller feature updates delivered with minimal downtime disruption. Feature releases are not subject to additional fees. The business mix is roughly 75% HCM and 25%
financials, with the latter growing faster than the former (low-20s versus mid-teens over the last few years). From a geographic standpoint, the US represents 75% of total
sales with the balance OUS. The company’s subscription backlog, or remaining performance obligations, which represents total contractual commitments for services that will
be performed in the future, topped $27bn in the most recent period, up from less than $4bn in fiscal 2017. They currently serve 11,500 customers, including 65% of the
Fortune 500 and have 80mn+ users generating 1.4tn transactions globally. Gross retention rate, which indicates stickiness of the existing customer base (and excludes upsell),
consistently exceeds 95% with churn mostly due to M&A. Net retention (including upsell) is north of 100%.
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect low-teens sales growth driven by growth in new customers or “logos” (going down market to medium enterprise
lines.lead_prefix: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return

lines.text: and capitalizing on the larger opportunity OUS) as well as cross-sell and upsell to existing customers. With margin expansion and opportunistic share buybacks, EPS should
grow mid-teens. There could be additional upside to total shareholder return if the multiple re-rates.
INVESTMENT THESIS: Fundamentals are solid with sales growing low-teens, operating
margin improvement, strong free cash flow and net cash on the balance sheet.
Multiple favorable trends in a large and growing market:While no longer early days,
lines.lead_prefix: Multiple favorable trends in a large and growing market

lines.text: ERP workload migration from on-premise to cloud remains a tailwind. A structural
shift to unified, single platform systems of record benefits vendors like Workday
compared with stitching together point solutions. AI is also (currently) a tailwind to
growth. The opportunity is estimated at nearly $200bn, with > 50% of the regional
opportunity in markets OUS and > 50% of the vertical opportunity in financials versus
core HCM. The opportunity has expanded over time as Workday expands the product
portfolio into non-core adjacencies like payroll, talent management (recruiting,
reskilling), workforce planning and analytics in HCM and financial planning
(budgeting, forecasting), procurement and spend management in FINS.
Gold standard in HCM software (contender in FINS) with a historically strong moat:
lines.lead_prefix: Gold standard in HCM software (contender in FINS) with a historically strong moat

lines.text: Workdayoffers thegold standard in HCM software, particularly for large enterprise.
They’ve been named a leader in Gartner’s magic quadrant for cloud HCM suites for
1,000+ employees for 10 consecutive years, competing mostly with Oracle and SAP. In
financials, they have consistently gained market share and have also been recognized
by Gartner as a magic quadrant leader (shorter duration than HCM). Workday
benefits from high switching costs, scale and distribution advantages in a market still
mid-migration (from on-premise to cloud), proprietary data feeding the AI layer, and a
unified system of record. Customer captivity is evidenced by 95%+ gross retention
revenue, as it’s painful to rip and replace mission-critical software. With HR and
finance on one unified platform, AI agents get richer context with people and money
data living in one graph as opposed to being stitched together across systems.
Pre-mortem: Seat-based subscription pricing doesn’t hold, and Workday is too slow to
respond (to a usage or consumption-based model). As they shift, agentic AI becomes
good enough that large customers reduce headcount rather than augmenting existing
staff. As agent use scales and becomes much larger as a percent of total business,
inference costs grow faster than revenues (despite declining per token price).
Operating margin expansion from headcount discipline is no longer able to offset
gross margin declines. Optionality embedded in the depressed multiple doesn’t pay
off, meaning the stock was closer to fairly priced than mispriced at initiation.
Competition: While incumbents SAP and Oracle are bundling HCM with broader ERP
suite offerings (and giving migration discounts to customers switching from on-prem
to cloud), traditional competition is nothing new and Workday has been successful
taking share over time. The newer competitive threat is cross-vertical encroachment.
ServiceNow and Salesforce, who historically competed in other verticals (IT service
management and CRM, respectively) are moving directly into HR. ServiceNow
orchestrating workflows across various systems of record (HR, ERP, CRM) means
Workday could be commoditized into the data plumbing underneath rather than the
customer facing platform capturing the AI value.
Ownership:Largest institutional shareholders include Vanguard (12.7%), Blackrock
(7.9%) and Hotchkis & Wiley (5.3%). Workday has a dual class share structure with
class A common stock carrying one vote per share and class B carrying 10 votes per
share. While economic ownership is mostly institutional, co-founders Dave Duffield
and Aneel Bhusri own 69% of total voting power.
Management and capital allocation: CEO Aneel Bhusri co-founded the business with Dave Duffield in 2005 and served as sole or co-CEO from 2009 to 2024. Before Workday, he
held several leadership roles at PeopleSoft, including vice chair of the board and senior vice president responsible for prod uct strategy, business development, and
marketing. PeopleSoft (acquired by Oracle in 2005) is an on-premise enterprise software company that provides HR, finance and other back office applications. Bhusri holds an
MBA from Stanford and a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and economics from Brown University. Note that after stepping down as co-CEO in 2024, naming Carl
Eschenbach sole CEO at the time, he returned earlier this year to “lead in the rapidly evolving AI era”. There was a gap between the official messaging and how it was received
externally, though I personally view it as a net positive. Much of the rest of the management team has been freshly reassembled. Both the Chief Commercial Officer and
President of Product and Technology have decades of experience at Google and SAP. CFO Zane Rowe was appointed in 2023 with ties to former CEO Carl Eschenbach, which
makes him a bit of a continuity figure though his tenure is short. On capital allocation, priorities include reinvesting back into the business, strategic M&A and returning excess
capital to shareholders through buybacks. While declining as a percent of total sales (currently high-20s), R&D remains a priority. Workday has spent $6.3bn on acquisitions over
the last decade+. Notable deals include Adaptive Insights for $1.5bn in 2018 (enhanced financial planning, budgeting and forecasting), Scout RFP for $500mn in 2019 (cloud-
based procurement), Peakon for $700mn in 2021 (real-time visibility into employee experience) and VNDLY, also in 2021 (cloud-based external workforce and vendor
management company). The earlier era of M&A helped the company build out the product suite, particularly in non-core financials, whereas the current era is focused on
building out AI capabilities and functionality. Recent notable acquisitions include HiredScore (AI recruiting and talent matching), Evisort (contract intelligence for legal and
procurement), Flowise (low-code AI agent building platform), Paradox (conversational AI for frontline/hourly worker recruiting) and Sana (AI native learning and agent platform).
Sana was largest with a $1.1bn price tag. Over the last few years, Workday has repurchased $4.1bn+ in shares, offsetting share dilution from stock-based compensation. In
September 2025, the board authorized an additional $4bn in repurchases. They’ve targeted a total of $5bn in repurchases through the end of fiscal 2027, which should more
Special items: SAP’s end of support for legacy ERP customers in 2027 should force a large install base to choose a cloud platform sooner than later (but they have been known to
kick the can down the road with prior end of support announcements).
Source: Bernstein, Gartner (market definitions are generally more narrow in scope than other third-party sources)

Workday, Inc. (WDAY-US) 
Fiscal 2Q27 earnings update 
 
 
 
Recommendation: Maintain position in PFOE 
Workday reported a solid second quarter for fiscal year 2027, beating on both top and bottom line. Subscription revenue grew 14% 
to $2.47bn versus $2.46bn guidance and operating non-GAAP operating margin reached 31.1% compared with guidance of 30%. The 
company benefited from strong execution in AI monetization and international markets, even as it navigates a transition toward a 
hybrid consumption-based pricing model. Management provided a definitive "de-risked" framework for FY28 that anchors 
expectations at 11% subscription revenue growth, while simultaneously signaling a shift toward aggressive margin expansion. The 
tone of the call was notably optimistic, with co-founder and CEO Aneel Bhusri stating “'This is Workday's moment. I've never felt 
better about where we're headed”. The strategic narrative has shifted from being a traditional applications vendor to an "enterprise 
context platform," where Workday provides the deterministic permissions and data context necessary for autonomous AI agents.  
 
Headline results 
Positives 
- 
Workday beat on both top and bottom line as revenue and non-GAAP EPS both topped Street estimates, with EPS growing 24% 
YoY on continued margin expansion. AI monetization is inflecting with AI products generating $100M+ new annual contract value 
(ACV) and driving 25%+ of total new ACV in the quarter. AI-related annual recurring revenue reached roughly $600M, up 200%+ 
YoY. Agent adoption is scaling quickly with 5,500+ customers now using one or more Workday AI agents, up 35% QoQ. Deal mix 
is broadening with medium-enterprise customer volume increasing more than 5x versus Q1, and more than half of net-new 
customer wins included an AI solution. Margin discipline continues, as non-GAAP operating margin expanded 210bps year-over-
year to 31.1%, and full-year margin guidance was raised. On capital return, the board authorized an incremental $4B share 
buyback alongside earnings, against a backdrop of continued engagement from activist investor Elliott Management. 
Negatives 
- 
Guidance raise was marginal with full-year subscription revenue guidance up only slightly ($7.5M at the midpoint, under 0.1%), 
which the market judged as insufficient given elevated expectations coming into the print and investors read as a sign organic 
momentum isn't yet accelerating. Forward growth is decelerating as Q3 current remaining performance obligation (cRPO) 
growth was guided to 11-12%, down from Q2's 14.2% actual. Q3 cRPO growth will be pressured by lapping the Paradox 
acquisition which added 1pp+ to prior year. Early commentary points to a preliminary FY2028 subscription growth framework of 
roughly 11%, down from the 13-14% pace of FY2027. One reason is that AI usage is still outpacing AI monetization. Only 200 
customers have signed up for consumption-based Flex Credit pricing versus 5,500+ using agents, underscoring an early-stage gap 
between adoption and revenue capture (revenue impact from consumption-based products tends to be lagged).

Geographic highlights 
- 
Management called North American performance "exceptional" as US revenue grew 12% year-over-year to $1.97B, driven by 
large enterprise. International sales grew 17% year-over-year to $682M, outgrowing the US. EMEA was described as "solid", 
driven by strong performance in France, Germany, and the Nordics. AI represented one-third of new ACV in the region, a higher 
AI mix than company average. Japan was highlighted as a standout market in the quarter, validating continued investment.  
 
Segment highlights 
- 
In new products, Adaptive Decision Intelligence has been purchased by 170 customers since general availability. The newly 
launched Adoption Agent signed 200+ customers within three days of launch. Sana Enterprise had an “exceptional” launch with 
12,000 internal active users and 22,000 custom agents built. Talent Acquisition Agent processed 30M candidate interactions and 
scheduled 8M interviews. The continued integration of Paradox (the AI-driven candidate-experience platform acquired in fiscal 
2026) alongside Workday Recruiting and HiredScore, deepens the company's talent-acquisition suite as competitors such as SAP 
push into the same space. For developers, custom application development on the Workday platform grew 90%+ year-over-year, 
with 3,000+ custom apps and agents built since the company's DevCon event. New logos in the quarter included BWX 
Technologies, Guess, KPMG, Danske Bank, Guidehouse and S-E-B, among others. Existing customers including Caterpillar, 
Delivery Hero, Lithia & Driveway, Merck, Novartis and AstraZeneca expanded their Workday footprints. Net expansion from 
existing customers is driving 60% of subscription revenue growth. 
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
Growth deceleration and elongated deal cycles – total revenue growth of 12.8% continues a gradual slowdown, and 
management's own framework points to further deceleration into FY2028. Analysts have flagged extended approval timelines on 
large HR and finance system implementations, which can push out bookings. 
- 
Monetization lag on AI/Flex Credit – large customers remain cautious about adopting consumption-based pricing for AI agents, 
creating uncertainty around how quickly agent usage converts into incremental revenue. 
- 
Competitive pressure and elevated customer acquisition costs – AI-native point solutions and larger platform competitors 
(including SAP's push into talent acquisition) are competing for the same AI-driven workflows Workday is targeting. Payback 
periods on new customer acquisition remain lengthy, a sign of a still-competitive enterprise software selling environment. 
 
Guidance 
- 
Full-year subscription revenue range was narrowed and nudged up only slightly at the midpoint (a raise of $7.5M, or under 
0.1%), which the market interpreted as confirmation rather than acceleration of the FY2027 plan. Preliminary commentary on 
FY2028 pointed to subscription revenue growth of roughly 11%, below the 13-14% range Workday is producing currently, the 
deceleration signal that weighed most heavily on sentiment. Full-year non-GAAP operating margin guidance for fiscal 2027 was 
raised 50bps to 31.0%, continuing a multi-year trend of margin expansion outpacing revenue growth.  
 
Rating actions and target price changes 
Heading into the print, WDAY shares had already re-rated sharply higher (roughly +26% from early June through mid-August) after 
Reuters reported that private equity firm Silver Lake was in talks to take the company private. That speculation drove a wave of price-
target increases across the Street in the two weeks before earnings even as a few firms used the rally to step off the bullish side, 
downgrading to Hold/Neutral on valuation grounds rather than on fundamentals. Analysts largely interpreted the Q2 results as a 
stabilization of the story, though debate remains regarding the durability of the 11% growth floor. Guggenheim Securities remains 
bullish with a $275 price target, arguing that underlying demand trends were stable and that concerns regarding AI-driven seat 
compression are overblown. They attribute the Q2 margin beat to efficient internal AI leverage but warn that free Sana trials could 
be a minor margin drag in the near term. TD Cowen notes that while AI ARR continues to ramp, subscription revenue remains on a 
deceleration path from 14% in Q1 to an expected 11% by Q4 FY27. The firm raised its price target to $220, focusing on the potential 
for a Silver Lake acquisition to provide a valuation floor. Jefferies Research maintains a Hold rating, expressing skepticism that 
Workday can significantly take share from SAP or Oracle without a "killer app." They view the 11% growth bar as more realistic but 
believe sustainable re-acceleration hinges on the successful GA of new Sana products in FY28. Piper Sandler highlights a "mixed" 
perception of Flex Credits, with 30% of surveyed partners finding the pricing confusing, which may lead to longer sales cycles as 
customers struggle to project ROI.

RPO reflects total contractual commitments (legally binding, non-cancelable and non-refundable) for services that will be performed 
in the future. Current RPO is expected to be recognized as revenue within 12 months, non-current is beyond 12 months. Minimum 
contract duration is typically three years.  
 
Why we own 
Workday is a cloud-native enterprise application software company with roots in enterprise resource planning, or ERP. They sell 
mission-critical products and services in human capital management, or HCM, and financial management systems, or FMS. As a 
software-as-a-service (SaaS) company, Workday sells subscriptions in-cloud. The company’s subscription backlog, or remaining 
performance obligations, topped $27bn in the most recent period, up from less than $4bn in fiscal 2017. They currently serve 11,500 
customers, including 65% of the Fortune 500 and have 80mn+ users generating 1.4tn transactions globally. Gross retention rate, 
which indicates stickiness of the existing customer base (and excludes upsell), consistently exceeds 95% with churn mostly due to 
M&A. Net retention (including upsell) is north of 100%. The market opportunity is estimated at nearly $200bn, with 50%+ of the 
regional opportunity in markets OUS and 50%+ of the vertical opportunity in financials versus core HCM. Workday offers the gold 
standard in HCM software, particularly for large enterprise. In financials, they have consistently gained market share and have been 
recognized by third-parties as an industry leader. With high switching costs, scale, distribution advantages, proprietary data feeding 
the AI layer and a unified system of record, Workday benefits from the continued ERP workload migration from on-premise to cloud. 
With AI as an additional tailwind to growth, trading at a relatively attractive valuation and with a seemingly wide margin of safety, 
Workday should remain a core position.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN POSITIONS IN PFOE AND IDVZ (REDUCE/SOURCE OF CASH FOR BETTER ALTERNATIVE) 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: What started as a failing joint venture between ASM International and Philips in a leaky shed, widely dismissed even by the engineers who worked 
there, ASML eventually became the sole supplier of one of the most critical tools in the entire global semiconductor supply chain. ASML is a capital equipment company with 
a dominant position in deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines and sole manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. Lithography machines are tools 
used by chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips. While the business mix is diversified by region, system and technology, 
the customer base is highly concentrated, with TSMC and Samsung representing 38% of total sales in 2025 (24% and 14%, respectively). Geographically, sales are split 
between China (41%), Taiwan (36%), Korea (35%) and the US (18%) with the balance in Japan, EMEA and the rest of Asia. By system, half of sales are generated from DUV 
machines and half are generated from EUV machines. 25% of total sales are install base management, which is essentially their aftermarket and servicing business. This 
includes maintenance and field service (ASML technicians are often embedded at customer fabs for regular upkeep), software upgrades, hardware (physical) upgrades and 
parts and consumables (for components that need to be replaced over time). Services grow as the install base grows, are recurring in nature, are less cyclical and provide a 
floor during downturns. 
 
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: At the 2024 investor day, management guided to €44-60bn in sales by 2030, implying 6-13% annual growth from 2025 
levels. They target 56-60% gross margin by 2030, mostly the result of mix shift to higher margin EUV products. With margin expansion and share buybacks, EPS should grow 
20%+, and with the dividend, total shareholder return should be slightly higher. 
INVESTMENT THESIS: The most advanced modern technology does not exist without 
ASML. Fundamentals are strong with sales growing low-teens, operating margin 35% 
and growing, solid free cash flow (margin 34%) and net cash on the balance sheet. 
 
Secular growth tailwinds trump short-term cyclicality in this trillion dollar market: 
Chips are the building blocks for the digital economy. They are pervasive, powering 
everything from smartphones and computers to datacenters, cars and medical 
devices. Global semiconductor sales have grown mid-single-digits annually for 
decades to $800bn in 2025, expected to top $1tn this year. Wafer fabrication 
equipment sales (including lithography machines) have grown high-single-digits 
annually since the late 1980s, with acceleration in recent years (5-year CAGR is 
15.8%). WFE is high-teens as a percent of global semi sales (and growing), and 
lithography represents 25-30% of total WFE spend (and growing). 
 
Monopoly in EUV lithography with an impregnable moat: ASML dominates its part 
of the value chain, with 90% of the DUV lithography market and 100% of EUV. The 
other two competitors in DUV are Nikon and Canon. ASML benefits from a system of 
interlocking barriers that make its position nearly impossible to replicate. Their 
technology is the embodiment of accumulated engineering knowledge across 
hundreds of interdependent subsystems (laser physics, vacuum engineering, mirror 
optics, etc.) which took decades of effort and significant resources to master. 
Switching costs are high (in time in and in money) as they co-develop technology 
roadmaps with customers who have each invested billions into integration. The 
services component deepens their already entrenched customer relationships.  
RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Pre-mortem: China represents 40%+ of total sales and has arguably been stockpiling 
DUV machines ahead of tightening export controls over the last few years. This pull 
forward in demand has skewed recent results and creates a near-term growth 
headwind. Proposed US legislation to ban sales and servicing of DUV machines to 
China would further reduce ASML’s total addressable market. AI demand from 
Taiwan, Korea and the US are not enough to fill the gap, and the stock, which has 
historically traded at a healthy premium, de-rates accordingly.  
 
Customer concentration: TSMC, Samsung and Intel are ASML’s three largest 
customers. Foundry cap ex funds the business and spend is lumpy as customers can 
meaningfully reduce or delay orders in any given year. Intel’s recent restructuring and 
significant scaling back of cap ex is case in point. 
 
Technological obsolescence: While no competitor is close to replicating ASML’s 
technology and there is no near-term substitute, breakthroughs in next generation 
technology required to manufacture the most advanced chips may come from 
alternative suppliers (not likely, but a consideration). 
 
Ownership: Largest institutional shareholders include Vanguard (3.8%), Norges Bank 
(2.3%) and Blackrock (2.2%).

Management and capital allocation: President and CEO Christophe Fouquet joined ASML in 2008 and held several management positions in marketing and product 
management prior to CEO, including Chief Business Officer from 2022 to 2024, EVP of EUV from 2018 to 2022 and EVP of Applications from 2013 to 2018. Prior to ASML, he 
worked at industry peers KLA Tencor and Applied Materials. Executives are long-tenured with decades of accumulated technical knowledge. While CFO Roger Dassen comes 
from a pure finance and audit background (previously at Deloitte), there are mostly engineers at the top (the CEO has a physics background, and the CTO is a mathematician).  
On capital allocation, the hierarchy follows a fairly classic framework for a capital-light, high-margin industrial business. Priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business, 
with R&D treated as sacrosanct and cap ex spend to scale production capacity, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. Over the 
last three decades, they’ve spent nearly €34bn on a cumulative basis on R&D, which is consistently low- to mid-teens as a percent of total sales. This spend is not discretionary, 
but rather the engine that sustains the monopoly. Since the mid-1990s, ASML has spent nearly €15bn on cap ex on a cumulative basis (typically mid- to high-single-digits as a 
percent of sales) to ensure sufficient manufacturing capacity to build enough machines to meet demand. ASML has returned €16.7bn in dividends over the last two decades, and 
they’ve repurchased €28.2bn in stock over that same time frame. Nearly 75% of buybacks have occurred in the last five years. While M&A is not a priority, ASML has made 
selective, strategic acquisitions over time, mostly to internalize critical technology dependencies (for example, acquiring Cymer for their industry leading laser light sources).  
 
Special items: ASML has granted a “stichting”, or preference share option, to a Dutch foundation established under Netherlands law that acts as a poison pill defense 
mechanism. This protects ASML’s independence and long-term strategic orientation (which is important for a company that sits at the center of global geopolitical contest over 
semiconductor technology). It also means ordinary shareholders have limited ability to influence change. The Dutch government has also made clear through policy signals that 
ASML is a strategic national asset, adding another layer of implicit protection beyond the preference share option.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN POSITIONS IN PFOE AND IDVZ (REDUCE/SOURCE OF CASH FOR BETTER ALTERNATIVE)
COMPANY DESCRIPTION:What started as a failing joint venture between ASM International and Philips in a leaky shed, widely dismissed even by the engineers who worked
there, ASML eventually became the sole supplier of one of the most critical tools in the entire global semiconductor supply chain.ASML is a capital equipment company with
a dominant position in deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines and sole manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. Lithography machines are tools
used by chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips. While the business mix is diversified by region, system and technology,
the customer base is highly concentrated, with TSMC and Samsung representing 38% of total sales in 2025 (24% and 14%, respectively). Geographically, sales are split
between China (41%), Taiwan (36%), Korea (35%) and the US (18%) with the balance in Japan, EMEA and the rest of Asia. By system, half of sales are generated from DUV
machines and half are generated from EUV machines. 25% of total sales are install base management, which is essentially their aftermarket and servicing business. This
includes maintenance and field service (ASML technicians are often embedded at customer fabs for regular upkeep), software upgrades, hardware (physical) upgrades and
parts and consumables (for components that need to be replaced over time). Services grow as the install base grows, are recurring in nature, are less cyclical and provide a
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: At the 2024 investor day, management guided to €44-60bn in sales by 2030, implying 6-13% annual growth from 2025
lines.lead_prefix: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return

lines.text: levels. They target 56-60% gross margin by 2030, mostly the result of mix shift to higher margin EUV products. With margin expansion and share buybacks, EPS should grow
20%+, and with the dividend, total shareholder return should be slightly higher.
INVESTMENT THESIS: The most advanced modern technology does not exist without
ASML. Fundamentals are strong with sales growing low-teens, operating margin 35%
and growing, solid free cash flow (margin 34%) and net cash on the balance sheet.
Secular growth tailwinds trump short-term cyclicality in this trillion dollar market:
lines.lead_prefix: Secular growth tailwinds trump short-term cyclicality in this trillion dollar market

lines.text: Chips are the building blocks for the digital economy. They are pervasive, powering
everything from smartphones and computers to datacenters, cars and medical
devices. Global semiconductor sales have grown mid-single-digits annually for
decades to $800bn in 2025, expected to top $1tn this year. Wafer fabrication
equipment sales (including lithography machines) have grown high-single-digits
annually since the late 1980s, with acceleration in recent years (5-year CAGR is
15.8%). WFE is high-teens as a percent of global semi sales (and growing), and
lithography represents 25-30% of total WFE spend (and growing).
Monopoly in EUV lithography with an impregnable moat:ASML dominates its part
lines.lead_prefix: Monopoly in EUV lithography with an impregnable moat

lines.text: of the value chain, with 90% of the DUV lithography market and 100% of EUV. The
other two competitors in DUV are Nikon and Canon. ASML benefits from a system of
interlocking barriers that make its position nearly impossible to replicate. Their
technology is the embodiment of accumulated engineering knowledge across
hundreds of interdependent subsystems (laser physics, vacuum engineering, mirror
optics, etc.) which took decades of effort and significant resources to master.
Switching costs are high (in time in and in money) as they co-develop technology
roadmaps with customers who have each invested billions into integration. The
services component deepens their already entrenched customer relationships.
Pre-mortem:China represents 40%+ of total sales and has arguably been stockpiling
DUV machines ahead of tightening export controls over the last few years. This pull
forward in demand has skewed recent results and creates a near-term growth
headwind. Proposed US legislation to ban sales and servicing of DUV machines to
China would further reduce ASML’s total addressable market. AI demand from
Taiwan, Korea and the US are not enough to fill the gap, and the stock, which has
historically traded at a healthy premium, de-rates accordingly.
Customer concentration:TSMC,Samsung and Intel are ASML’s three largest
customers. Foundry cap ex funds the business and spend is lumpy as customers can
meaningfully reduce or delay orders in any given year. Intel’s recent restructuring and
significant scaling back of cap ex is case in point.
Technological obsolescence: While no competitor is close to replicating ASML’s
technology and there is no near-term substitute, breakthroughs in next generation
technology required to manufacture the most advanced chips may come from
alternative suppliers (not likely, but a consideration).
Ownership:Largest institutional shareholders include Vanguard (3.8%), Norges Bank
Management and capital allocation: President and CEO Christophe Fouquet joined ASML in 2008 and held several management positions in marketing and product
management prior to CEO, including Chief Business Officer from 2022 to 2024, EVP of EUV from 2018 to 2022 and EVP of Applications from 2013 to 2018. Prior to ASML, he
worked at industry peers KLA Tencor and Applied Materials. Executives are long-tenured with decades of accumulated technical knowledge. While CFO Roger Dassen comes
from a pure finance and audit background (previously at Deloitte), there are mostly engineers at the top (the CEO has a physics background, and the CTO is a mathematician).
On capital allocation, the hierarchy follows a fairly classic framework for a capital-light, high-margin industrial business. Priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business,
with R&D treated as sacrosanct and cap ex spend to scale production capacity, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. Over the
last three decades, they’ve spent nearly €34bn on a cumulative basis on R&D, which is consistently low- to mid-teens as a percent of total sales. This spend is not discretionary,
but rather the engine that sustains the monopoly. Since the mid-1990s, ASML has spent nearly €15bn on cap ex on a cumulative basis (typically mid- to high-single-digits as a
percent of sales) to ensure sufficient manufacturing capacity to build enough machines to meet demand. ASML has returned €16.7bn in dividends over the last two decades, and
they’ve repurchased €28.2bn in stock over that same time frame. Nearly 75% of buybacks have occurred in the last five years. While M&A is not a priority, ASML has made
selective, strategic acquisitions over time, mostly to internalize critical technology dependencies (for example, acquiring Cymer for their industry leading laser light sources).
Special items: ASMLhas granted a “stichting”, or preference share option, to a Dutch foundation established under Netherlands law that acts as a poison pill defense
mechanism. This protects ASML’s independence and long-term strategic orientation (which is important for a company that sits at the center of global geopolitical contest over
semiconductor technology). It also means ordinary shareholders have limited ability to influence change. The Dutch government has also made clear through policy signals that
ASML is a strategic national asset, adding another layer of implicit protection beyond the preference share option.

ASML Holding NV (ASML-US) 
2Q26 earnings update 
 
 
 
Recommendation: Maintain positions in PFOE and IDVZ 
ASML delivered a clean beat-and-raise quarter. Net sales and gross margin both came in above the top of guidance, and management 
raised full-year 2026 guidance for the second time this year on the back of accelerating AI-driven capacity investment. The stock 
nonetheless dipped modestly on the print as investors weighed the strength against a steep implied second-half ramp and lingering 
China/geopolitical overhang.  
 
Headline results 
Positives 
- 
Total net sales of €9.3B were above the €8.4-9.0B guided range, up 21% year-over-year (€7.7B in Q2 2025) and 6% sequentially 
(€8.8B in Q1 2026). Gross margin of 54% exceeded the 51-53% guided range. Net income rose 26% year-over-year to €2.9B 
(basic EPS of €7.59). Installed Base Management (service) sales of €2.76B came in roughly €300M above guidance, underscoring 
a high-margin, recurring revenue engine that management expects to grow >30% annually. Full-year 2026 outlook lifted to €43-
45B net sales and 54-56% gross margin, the second upward revision in 2026. Intel Foundry reached a production milestone using 
High-NA EUV on its 18A process for Core Ultra Series 3 chips, which is the first concrete commercial validation of the platform. 
Management said ASML has “already received substantially all orders needed for 2027 and a large number of orders for 2028,” a 
multi-year demand signal well beyond the normal order book. On capital returns, the interim dividend was raised to €1.88/share 
(from €1.60 in the prior interim), plus €1.1B of share buybacks in the quarter.  
Negatives 
- 
Shares fell 3.8% following the print despite the beat-and-raise, reflecting the demanding scale of the implied second-half ramp 
and unresolved China policy risk. First-half 2026 free cash flow was negative (€1.3B) despite €5.7B of net income over the same 
period, as inventory and prepayments built ahead of the H2 shipment ramp. The raised full-year guidance implies €14B+ of net 
sales in Q4 2026 alone, an unusually demanding execution requirement in a single quarter. EUV fell to 57% of system sales in Q2 
(from 66% in Q1) as DUV/immersion (29%) and metrology gained share. Not necessarily negative, but a reminder that near-term 
mix will swing quarter to quarter. A small number of customers (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, and memory makers) continue to 
account for the large majority of sales (roughly 61% from the top four customers in 2025).

Geographic highlights 
- 
Regional mix shifted markedly within the quarter, driven mainly by the pace of individual customers' fab buildouts rather than 
any broad-based regional trend. South Korea remained the largest market at 43% of Q2 sales, though down slightly from 45% in 
Q1, reflecting the phasing of Samsung and SK Hynix memory and logic tool deliveries. Taiwan surged to 30% of Q2 sales from 
23% in Q1, driven by TSMC's continued advanced-node and AI-accelerator capacity expansion. China fell sharply to 14% of Q2 
sales, down from 19% in Q1 and well below the 36% peak in Q4 2025, as the prior pull-forward buying ahead of export-control 
deadlines normalizes. Management reiterated that China should still average around 20% of full-year 2026 sales, driven primarily 
by mainstream/legacy logic demand rather than leading-edge tools. US was 9% of Q2 sales, tied to Intel's foundry buildout, 
including its High-NA-enabled 18A ramp. Net takeaway is that the geographic story in 2026 is increasingly a Korea/Taiwan/China 
rotation tracking each region's AI and memory capex cycle, with China's quarterly swings creating more optical volatility than the 
steadier 20% full-year run-rate management is guiding to. 
 
Segment highlights 
- 
EUV lithography was 57% of Q2 system sales. Full-year 2026 EUV business is guided to grow 45%. ASML plans 65 Low-NA EUV 
units in 2026, stepping up to a 30% unit increase in 2027. One High-NA system was recognized in revenue in Q2, with 4-5 
expected for the full year. DUV/immersion was 29% of Q2 system sales. 130 immersion DUV units are planned for 2026 (in line 
with 2025), rising in step with the 2027 30% capacity increase. Metrology and inspection demand is being lifted by greater 
process-control intensity at advanced nodes, guided to grow 25% for the full year. Installed Base Management (services) was 
€2.76B in Q2 sales, €300M above guidance, from field upgrades and service contracts on the growing installed fleet. This is 
guided to grow >30% annually. Logic-related sales are guided to grow 25%+ in 2026 on 3nm capacity expansion for AI 
accelerators and initial 2nm ramps. Memory has become the more explosive driver with DRAM/HBM-related sales guided to 
grow 75%+ in 2026 as supply-constrained DDR/HBM pricing motivates aggressive fab expansion. Memory is now management's 
single largest incremental growth driver for the year. On the 2027-2028 capacity plan, ASML intends to raise 2027 capacity by 
30% in units for both Low-NA EUV and DUV immersion (equivalent to 45% more wafer capacity once productivity gains are 
included), achievable within its existing manufacturing footprint. A further 30% expansion for 2028 is under investigation, 
though not yet fully secured in orders. The 2027 tool mix shifts toward higher-ASP, higher-productivity E- and F-model systems.  
 
Headwinds and risks 
- 
China / export policy – the proposed US MATCH Act could tighten DUV export restrictions to China further. China's quarterly 
sales share has already fallen from 36% (Q4 2025) to 19% (Q1 2026) to 14% (Q2 2026), and while management still expects 20% 
for the full year, the policy overhang keeps this a recurring source of headline risk.  
- 
High-NA adoption pace – TSMC, the industry's largest foundry, has said it will skip High-NA EUV for its upcoming A14 node, 
pushing broad commercial adoption out toward 2029 and leaving Intel as the primary near-term High-NA reference customer. 
Customers are also pushing back on High-NA pricing relative to Low-NA multi-patterning economics, and ASML has said platform 
maturity is key to proving out the cost case.  
- 
Supply chain and customer concentration – ASML depends heavily on Zeiss for EUV optics, and management confirmed there is 
no fungibility between High-NA and Low-NA optics, limiting flexibility to reallocate capacity if demand mix shifts. A handful of 
customers account for the majority of revenue, so any pause or delay by a single large customer (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK 
Hynix, Micron) can move results materially.  
- 
Execution risk and valuation – the raised full-year guide implies an unusually steep H2 ramp (€14B+ required in Q4 alone) and 
negative H1 free cash flow from working-capital build, raising the bar for flawless execution into year-end. Shares trade around 
38x estimated 2026 EPS, a multiple that assumes another strong year in 2027-28, leaving limited room for disappointment.  
 
Guidance 
- 
UPDATED full-year 2026 guidance to EUR 43-45bn in total net sales with 54-56% gross margin. The current FY2026 sales guide is 
roughly 16% above the April guidance at the midpoint and roughly 20% above the initial January 2026 guidance midpoint. For 
Q3 2026, the company expects EUR 11-12bn in total net sales, EUR 2.9bn in installed base management sales, and 55-57% gross 
margin. The company also plans to INCREASE low NA EUV capacity by 30% in 2027 and is investigating a further 30% expansion 
for 2028, with similar 30% increases planned for immersion systems. This effectively extends the guidance conversation two 
years further out than is typical for ASML.  
3 
 
Rating actions and target price changes 
The investment community responded to the print with broad upward revisions to earnings estimates and price targets, though 
some brokers remained cautious regarding valuation and geopolitical risks. Bernstein maintained an Outperform rating with a street-
high target price of €2,500, arguing that ASML's 2028 earnings potential is dramatically underappreciated and forecasting a 30% 
revenue CAGR through 2028. JPMorgan reiterated an Overweight rating and raised its price target to €2,100 (from €1,900), noting 
that the 85 EUV tool capacity for 2027 is likely a "floor" rather than a ceiling. UBS reiterated a Buy rating and increased its target price 
to €2,250 (from €2,100), highlighting that demand visibility is extending unusually far, and capacity adds more than compensate for 
any near-term "noise." HSBC maintained a Buy rating and raised its target price to €2,149 (from €1,883), driven by increased 
confidence in 2028 EPS power reaching over €78. Jefferies maintained a Hold rating but raised its target price to €1,650 (from 
€1,560), cautioning that the stock may face cyclical de-rating as it trades close to peak multiples. Santander reiterated an 
Underperform rating with a target price of €1,291, citing risks from Chinese competitors developing immersion tools and potential 
export restrictions.

Net bookings are a demand signal for future revenue. This reflects the value of new orders received minus any cancelations or order 
adjustments. 
 
Why we own 
ASML is the sole supplier of one of the most critical tools in the entire global semiconductor supply chain. Specifically, ASML is a 
capital equipment company with a dominant position in deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines and sole manufacturer of 
extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. Lithography machines are tools used by chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel to 
manufacture the world’s most advanced chips. While volumes are relatively low (500+ unit sales annually), the price for a leading 
edge EUV machine is north of $200mn. Chips are the building blocks for the digital economy, powering everything from smartphones 
and computers to datacenters, cars and medical devices, which is a substantial tailwind to the business. Semiconductor industry sales 
are expected to reach $1.5tn this year and could top $2tn by the end of the decade. ASML’s technology is the embodiment of 
accumulated engineering knowledge across hundreds of interdependent subsystems (laser physics, vacuum engineering, mirror 
optics, etc.) which took decades of effort and significant resources to master. With a dominant position in its part of the value chain 
(90% of the DUV lithography market and 100% of EUV), derived from high switching costs and deeply entrenched customer 
relationships, ASML benefits from the ever-increasing pervasiveness of chips. While the semiconductor industry is inherently cyclical, 
much like TSMC, the most advanced modern technology does not exist without ASML, and it should remain a core position.

lines.text: Recommendation: Maintain positions in PFOE and IDVZ
ASML delivered a clean beat-and-raise quarter. Net sales and gross margin both came in above the top of guidance, and management
raised full-year 2026 guidance for the second time this year on the back of accelerating AI-driven capacity investment. The stock
nonetheless dipped modestly on the print as investors weighed the strength against a steep implied second-half ramp and lingering
Total net sales of €9.3B were above the €8.4-9.0B guided range, up 21% year-over-year (€7.7B in Q2 2025) and 6% sequentially
(€8.8B in Q1 2026). Gross margin of 54% exceeded the 51-53% guided range. Net income rose 26% year-over-year to €2.9B
(basic EPS of €7.59). Installed Base Management (service) sales of €2.76B came in roughly €300M above guidance, underscoring
a high-margin, recurring revenue engine that management expects to grow >30% annually. Full-year 2026 outlook lifted to €43-
45B net sales and 54-56% gross margin, the second upward revision in 2026. Intel Foundry reached a production milestone using
High-NA EUV on its 18A process for Core Ultra Series 3 chips, which is the first concrete commercial validation of the platform.
Management said ASML has “already received substantially all orders needed for 2027 and a large number of orders for 2028,” a
multi-year demand signal well beyond the normal order book. On capital returns, the interim dividend was raised to €1.88/share
(from €1.60 in the prior interim), plus €1.1B of share buybacks in the quarter.
Shares fell 3.8% following the print despite the beat-and-raise, reflecting the demanding scale of the implied second-half ramp
and unresolved China policy risk. First-half 2026 free cash flow was negative (€1.3B) despite €5.7B of net income over the same
period, as inventory and prepayments built ahead of the H2 shipment ramp. The raised full-year guidance implies €14B+ of net
sales in Q4 2026 alone, an unusually demanding execution requirement in a single quarter. EUV fell to 57% of system sales in Q2
(from 66% in Q1) as DUV/immersion (29%) and metrology gained share. Not necessarily negative, but a reminder that near-term
mix will swing quarter to quarter. A small number of customers (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, and memory makers) continue to
account for the large majority of sales (roughly 61% from the top four customers in 2025).
Regional mix shifted markedly within the quarter, driven mainly by the pace of individual customers' fab buildouts rather than
any broad-based regional trend. South Korea remained the largest market at 43% of Q2 sales, though down slightly from 45% in
Q1, reflecting the phasing of Samsung and SK Hynix memory and logic tool deliveries. Taiwan surged to 30% of Q2 sales from
23% in Q1, driven by TSMC's continued advanced-node and AI-accelerator capacity expansion. China fell sharply to 14% of Q2
sales, down from 19% in Q1 and well below the 36% peak in Q4 2025, as the prior pull-forward buying ahead of export-control
deadlines normalizes. Management reiterated that China should still average around 20% of full-year 2026 sales, driven primarily
by mainstream/legacy logic demand rather than leading-edge tools. US was 9% of Q2 sales, tied to Intel's foundry buildout,
including its High-NA-enabled 18A ramp. Net takeaway is that the geographic story in 2026 is increasingly a Korea/Taiwan/China
rotation tracking each region's AI and memory capex cycle, with China's quarterly swings creating more optical volatility than the
steadier 20% full-year run-rate management is guiding to.
EUV lithography was 57% of Q2 system sales. Full-year 2026 EUV business is guided to grow 45%. ASML plans 65 Low-NA EUV
units in 2026, stepping up to a 30% unit increase in 2027. One High-NA system was recognized in revenue in Q2, with 4-5
expected for the full year. DUV/immersion was 29% of Q2 system sales. 130 immersion DUV units are planned for 2026 (in line
with 2025), rising in step with the 2027 30% capacity increase. Metrology and inspection demand is being lifted by greater
process-control intensity at advanced nodes, guided to grow 25% for the full year. Installed Base Management (services) was
€2.76B in Q2 sales, €300M above guidance, from field upgrades and service contracts on the growing installed fleet. This is
guided to grow >30% annually. Logic-related sales are guided to grow 25%+ in 2026 on 3nm capacity expansion for AI
accelerators and initial 2nm ramps. Memory has become the more explosive driver with DRAM/HBM-related sales guided to
grow 75%+ in 2026 as supply-constrained DDR/HBM pricing motivates aggressive fab expansion. Memory is now management's
single largest incremental growth driver for the year. On the 2027-2028 capacity plan, ASML intends to raise 2027 capacity by
30% in units for both Low-NA EUV and DUV immersion (equivalent to 45% more wafer capacity once productivity gains are
included), achievable within its existing manufacturing footprint. A further 30% expansion for 2028 is under investigation,
though not yet fully secured in orders. The 2027 tool mix shifts toward higher-ASP, higher-productivity E- and F-model systems.
China / export policy – the proposed US MATCH Act could tighten DUV export restrictions to China further. China's quarterly
sales share has already fallen from 36% (Q4 2025) to 19% (Q1 2026) to 14% (Q2 2026), and while management still expects 20%
for the full year, the policy overhang keeps this a recurring source of headline risk.
High-NA adoption pace – TSMC, the industry's largest foundry, has said it will skip High-NA EUV for its upcoming A14 node,
pushing broad commercial adoption out toward 2029 and leaving Intel as the primary near-term High-NA reference customer.
Customers are also pushing back on High-NA pricing relative to Low-NA multi-patterning economics, and ASML has said platform
maturity is key to proving out the cost case.
Supply chain and customer concentration – ASML depends heavily on Zeiss for EUV optics, and management confirmed there is
no fungibility between High-NA and Low-NA optics, limiting flexibility to reallocate capacity if demand mix shifts. A handful of
customers account for the majority of revenue, so any pause or delay by a single large customer (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK
Hynix, Micron) can move results materially.
Execution risk and valuation – the raised full-year guide implies an unusually steep H2 ramp (€14B+ required in Q4 alone) and
negative H1 free cash flow from working-capital build, raising the bar for flawless execution into year-end. Shares trade around
38x estimated 2026 EPS, a multiple that assumes another strong year in 2027-28, leaving limited room for disappointment.
UPDATED full-year 2026 guidance to EUR 43-45bn in total net sales with 54-56% gross margin. The current FY2026 sales guide is
roughly 16% above the April guidance at the midpoint and roughly 20% above the initial January 2026 guidance midpoint. For
Q3 2026, the company expects EUR 11-12bn in total net sales, EUR 2.9bn in installed base management sales, and 55-57% gross
margin. The company also plans to INCREASE low NA EUV capacity by 30% in 2027 and is investigating a further 30% expansion
for 2028, with similar 30% increases planned for immersion systems. This effectively extends the guidance conversation two
years further out than is typical for ASML.
Rating actions and target price changes

lines.text: The investment community responded to the print with broad upward revisions to earnings estimates and price targets, though
some brokers remained cautious regarding valuation and geopolitical risks. Bernstein maintained an Outperform rating with a street-
high target price of €2,500, arguing that ASML's 2028 earnings potential is dramatically underappreciated and forecasting a 30%
revenue CAGR through 2028. JPMorgan reiterated an Overweight rating and raised its price target to €2,100 (from €1,900), noting
that the 85 EUV tool capacity for 2027 is likely a "floor" rather than a ceiling. UBS reiterated a Buy rating and increased its target price
to €2,250 (from €2,100), highlighting that demand visibility is extending unusually far, and capacity adds more than compensate for
any near-term "noise." HSBC maintained a Buy rating and raised its target price to €2,149 (from €1,883), driven by increased
confidence in 2028 EPS power reaching over €78. Jefferies maintained a Hold rating but raised its target price to €1,650 (from

ASML is the sole supplier of one of the most critical tools in the entire global semiconductor supply chain. Specifically, ASML is a
capital equipment company with a dominant position in deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines and sole manufacturer of
extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. Lithography machines are tools used by chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel to
manufacture the world’s most advanced chips. While volumes are relatively low (500+ unit sales annually), the price for a leading
edge EUV machine is north of $200mn. Chips are the building blocks for the digital economy, powering everything from smartphones
and computers to datacenters, cars and medical devices, which is a substantial tailwind to the business. Semiconductor industry sales
are expected to reach $1.5tn this year and could top $2tn by the end of the decade. ASML’s technology is the embodiment of
accumulated engineering knowledge across hundreds of interdependent subsystems (laser physics, vacuum engineering, mirror
optics, etc.) which took decades of effort and significant resources to master. With a dominant position in its part of the value chain
(90% of the DUV lithography market and 100% of EUV), derived from high switching costs and deeply entrenched customer
relationships, ASML benefits from the ever-increasing pervasiveness of chips. While the semiconductor industry is inherently cyclical,
much like TSMC, the most advanced modern technology does not exist without ASML, and it should remain a core position.

RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN IN PFOE, CANDIDATE FOR DIVZ 
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Nike designs and markets athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment, including running shoes, basketball sneakers, sports jerseys, and gym gear. 
They do not manufacture anything in-house. Instead, they outsource to third-parties in Vietnam, Indonesia and China. They sell mostly through 1) wholesale channel partners 
like Dick’s Sporting Goods and Footlocker and 2) direct-to-consumer through Nike.com and roughly 1,000 owned retail stores. Within overall Nike brand sales, wholesale 
represents 58% of total with DTC at 42%. They also own the Converse brand, which generates just under 4% of total sales. From a category standpoint, footwear is largest at 
2/3 of total sales with apparel at 29% and equipment at 5%. From a regional perspective, Nike generates 44% of sales from North America, 27% from EMEA, 15% from China 
and 14% from APAC and Latin America. Through their demand creation (marketing) budget, which topped $4bn in each of the last three years, they attach the Nike brand to 
the world’s most aspirational athletes and moments. Athlete endorsements span from Michael Jordan and Lebron James to Cristiano Ronaldo, Serena Williams and Kevin 
Durant. They organize around specific sports, like basketball, running and football, in an attempt to own performance credibility.  
 
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect mid-single-digit sales growth in-line with the market and some potential upside from share gains. With operating 
margin expansion and opportunistic share buybacks, EPS growth should be low-double-digits and with a 1-2% dividend, total shareholder return should be low-teens. 
INVESTMENT THESIS: As one of the strongest consumer brands in the world, Nike 
should overcome the strategic missteps that led to deteriorating fundamentals over 
the last few years. The turnaround, which includes restoring wholesale channel 
partner relationships, clearing excess inventory and refreshing the product lineup 
should result in a return to profitable growth. 
 
Secular trends favorable in a massive and fragmented market: Increasing 
participation in sports and fitness activity drives demand for performance-oriented 
footwear and athletic apparel. This is even more notable in emerging markets like 
China and other parts of southeast Asia where disposable incomes are rising. 
Increasing chronic disease is also leading to government investment in sports 
infrastructure more broadly. Athleisure (performance gear becoming part of everyday 
wear) also drives demand. On a combined basis (athletic footwear and apparel), the 
market is sized at $500bn, growing mid-single-digits annually. The market is even 
larger if you expand to include all athleisure. 
 
Leading brand in athletic footwear and apparel with a strong and defensible moat: 
In a highly fragmented market, Nike is a standout. It is multiples larger than most 
peers, with the exception of adidas. Nike benefits from tremendous scale (they spend 
$4bn on demand creation annually) which gives the company a distribution 
advantage as well, namely with wholesale channel partners that need Nike on their 
shelves. When you’re the dominant brand in athletic footwear, you’re too important 
for any major retailer to drop. Nike’s brand is consistently ranked among the most 
valuable brands globally, alongside companies like Apple and Coca Cola. Its brand is 
one of the most culturally embedded and globally recognized, which gives the 
company sustained pricing power. 
 
RISKS AND CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Pre-mortem: Wholesale relationships are reparable, but Nike is unable to dominate 
shelf space at retail partners like they once did. New entrants like On and Hoka are 
now large and established enough to compete effectively. China remains a structural 
headwind, and brand heat never returns in a meaningful way. As a result of these 
things in combination, underlying fundamentals never fully recover and the stock 
trades accordingly. 
 
Execution risk: There is a lot of damage to repair from former CEO John Donahoe’s 
time at the helm. His strategy included 1) massively deprioritizing the wholesale 
channel in favor of DTC sales, 2) eliminating categories like running and basketball, 
and 3) shifting away from brand marketing to direct response advertising. It was a 
strategically coherent failure on every front, to quote Ben Thompson. Rebuilding 
wholesale relationships with key retail partners takes time and goodwill. Restoring 
cultural relevance (and brand heat) requires investing in the product pipeline and 
ensuring the right mix, not to mention better storytelling and athlete partnerships. 
Tariffs are out of management’s control, and supply chain diversification (shifting 
production to countries with lower or more favorable tariff treatment) requires time 
and resources. Stabilizing China will be difficult to execute not because of the excess 
inventory (this isn’t their first rodeo) but increasing competition from local brands 
that are benefiting from nationalist sentiment. Adidas provides a good case study for 
Nike’s turnaround as they experienced similar operational challenges several years 
prior to Nike’s, but Nike’s issues are arguably more self-inflicted and structural. 
 
Ownership: Top institutional investors include Vanguard (8.8%), Blackrock (5.3%), 
SSGA (5%), Capital (4.1%) and Wellington (2.6%). 
 
 
 
 
 
4_7_2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
 
 
Management and capital allocation: CEO Elliott Hill, age 61, is a Nike lifer, unlike his predecessor John Donahoe, a tech-oriented outsider who was CEO of eBay and ServiceNow 
before joining Nike in 2020. The transition from Donahoe to Hill in 2024 was a deliberate move to rebuild a leadership team with deep Nike DNA (in other words, those that 
know the brand, the product and the wholesale ecosystem). Hill started at Nike in 1988 as an intern, working his way up to oversee all commercial and marketing operations for 
Nike and the Jordan brand. Capital allocation priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business, mostly through demand creation and product innovation, and more recently 
through supply chain restructuring and rebuilding wholesale relationships, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through the dividend and opportunistic share 
repurchases. Nike is not acquisitive. The dividend is treated as sacrosanct, as they’ve raised the dividend for 24 consecutive years, despite recent operational challenges. Since 
1995, Nike has paid out $23bn+ in dividends, and they’ve repurchased $53bn+ in shares. They’ve reduced the pace of buybacks in recent years due to the ongoing turnaround, 
but management is likely to pick up the pace following a return to more profitable growth.  
 
Special items: The dramatic decline in EPS in 2018 was due to a non-recurring tax impact from the US Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.

lines.text: Upside assumptions: mid-single-digit top line growth, margin
Base (consensus) assumptions: low-single-digit top line growth
slowly recovering to mid-single-digit, operating margin
Downside assumptions: sales growth flat to slightly positive, no
operating margin recovery, meaningful multiple compression
RECOMMENDATION: MAINTAIN IN PFOE, CANDIDATE FOR DIVZ
COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Nike designs and markets athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment, including running shoes, basketball sneakers, sports jerseys, and gym gear.
They do not manufacture anything in-house. Instead, they outsource to third-parties in Vietnam, Indonesia and China. They sell mostly through 1) wholesale channel partners
like Dick’s Sporting Goods and Footlocker and 2) direct-to-consumer through Nike.com and roughly 1,000 owned retail stores. Within overall Nike brand sales, wholesale
represents 58% of total with DTC at 42%. They also own the Converse brand, which generates just under 4% of total sales. From a category standpoint, footwear is largest at
2/3 of total sales with apparel at 29% and equipment at 5%. From a regional perspective, Nike generates 44% of sales from North America, 27% from EMEA, 15% from China
and 14% from APAC and Latin America. Through their demand creation (marketing) budget, which topped $4bn in each of the last three years, they attach the Nike brand to
the world’s most aspirational athletes and moments. Athlete endorsements span from Michael Jordan and Lebron James to Cristiano Ronaldo, Serena Williams and Kevin
Durant. They organize around specific sports, like basketball, running and football, in an attempt to own performance credibility.
Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect mid-single-digit sales growth in-line with the market and some potential upside from share gains.With operating
lines.lead_prefix: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return

lines.text: margin expansion and opportunistic share buybacks, EPS growth should be low-double-digits and with a 1-2% dividend, total shareholder return should be low-teens.
INVESTMENT THESIS: As one of the strongest consumer brands in the world, Nike
should overcome the strategic missteps that led to deteriorating fundamentals over
the last few years. The turnaround, which includes restoring wholesale channel
partner relationships, clearing excess inventory and refreshing the product lineup
should result in a return to profitable growth.
Secular trends favorable in a massive and fragmented market: Increasing
lines.lead_prefix: Secular trends favorable in a massive and fragmented market

lines.text: participation in sports and fitness activity drives demand for performance-oriented
footwear and athletic apparel. This is even more notable in emerging markets like
China and other parts of southeast Asia where disposable incomes are rising.
Increasing chronic disease is also leading to government investment in sports
infrastructure more broadly. Athleisure (performance gear becoming part of everyday
wear) also drives demand. On a combined basis (athletic footwear and apparel), the
market is sized at $500bn, growing mid-single-digits annually. The market is even
larger if you expand to include all athleisure.
Leading brand in athletic footwear and apparel with a strong and defensible moat:
lines.lead_prefix: Leading brand in athletic footwear and apparel with a strong and defensible moat:

lines.text: In a highly fragmented market, Nike is a standout. It is multiples larger than most
peers, with the exception of adidas. Nike benefits from tremendous scale (they spend
$4bn on demand creation annually) which gives the company a distribution
advantage as well, namely with wholesale channel partners that need Nike on their
shelves. When you’re the dominant brand in athletic footwear, you’re too important
for any major retailer to drop. Nike’s brand is consistently ranked among the most
valuable brands globally, alongside companies like Apple and Coca Cola. Its brand is
one of the most culturally embedded and globally recognized, which gives the
Pre-mortem: Wholesale relationships are reparable, but Nike is unable to dominate
shelf space at retail partners like they once did. New entrants like On and Hoka are
now large and established enough to compete effectively. China remains a structural
headwind, and brand heat never returns in a meaningful way. As a result of these
things in combination, underlying fundamentals never fully recover and the stock
Execution risk: There is a lot of damage to repair from former CEO John Donahoe’s
time at the helm. His strategy included 1) massively deprioritizing the wholesale
channel in favor of DTC sales, 2) eliminating categories like running and basketball,
and 3) shifting away from brand marketing to direct response advertising. It was a
strategically coherent failure on every front, to quote Ben Thompson. Rebuilding
wholesale relationships with key retail partners takes time and goodwill. Restoring
cultural relevance (and brand heat) requires investing in the product pipeline and
ensuring the right mix, not to mention better storytelling and athlete partnerships.
Tariffs are out of management’s control, and supply chain diversification (shifting
production to countries with lower or more favorable tariff treatment) requires time
and resources. Stabilizing China will be difficult to execute not because of the excess
inventory (this isn’t their first rodeo) but increasing competition from local brands
that are benefiting from nationalist sentiment. Adidas provides a good case study for
Nike’s turnaround as they experienced similar operational challenges several years
prior to Nike’s, but Nike’s issues are arguably more self-inflicted and structural.
Ownership: Top institutional investors include Vanguard (8.8%), Blackrock (5.3%),
Management and capital allocation: CEO Elliott Hill, age 61, is a Nike lifer, unlike his predecessor John Donahoe, a tech-oriented outsider who was CEO of eBay and ServiceNow
before joining Nike in 2020. The transition from Donahoe to Hill in 2024 was a deliberate move to rebuild a leadership team with deep Nike DNA (in other words, those that
know the brand, the product and the wholesale ecosystem). Hill started at Nike in 1988 as an intern, working his way up to oversee all commercial and marketing operations for
Nike and the Jordan brand. Capital allocation priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business, mostly through demand creation and product innovation, and more recently
through supply chain restructuring and rebuilding wholesale relationships, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through the dividend and opportunistic share
repurchases. Nike is not acquisitive. The dividend is treated as sacrosanct, as they’ve raised the dividend for 24 consecutive years, despite recent operational challenges. Since
1995, Nike has paid out $23bn+ in dividends, and they’ve repurchased $53bn+ in shares. They’ve reduced the pace of buybacks in recent years due to the ongoing turnaround,
but management is likely to pick up the pace following a return to more profitable growth.
Special items: The dramatic decline in EPS in 2018 was due to a non-recurring tax impact from the US Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
